item.title: [YC Root Access] Improving Small Language Model Reasoning With A* Search
item.dc:creator: YC Root Access
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的观察：小模型的"自我怀疑"竟是它最锋利的武器

大多数人以为小模型的短板是"知识不够"，所以要靠更大的老师模型蒸馏、要靠外部奖励模型评分。但 Alex 的方法揭示了一个几乎相反的真相——小模型不是不知道对错，它只是不知道自己知道。当你把同一个小模型的"生成能力"和"批判能力"拆成两个角色使用时，它突然获得了近似大模型的推理能力。这不是能力的注入，而是能力的解耦。换句话说，小模型的瓶颈从来不是"智力上限"，而是"元认知的调用方式"。

跨领域连接：这其实是把"皮亚杰的形式运算"嵌进了 A* 搜索

有意思的是，这套 self-critique + A* 的组合，在结构上非常接近发展心理学里儿童从"具体运算"跃迁到"形式运算"的过程——能够对自己的思考进行思考（metacognition）就是那道分水岭。而 A* 的启发式函数 h(n) 本质上就是"对未来的一种直觉估计"，这与人类下棋时的"棋感"、老练医生的"直觉诊断"是同源的。Alex 的方法之所以有效，某种程度上是因为它把认知科学里的双系统模型（System 1 生成 + System 2 批判）硬编码进了搜索算法。这也解释了为什么它在同等 token 预算下仍能提升 3-4 个百分点——它并不是"想得更久"，而是"想得更有结构"。

藏在演讲最后的伏笔：他真正的野心不在 test-time scaling

注意他最后跳到"因果 RL"和"credit assignment"这个转向——这不是一个附带项目，而是同一个哲学的下一步。Test-time A* 解决的是"如何在搜索空间里做对的选择"，而反事实推理解决的是"如何知道是哪个选择导致了结果"。前者是空间维度的剪枝，后者是时间维度的归因。两者合在一起，就是在给语言模型装上一个能"回头看"和"向前看"的完整因果引擎。

更耐人寻味的是一个跨领域的隐喻：金融领域的"归因分析"（attribution analysis）几十年来一直在解决同一个问题——一个投资组合赚了钱，是哪只股票、哪个决策、哪次调仓的功劳？RL 里的 credit assignment 与之几乎是同构问题。也就是说，Alex 正在把基金经理的绩效归因方法论搬到 agent 训练里。这个方向如果走通，未来的小模型 agent 不会因为"更大"而变强，而会因为"更懂自己为什么做对/做错"而变强——这是一种从规模驱动到反思驱动的范式迁移。

📝 转录文本

开场

[music] We're here with Alex at our inaugural YCML at Startup School. Alex, tell us what you're working on.

研究背景：小语言模型的推理困境

So, today I'm going be talking about my recently submitted paper to um AI stats and it was accepted to a Europe's workshop. It's test time scaling for LM reasoning via our method of AAR search.

So, the main problem we focus on is LM reasoning. However, specifically for small language models, in a lot of cases, small language models are actually preferred to LLMs because of lower cost, lower latency, and also lower comput required. However, small language models actually lack the complex reasoning skills that larger language models have.

This begs our like main research question: How can we provide high quality reasoning to resource constraint models?

Makes sense.

已有方案的局限：蒸馏与 MCTS

So previously there was two avenues for solutions. There was distillation and then Monte Carlo research or other tree search methods.

So distillation — essentially you transfer knowledge from a larger teacher model, say like a few hundred billion parameters, to a smaller like learner model or student model, right? However, this has some issues. For example, you have to have access to a larger teacher model and also run the model, and then also this training process also takes compute resources, time, etc. So it isn't the most convenient for a lot of applications and small language models.

Additionally, there's tree search methods such as MCTS, where you have an LLM sample multiple paths, evaluate them, and then choose, for example, the most correct or most like highly rated answer. However, a lot of times evaluation actually requires external reward models, which are difficult to train and then also host because they're external.

Of course, you might not have that.

Yes, of course.

方法核心：Test-Time A* 与 Self-Critique

So at a high level, I will talk about what our method does. Test time a star. So we still like to view reasoning as a search — or tree search in this case — and we want to find the correct answer, or in this case the destination node. For example, in this picture, say 60 is the correct answer. We want to traverse the tree and get to 60.

However, instead of using a sterile reward model, we use the model's own self-critique as a heuristic. And in this case, it allows us to traverse the tree without any external reward models.

Can you define self critique?

So for example, right, say I ask an LLM to answer 5 plus 5, right? And then it says 10, and I ask the model — the same model — okay, this is the question, this is the answer, what would you give it on a scale of 0 to 100? This is a self critique, for example, right?

Cool.

If it was like — if it said 10 plus 10 is five — it would be wrong.

And then we use this — we search the tree using an A* inspired cost function that includes a score from this like self-critique tree.

Okay, cool. Makes sense. So the self critique is part of the value function.

Of course. Yes.

算法流程与直觉

This is a diagram. So essentially you start off with a question and then you generate the root node of the tree, and then you have this iterative cycle where you generate children to a selected node and then you keep exploring based on the currently high — sorry, currently lowest cost node — which is generated using this formula, which I don't think we have time to go into depth. And then you essentially traverse the tree till you reach like a solution — like the correct solution node — and then you obviously output the final answer.

So what's the intuition for why the self-critique improves this here?

Um, so essentially see here this 34 is lower than the 71. In this case they're the same depth. So the only factor differentiating them is the critique, right? So this part of the tree has been essentially pruned, because we saw this — the LM who's critiquing its own LM realized this like answer was essentially hallucinated. Almost where it can keep exploring here because of course it was much like higher than this.

Yes. So this can be actually seen better in this example with like a math word problem. So first you generate the root node, which is just an LLM call to this answer, and then at each step you expand it into two branches, two children, using just this in the prompt and then the self critique in the prompt. Additionally you just traverse the tree. In this case you can see the final answer, the correct one, is on the bottom left.

Does this visualize it well?

Makes sense.

Awesome. Yeah.

实验结果：GSM8K 与 MATH500

And then for experiments, we check on some various mathematical reasoning benchmarks including GSM8K and MATH 500. Here's GSM8K — in red is our methodology. You can see here it increased the reasoning accuracy compared to this other test time scaling method.

Can you briefly explain what GSM8K?

So it's a mathematical reasoning data set that's around high school level. It depends like what you define, but it's just like basic mathematical reasoning.

So these are basically like off-the-shelf small models and these are ones in which you use your research method.

So it all uses the same model. It's Qwen 34 billion. However, these are just other algorithms to test time — to do test time reasoning.

效率消融：Token 与时间

However, of course with test time scaling, there's a big concern of you're using obviously more time and also more resources to increase accuracy. So we did an ablation to see: for the amount of tokens and the amount of time, are we being efficient in how much we're actually improving the accuracy of the model?

So on the right is the tokens and on the left is the time. So for the same amount of tokens — in purple is us — we actually increase by two to — sorry — 3 to 4 percentage points. And on the right, for the same amount of time, we're also increasing by 3 percentage points. This shows that not only are we — sorry — we're not just only increasing the time used or just other like kind of cheating factors almost.

Yeah, makes sense.

Additionally, if you wanted to see the raw numbers. Yeah.

后续方向：因果强化学习与信用分配

And as for that paper — and then this is some ongoing work. I'm still working on LM reasoning. However, more — I'm now more focused on RL for LM reasoning, and specifically causal RL.

So classical RL is mainly based on correlation. However, like if I'm driving a car, for example, and I turn right and I crash into a tree, I know that that turn of the wheel is what crashed the car, right? But in a lot of aspects with LM agents, there's a lot of like moving parts. The LM can't always assign credit to where credit's due. And it's actually known as the problem in RL as credit assignment. It's a very like big open problem.

So instead of MCTS as your iteration method, you're using RL?

Well, this is for an ongoing — this is new work. Yeah. This is a separate from test time scaling. Yeah.

And so this is working on counterfactual reasoning to essentially isolate like — and give credit — do credit assignment. To create like agents that go from just like correlation to knowing like cause and effect. Because correlation ≠ causation, and to have true intelligence, true visiting agents, you need like this causation — like you need this understanding.

结束语

Yeah. And then in terms of other work, these are two other previous papers. This is a systems paper and this is a LM hallucination paper. My website and LinkedIn are here if this is relevant.

Thank you so much.

Thanks so much for coming here. This is awesome.

item.title: [YC Root Access] LeanAgent: Lifelong Learning for Formal Theorem Proving
item.dc:creator: YC Root Access
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的悖论：数学恰恰是"遗忘"最有价值的领域

大多数人的直觉——包括访谈者本人——都认为数学是纯粹累积性的：你不能忘记代数就去做微积分。但 Adish 揭示了一个反直觉的真相：在数学中，早期的前提常常被后期获得的更高阶直觉"吞并"（subsumed）。这就是所谓的"反向迁移"（backwards transfer）。

换句话说，数学不是砖块的堆叠，而是语义的重构。学了拓扑之后，你对代数的理解并不是"保留下来"，而是被重新编码了。这解释了为什么数学家会说"我现在才真正理解当年学的东西"——不是记忆强化，而是旧知识在新框架下被彻底翻译了一遍。这也意味着：一个"完美记住所有前提"的系统，反而不是最好的数学家。

二、跨领域连接：LeanAgent 的架构其实是"皮亚杰认知发展论"的机器实现

这里有一个让人拍案的隐藏对应关系。皮亚杰（Piaget）提出人类认知发展有两个机制：同化（assimilation）（新信息纳入旧结构）和顺应（accommodation）（旧结构被新信息改造）。稳定性 vs. 可塑性的权衡，本质上就是同化与顺应的权衡。

而 LeanAgent 的"一个 epoch 训练 + 动态数据库 + 课程排序"结构，几乎是皮亚杰理论的算法化重构： - 课程排序（易到难） ≈ 皮亚杰的"发展阶段" - 反向迁移 ≈ "顺应"（旧图式被新经验重写） - 一次 epoch 的克制训练 ≈ 儿童学习中的"最近发展区"（Vygotsky 的补充）

更有意思的是，生物进化中的"外适应"（exaptation） 也是同一种模式：羽毛先为保温进化，后被用于飞行——原始功能被更高阶的用途"吞并"但没有消失。LeanAgent 事实上在数学定理网络中实现了一种"知识的外适应"。

三、意外观察：Adish 有意选择"小模型"，这不是妥协，而是设计哲学

访谈里最容易被忽略的一句话是："我们的模型故意做得很小，这样 Terence Tao 之类的人可以自己跑。"

表面看这是工程选择，但深层是一个关于科学生产模式的赌注。当整个 AI 行业都在冲向"越大越好"时，LeanAgent 押注的是：数学突破不会来自云端的巨型模型，而来自能在数学家笔记本上运行的、可被个人反复调教的小工具。

这里有一个更大的隐喻——数学历史上真正的突破往往发生在极高带宽的私人思考回路中（庞加莱洗澡、拉马努金梦中）。任何需要 API 往返、需要排队、需要付费的工具，都会破坏这种"思维密度"。Adish 实际上在赌：未来最重要的数学 AI，会像 Vim 或纸笔一样"隐形"，而不是像 ChatGPT 一样"在场"。

这个赌注如果对了，"lifelong learning for a single mathematician"（为单个数学家而生的终身学习系统）会是一个比"通用数学 AI"更精准的产品形态。

📝 转录文本

开场

[music] We're here at YCML. I'm here with Adish who's going to present his work on formal theorem proving that he presented on ICLR last year.

Others, tell us what you worked on.

Yeah, so this is LeanAgent. It's a lifelong learning framework for formal theorem proving, and this is work I did when I was at Caltech.

稳定性 vs. 可塑性：终身学习的核心张力

So one of the hottest problems right now in AI is the continual or lifelong learning problem. How do you learn new things without forgetting what came previously?

And so it's kind of two sides of the coin here. So if you have excessive stability, then your model is effectively frozen. It's not able to learn new things.

Or if it's too plastic, it's learning so fast that it's completely forgetting what came before.

Yeah. So the key to lifelong learning is to be in the sweet spot in between. And for this, we chose the domain of formal math because it's one of the hardest places where you can do this. Math is inherently very cumulative and additive. You have to learn algebra before you do calculus and analysis. And so that's why we chose this domain.

为什么"遗忘"在数学中反而有用？

You know, I don't necessarily think of math intuitively as a domain in which any amount of forgetting is necessarily useful. Like what's the intuition behind why you would put math kind of in the center of these two things?

Yeah. So sometimes what you have is that your very early premises are actually subsumed by later intuitions that you can gain. And it was kind of a little teaser to later — this is called backwards transfer. So as you learn new things, you actually already improve what you learned previously. So that's why you can have this sort of trade-off here.

Makes sense. Cool.

Lean 语言与前提检索问题

So I mentioned formal math and the reason behind this is that we're using this language called Lean. So it's a programming language where you code your proof and the compiler checks that your proof is correct.

So as an example, I'm in VS Code here. I've written out my theorem in code. And what we have on the right is we see a lot of hypothesis and my current goal. And we want this goal to say "no goals left." And we do this by writing line by line of this format.

So here exact is what's called a tactic. A tactic is a function call. And the argument is what's called a premise. And premises are just anything that's previously proven — so any theorems or definitions or lemmas or such.

And as you can tell, there's so many premises in math that one of the hardest problems is: how do you retrieve the relevant premises at each step of the proof? So that's one of the core challenges. And it's hard, especially in math, because within math, everything is connected. And so as everything is connected and as it grows, as people keep adding new theorems, how do we know over time how to retrieve but also not forget previous theorems?

So that's the goal of LeanAgent.

LeanAgent 的架构：一个 agentic 循环

So there's a lot going on here. I'll cover at a high level. So it's effectively an agentic loop.

第一步：抓取与课程构建。 It starts off by scraping GitHub and finding different Lean repositories — because code — and then it needs to figure out the curriculum, the easy-to-hard of all the repos, because you need to learn the foundational math before the more difficult math.

Oh, interesting. So it literally continually — it's, you know, continual learning agent in that you are giving iteratively harder math to build up its premises.

Exactly. The same way that we would do as humans.

第二步：复杂度度量。 And the way that we do this is that, as I showed you, we have these line by line of different steps. And so the complexity of a theorem is e to the number of proof steps. We do this for all the theorems and repos. Then for each repo, we have a distribution of easy, medium, and hard. And we sort the repos to descending number of easy theorems.

第三步：动态数据库。 Once you have that, that curriculum goes into your dynamic database. So that is sort of the brain of LeanAgent. It stores all the theorems, all the premises, all the proofs, all those things.

第四步：学习。 And then now you have to learn. So we take the latest retriever — so this is the one that has the most knowledge — and we actually just train it for one epoch. Pretty simple. And that's the best way to balance stability and plasticity. So you're learning the new premises without forgetting the previous ones. That gives you a new retriever.

第五步：证明与回填。 And then you do your best-first tree search for your proving. So you have this new retriever, you retrieve premises, that goes into your tactic generator to generate different nodes of the tree. And then you do your research, you can do backtracking, timeout, all those things. And if you have a new proof which is generated, that goes back into your database.

So over time, LeanAgent is getting better and stronger the same way that humans win.

All of this is just code. And so when you say "train for one epoch," you basically mean one pass through your code repository is given to this LLM that is getting updated with that code.

Exactly.

Cool.

结果与"反向迁移"的涌现

Yeah. So after doing all of this, we were able to prove 155 new formal proofs across 23 domains. Some of them are nebulous domains as well — so we had some comics domains and such.

And as I mentioned, the original motivation was lifelong learning, and what we actually also noticed in addition to that was, as I mentioned, backwards transfer. So as you learn, you actually do better on previous domains. So if I learn algebra and then topology, now I'm better at algebra. That's a cool emergent ability from this framework.

总结： And so to summarize, we are the first lifelong learning or continual learning framework for formal theorem proving. We were able to learn without forgetting and have backwards transfer. Proved a lot of theorems across different repositories, and we learned from basic to advanced concepts. And the QR code for the paper is right here.

展望：如果今天重做，会怎么做？

Cool. Yeah. My final thought for you is: you know, this paper was from ICLR last year. Since then there's been a lot of work in people using the latest coding agents for math. I'm curious how you see — you know, if you were to start and embark on this type of thing today, are there new emergent capabilities of the base models that would mean that you would approach this very differently versus this kind of like iterative buildup approach? Like, is that still relevant even with today's best models, or is there like a new version of that that you would do today?

It's a good question. So I think there's sort of a debate right now to what extent Lean itself is useful. Some people think that for specific domains it's more useful than others.

I think what I've seen is we've seen a lot of open-source models get very, very strong at writing Lean. And so the models that we use here are what's called ByT5 from Google — but probably putting a Kimi or someone else on there would be much better. I didn't mention this, but our models are pretty small on purpose, so that people like Terence Tao can just run it themselves. But now we have lots of like Gemma and other small models, so that would be a good approach.

I still feel like this tree-search approach, where we go step by step, is still quite useful. You can also just generate it all at once, and maybe just test-time RL. Those work, but it's very computationally expensive. We've taken sort of an AlphaEvolve-type approach where you can just search and not do RL and still get some great results.

So I think that there's some distinctions that could be made in different fields, but within math, it seems like a lot of things work.

Cool. Thanks so much, man. This is great.

Thank you. Appreciate it.

item.title: [a16z] How Open Source Became AI's Backbone | Inferact with a16z
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、开源的悖论：越"关键"的东西，越不能被"关闭"

有一个让人意外的观察：在这场 AI 军备竞赛中，闭源模型看起来在赢，但真正跑在生产系统底层的，反而是开源基础设施。 VLLM 已经在任意时刻运行在 50 万张 GPU 上——这个数字比大多数"闭源"公司的私有部署都要大。Cursor、Decagon、Harvey 这些最锋利的应用层公司，最后都得出同一个结论：不能只在 OpenAI 之上做壳。

这里藏着一个反直觉的动力学：越是被大量真实业务依赖的东西，越会被"引力"拉向开源。 因为闭源意味着别人可以随时改你的 API、改你的价格、改你的 guardrail——而当你的业务已经跑在上面，这种不可控就是致命的。所以你会看到一个奇妙的分层：上层越闭，下层越开。Nvidia、AMD、Google 的新芯片都要拿 VLLM 作为 benchmark——这意味着一个开源项目，反过来成为了万亿美元硬件生态的"验收标准"。

二、跨领域连接：AI 模型的经济结构，其实是"制药业 + 社交媒体"的怪异混合体

Simon 自己提到了制药类比：R&D 极贵、失败率极高、需要一次爆款收回多次失败。但我想推得更远——开源 AI 模型的经济结构，本质上是"制药 R&D 成本 + 社交媒体的分发结构 + 开源软件的贡献模型"三者的嵌合体，而这三种范式之间是相互冲突的：

  • 制药靠分子专利收回成本 → 但开源模型一旦发布，"分子"就在所有人硬盘里
  • 社交媒体靠Section 230 豁免免于为用户行为负责 → 但 AI 平台没有这层豁免，所以 Anthropic 只能过度谨慎
  • 开源软件靠业余时间捐赠 → 但没人能在自家地下室训练一个 frontier 模型

这就解释了一个更深的模式：为什么 Llama 的许可证会写"日活超过某个数就必须谈商务"——那不是贪婪，那是一种在三种不兼容范式的夹缝里发明出来的"半开源经济学"。 而 Kimi K2、MiniMax M2 加上使用条款，其实是这种新型经济结构正在快速成熟的信号。

三、一个几乎没人注意到的隐藏真相："安全对齐"正在把高价值工作流悄悄推向开源

访谈中最容易被略过、但最爆炸性的一段是 Simon 说的：他们自己团队的开发者正在从 Claude 迁移到 Kimi K2，因为在写 GPU kernel 时，"invalid memory access error"会触发安全 red line，导致两小时的工作作废。

这里发生的事情，比表面上"用户抱怨误杀"要深得多：

闭源模型的 guardrail 是一种"外部性负债"——它把"内容审核成本"通过 false positive 转嫁给了最高价值的用户。 而最高价值的用户（做底层系统、做安全研究、做金融合规、做医学研究的人），恰恰是最容易被误伤的人。于是产生一个自我加强的分选机制：任务越有价值、越接近边界、越技术密集，就越会被推到开源侧。 长期看，闭源模型在服务"平均用户"，而开源模型在承接"边缘 + 高价值"这两端。

跨领域的类比：这几乎是精确复制了 1990 年代 Linux 蚕食 Unix 的路径——不是因为 Linux 一开始更好，而是因为闭源系统对"非标准需求"的响应成本太高，导致所有"边缘 + 硬核"用户全部往开源迁移，最终边缘变成主流。

啊哈时刻：如果这个模式成立，那么 Anthropic 越是在道德立场上"往前一步"，就越是在把自己最有价值的核心用户群往 Kimi、Qwen、DeepSeek 那边推。Safety 与 Market Share 在这个时代不是 tradeoff，而是负相关的因果链。 而这件事，可能连 Anthropic 自己都还没完全意识到——因为他们看到的 churn，是以"个别开发者抱怨"的形式发生的，而不是以"季度营收下滑"的形式。

开场：一些关键论点

"The fun thought experiment is if GPUs dropped in price by 99%. Then do we get back to a real open-source world?"

"If moderation is never solved in the future, people will go to open way by default because that is where you know for sure you can control your guardrail for trusted use cases."

Q: Can you talk about where VLM sits in that stack?

VLM is a inference engine. It is kind of like databases and operating system — other critical software to power AGI. Nvidia, AMD, Google, their newest chip will make sure VM can run on them. And in a lot of cases, they use VM as a benchmark.

We're bridging almost a 10x gap. For proprietary model, there is a regular mode and fast mode. But for open weight, every provider can offer potentially even 10 different levels of speed.

Q: 5 years from now, open source AI models — have they closed the gap with frontier models?

Capability wise, I don't really see a big gap. Not even today.

一、嘉宾介绍与 VLLM 起源

Today we're here with Simon Mo, co-founder of Infact and a lead maintainer of VLLM, the open-source inference engine now running on half a million GPUs at any moment. We're also joined by Matt Bornstein, an A16Z general partner. Simon, Matt, thank you so much for joining us.

I think first we should start with open-source AI and kind of the more recent history of open source AI. So VLM actually has its origins back in 2022, pre-ChatGPT, and your team set out to make a slow open-source demo faster and instead just found this pile of unsolved problems.

Q: So can you talk about what made serving an LLM so fundamentally different from the ML workloads everyone already knew how to run?

Simon: Yep, good to be here. So serving large language model is a fundamentally different problem because serving it requires to run it on accelerators like GPUs or TPUs, and it is a computationally intensive process that will require a lot of engineering and ensuring that for each request user can see the LLM's response quickly and efficiently.

So this typically means we need to handle differences in input distribution — how long each request is — output distribution which is non-deterministic, and batching and scheduling, and a lot more at the core of the inference engine.

二、从开源项目到关键基础设施

Q: Um, so the project has been around for about four years now, but the company is a little bit more recent. So I want to throw this out to either of you. Matt, I know you've known the team and observed the team for a very long time. At what point did you see this sort of transitioning from being a much-beloved open-source project to critical infrastructure and then a company?

Matt: Yeah, I mean I think you have to go back a little bit, right? Open source was the norm for AI models early on. I mean, we literally have this company called Open AI, which — you know, it's come a little bit of a joke. It's not as open as it once was, or not nearly as open as it once was. But early on, all the frontier AI work was being open sourced, or at least released into open weights, which is a little bit different than true open source.

And people could mostly run these models sort of on hardware or computers that they already had.

Q: Simon — what was the first model that you actually needed to go out and get special software and a special set of computers to be able to run?

Simon: Probably BERT. And before that it was like ResNet for computation — like for images, computer vision classification. So ResNet already needed to run on Nvidia K80, which is kind of one of the first on AWS and other places. But even at this point ResNet you can still kind of run on a commodity even CPU devices — it's just very slow.

But for BERT, when running it, it is like: wow, you have to run it on GPU to make it anything faster and efficient for anything — translation, any task. So that was like before 2020 even.

Matt: Yeah, it's so funny thinking about this. All the memories are flooding my head. Like Hugging Face had like a thousand BERT variants on it. You have to go find the right BERT variant for your particular task. Some people had their own GPUs and could run it, but a lot of people had to go provision cloud and stuff like that.

So look, BERT was an early language model. Newer models are much bigger, much more sophisticated, take up a lot more memory, a lot more compute. And so VLM really, from the early days, was about running these more powerful models that you couldn't just sort of figure it out on your own.

三、开源何时成为"关键基础设施"

Q: At what point did it really become critical infrastructure for these larger open-source models, and when did we start to see these larger open-source models come into the field?

Simon: What we really see the criticality of the software stack is always about bringing open frontier intelligence. This is a catchphrase for the K2 model release this time, and is also about VLM's mission about inferencing infrastructure.

So if we look at it — when do they start being critical? It is when people are relying on it for their application, for their day-to-day productivity. So maybe 2023, when GitHub Copilot and ChatGPT are something that people just cannot live without anymore. At that point open-weight model is already backing it and becomes a cornerstone of how people are living every day.

And at that point we will need the accelerator running open weight model and open source software to make sure it works well — and have all flexibility and control over it.

Matt: Yeah, it's sort of interesting from a startup standpoint. Like GPT-3 or early ChatGPT — those closed source solutions were starting to become critical to a small group of people around that time, and open source existed but it was a little bit of a curiosity or sort of an enthusiast thing.

As the frontier has expanded, particularly with closed source models, more and more open source has been dragged in as kind of critical behind it. At any given point in time — including now — I think models from OpenAI and Anthropic are more widely used and more critical kind of in general than open source models.

But I do think we passed a threshold about a year ago, where a bunch of smaller companies or new application companies, as they were trying to figure out how do I really build an AI without just being a wrapper on top of OpenAI, the answer to that question turned out to be open source.

I mean, this is what Cursor did. This is what Decagon and Harvey are in the process of doing now, and a bunch of other really strong application-level startups made the determination: we can't build just on closed source. We need to do our own mid-training, our own post-training, our own inference and deployment tricks — and all of that means it must be built on top of open source. The closed source vendors won't give you the access to do this.

So my read is: about a year ago, open source became really central in a way that's not always visible, because it's deeply embedded in some of these products. But some of the most innovative products and applications now really depend on this very deeply.

四、VLM 在 stack 中的位置

Q: Can you talk about where VLM sits in that stack — where we do have these larger enterprise companies that are choosing to use open source models?

Matt: Yeah, I mean just about everybody uses VLM. You should describe it.

Simon: Just about everybody uses VLM. VLM is an inference engine. That means its job is to turn available GPUs into a running endpoint for intelligence. So that means it is kind of like databases and operating system — other critical software to power this economy or power the AGI that everybody really uses today — to ensure they can have cost effectiveness, efficiency, reliability, and also always staying on the frontier.

Because for VLM we support more than a thousand model architectures up to today, and a lot of those are proprietary. But also a lot of those are open weight, right? And a lot of those model architectures, when they're transitioning from a research prototype to world-accessible open-weight model architecture, they are live on VLM immediately. So that's a process we call day-zero model release.

Additionally, VLM also works closely with all the hardware vendors — across Nvidia, AMD, Google and Amazon, Intel and a lot more — their newest chip will make sure VLM can run on them. And in a lot of cases they use VLM as a benchmark to make sure it runs well on them.

So this kind of fusion of where models run and where hardware gets to meet — that's where the magic happens, and this is where VLM is.

五、模型发布背后的"戏剧"

Q: You've told me some of the behind-the-scenes stories — it's actually not easy these days. Model releases have a lot of human drama in addition to technical work. Are there any stories there that you think are okay to share?

Simon: Oh, it's actually a very fun co-design process. Because from model labs' point of view, these are brilliant researchers who have built this model. Now their biggest question becomes: how do we get this out to the world and make sure everybody's able to use it and run it well?

And we have worked with model labs that — because they just use VLM already in production or in their research process — will just have done everything for you. This is a moment when we go to them and say "hi, we're the VLM team and we would like to support your open source model, we would like to offer this open-source-but-white-glove service to get your model running well on architecture" — and then they return and it's like "oh, we got it working already because we're running it for the RL process — here you go, just review our code and merge our pull request."

And then on the other end we really have model labs that just don't know how this can work — because systems is not their core. They have been training, or maybe they have their internal inference engine that just doesn't know how it will adapt to the open-weight ecosystem.

And by the way, this is also very much a multi-party involvement process. Every model release typically involves:

  • the model lab
  • the primary or secondary hardware vendors
  • us (VLM)
  • Hugging Face, who are the model format and model hub vendors
  • and depending on the appetite of the model lab, 10 or 20 different kinds of release partners — inference clouds, public hyperscalers, whoever is going to run this model

So even up to today if you look at the K2 model release, it's a whole partnership and a drive to make sure that once the model is released — because it's just a few terabytes of files sitting on the internet — that people are actually going to use it really well.

Even from the beginning of 2023–2024, if you remember when Mistral dropped their first model, they just dropped a torrent link for P2P and then everybody was struggling and trying to get it up and running. We were working behind the scene with the Mistral team trying to get the inference engine support working in VLM. That was one of the most exciting weekends early on that we were able to spend on this. And then after the weekend, when everybody's trying to really analyze what's going on, Monday–Tuesday, Mistral and us just announced "here, you can run it on VLM successfully" — and everybody was able to easily reuse a lot of the work and start building on top of it.

Matt: That was sort of a fun time where enthusiasts like me could just scramble to download the model and get it running somewhere. I'm glad the professionals have taken over, because it never worked very well, but it was a fun moment in time.

六、Open-Weights 联署信与生态立场

Q: So to bring things forward to the present — open source models and also distillation have been in the news recently. Infact signed the NVIDIA Open Weights and American AI Leadership letter, that was signed by also A16Z, Meta, Amazon, dozens of other companies. Can you talk about your decision to sign that and what you were really responding to in the market and in the news?

Simon: Yeah. So for us, what really we want to stand behind is: open weight absolutely matters in the ecosystem. The world cannot just be controlled by proprietary APIs, and where open weight, open development and research of these models are blocked or banned.

The pledge that Infact signed up for is: we want to help and foster this ecosystem, where we are typically a little bit downstream — inference engines are not part of the pre-training process nor the RL process, but we're where the model actually meets the world. And from what we're seeing, people are just really using their imagination and ability to materialize this imagination of open-weight models. They're able to leverage these open-weight models so much more effectively.

七、成本 vs 控制：客户到底在意什么？

Matt: There's almost two pieces to this, right? There's the cost thing — the closed models are too expensive — and then there's the control thing where I want to be in control of my infrastructure and in control of the model, if I need to extend it or put on my own guardrails.

Q: Are both those things important to customers, or are they willing to pay as long as they have the control? Or maybe they're different use cases?

Simon: I think it fluctuates over time. So control matters a lot over the last few years, and then costs just start to matter over the last few months.

Cost really matters starting from people trying to migrate off very expensive coding plans, and skyrocketing token-maxing spend. But control has always been on in the backbone — they want to control the cost, but also it's about controlling the system performance against what they're paying for.

For example, for a voice agent company, they want to control their own model so that they can make sure the model actually responds by their required time. So the customer, when they're on the phone, they can ensure the agent is responding according to an SLA. And this sometimes is only what you can do with your controlled intelligence — because you know the whole hardware you're running and the whole system you're monitoring, versus signing up and relying on your critical infrastructure with a proprietary API where they might go down anytime or have violation of the contract anytime.

八、Kimi K2 与"经济性并非重点"

Q: Simon, to go back to the cost point — you actually make the point in an essay you recently wrote about the release of Kimi K2 that actually the economics is besides the point. In the case of these really great open-weight models on the frontier, designed by really brilliant researchers, these models are in some cases just as expensive as the closed source models. In those cases, what is the point of running them, and what do we learn architecturally in the course of running them?

Simon: Yeah. So first on cost — it's not necessarily that they are as expensive as a proprietary model. The cost discourse has been discussed over and over again, even with GLM 4.6 a few months back. Open-weight models are sometimes definitely a lot cheaper. But for this model there's a big sort of step change where we're bridging almost a 10x gap.

Kimi K2 strikes somewhere in the middle — it is not as expensive as Claude or GPT-5, but it is a lot more expensive than GLM 4.6. Why is that? I do believe this is the point of pricing intelligence with the market correctly and understanding where it is.

But then the majority part of the discourse should be focusing on: wow, this model is bringing an Opus 4.5-level model to our own infrastructure that I can use, I can run, I can fine-tune, I can understand exactly how many tokens I need, understand the exact performance profile.

For example: for proprietary model there is a regular mode and fast mode, and that's only the two switches. But for open weight, when you're running it, every provider can offer potentially even 10 different levels of speed — going from the slowest mode which can be a lot cheaper, up to 400 tokens per second, almost up to 500 in many cases. For some workloads this is typically 2x or 3x faster than the fast mode out there today.

So this kind of level of control — even in terms of performance — let alone control over how customer interacts with the model, control over data retention (keeping in mind Fable doesn't have zero data retention policy, and a lot of the data needs to stay there), control over security and compliance. Yeah, this is why I'm particularly excited about K2 — not just from the cost perspective, but a lot more on bringing this level of intelligence to something people can own.

九、用户如何"调校"开源模型

Q: In terms of calibrating things like speed, calibrating other things on the back end, what needs to happen, and what are you seeing your users do? Who is being really clever about this?

Simon: So we do see users are able to get the maximum benefit out of this model when they enable fast mode — VLM's own fast mode, getting up to 400 and 500 tokens per second — because it is really a big step change. Especially when developers are interacting with the model they can see: "oh, I can really just get my task done faster here, and the model is no longer stuck in thinking; rather it is just executing, interacting with the environment."

So for premium developer blocking-focus tasks, we're seeing it's very benefiting. But also K2 just has the ability for people to modify it and fine-tune on top of it, allowing them to make it better for their own workload, and this is definitely happening today as well.

十、开源模型的许可证正在演变

Q: Can you explain what the licensing term is for the most recent open source models compared to the past, and why you think they're doing that?

Simon: Oh yeah. So historically the open-weight models are just like Apache 2 — like our software — "take it, modify it, do whatever you want with it, here is a gift to the world."

And then recently the model labs are trying to understand a way to economically fund their own model development. After all, model training and research and the data are very expensive. So we have been starting to see terms even in the Llama days — when Meta was releasing Llama, they had a term of: if you're daily active user or annual recurring revenue exceeds some threshold, please enter into a commercial agreement with Meta specifically.

Matt: I do remember that the numbers were specifically chosen at that time — you could go find that it was like two companies in the world that fit the definition that they had excluded from their license.

Simon: Exactly. But people have taken a hint from that, especially now the labs are trying to figure out a way to economically fund it — especially when they're open sourcing the model, everybody can just take it and run it themselves, whereas nobody will use your API anymore in many cases, while their API currently still taking up shape.

And now we're seeing a very healthy ecosystem development. Starting from even MiniMax recently, when they were releasing the M2 model, they have a term specifically focusing on usage. And Kimi initially also has, like, if you have derivative works — this was kind of big news back then, with Fireworks and Cursor about how they built on top of Kimi model.

十一、Open Source 与 Open Weights 的经济学

Matt: And I'll expand on that a little. I don't think it's greed — at least what I've seen from open source model labs. Open source models — really what we're talking about are open weights. It's just not software. Like an AI model is not software at the end of the day.

And so open-source software used to be supported by people donating their time, or big companies kind of authorizing their employees to donate their time. So it was sort of like a bulk in-kind donation of people's time. That really doesn't work in AI. Like I can't just go home at night and train a frontier open-source model with friends for fun. We need millions or billions of dollars of computing resources in order to do it.

So I think it does support your point that obviously there need to be economic incentives and there need to be funding mechanisms in place. Frankly, I think even more so with Chinese models than with domestically produced models. If there's no source of funding for Moonshot to continue to train models — like, we know where the funding will come from instead, and it's government and things that are actually worse for us, I think.

So I think you raised an interesting point that this is an important economic structure, and I think this means we'll see more of this in the future.

Simon: Yeah, it's really about sustainability in the end. It's about how do you make sure that all this initial capex almost to train the model, fail again and again, and train the model again — how do you really pay it back, and how do you make sure that there's enough confidence and funding from everybody involved to go do the next one.

I recently heard someone making an analogy to the pharmaceutical industry — it is almost like how do you make sure that the R&D process of new drugs are properly funded, and there's a proper sustainable method to making sure that people are willing to take big risk, big bet to go to do research for new drugs. And then later, because they know there's an economic incentive in the end when the new drug is released to the market, a portion of that — besides just distribution channels — a portion of that revenue will flow back to continue to fund the next R&D effort. And this is where we're kind of seeing similar dynamics in the model development now.

Matt: Yeah, that's a really interesting analogy. Because once a drug — a molecule — is released, you have the strongest possible control, which is nobody else can manufacture it at all. It's like the most closed possible source. But in the case of models — especially open source models — once it's there anybody can take it, use it, extend it, etc. So having some economics attached to it probably does make sense.

十二、开源 AI 模型需要维护什么？

Q: When it comes to open-source AI, what actually needs to be maintained? Is it the infrastructure around it? Do the models themselves need maintenance at all? What are those dynamics — the developer behavior around it is pretty different.

Matt: You see the results of a big training run — where training now means pre-training, then RL kind of mid-training or post-training, or pre-training, SFT, RL. It's sort of a complicated pipeline. We see only the result of this at the end and the numbers are big. You're like "oh, this was a $100 million training run." But what you often forget is like there may have been five failed training runs, large-scale failed training runs, before you even get to —

Q: The blood, sweat, and tears.

Matt: Yeah. Exactly. One of my favorite artifacts — maybe we could even track down the link — is one of the early Llama models. They published the whole conversation log between the people who were babysitting the training clusters while the models were training. And it's so funny. It's just like "oh no, everything's gone wrong." Like chaos. Like panic. And then the next comment is like "okay, we solved it. Everything's okay." Clusters up, losses going down.

So there's a lot that goes in behind the scenes before these models get released. Once they're out there, I guess it's a little bit more in your zone to make sure it's operationalized.

Simon: Oh yeah. But this is also a very interesting point. Once it's out there, it is a whole community effort trying to adapt this model — because the model is trained on a given type of hardware, on a given type of architecture. But when it's out in the wild, everybody has different cluster topology and use cases. And it's about: how do you turn a use case of one now to a use case of almost infinity?

Now you have people trying to adapt it to the edge devices, and people trying to run at largest scale ever, adapting it — making sure it runs for voice agent, but also for coding agent, which are entirely different kinds of use cases.

So this is a whole community effort trying to further optimize, specialize, and making sure the running of it is reliable and continues to be able to optimize against it. So that's a whole village later throughout the open source, to make sure it's improved.

Matt: And that's cool because that really is like open source software — anybody can contribute and make these better.

The fun thought experiment: if GPUs dropped in price by 99% — if GPU-based compute actually became cheap and widely available — then do we get back to a kind of real open-source world where one person sitting in their basement, or a hundred people working in their free time, can come up with something new, try many of these sort of model training paths that are in the queue somewhere at one of the big companies, and really expand and advance the field collectively?

Speaker: Yeah, this relates to what you were talking about at the beginning. At the beginning, the amount of compute you needed to be at the quote-unquote frontier was negligible, and now it's enormous. How do you get that back to consumer parity again?

Matt: I've said this on the podcast before, but I'll keep saying it. AlexNet — the first neural network to run on GPUs that we care about — ran on two GPUs. And that's not — there are no missing decimal points or commas in there. Literally two. Now that would get you literally nowhere.

十三、推理为何越来越难

Q: Inference has gotten harder over the past 18 months because of this combination of scale and diversity and the kinds of models that we have, and of course agents that are doing increasingly long-running tasks. What makes open source in this world not just a nice thing to have, but absolutely necessary?

Simon: Yeah, so scale comes from a few points:

  • Whether or not you can run this gigantic model on a data center rack
  • Whether you can optimize it to the extreme, to the speed of light, so that you're getting the most value out of it
  • Whether you have a whole community and collaboration and partners of effort to validate it, and make sure that there's no last remaining bugs that appear like 0.00001% of the time

So this is where scaling up the deployment, and then making sure more people are running it — the largest footprint possible — will ensure everybody's experience of running this model is better.

And this is why open-source inference is the current leading way right now, instead of closed source inference engine. Frankly, a lot of the inference cloud and API-as-a-service today do use and leverage open-source inference engine under the hood. The reason to do that is: there's just so much battle-tested and learned recipes and things that they can build on top of. This is where open source is the current leading way to run models.

Q: Something I find kind of funny — looking back at not just the history of VLLM and Infact, but also a company like Open Router or even Ollama — all of these different teams kind of got started around 2022 and 2023. Some of them even before ChatGPT in your case, built around open models. What special thing was happening at that time in the world of research and in the world of AI? Where we see these companies now and think of VLLM as mission critical or Open Router as mission critical — how did you guys know?

Simon: I think there's two parts to this. Our team always had an open source angle — we're from UC Berkeley, a long tradition of open source software and our system research principles. But also just curiosity overall — everybody was so curious about how are these AI models going to benefit humanity and how can we use it better.

And this is where open source is where you meet the most missional-aligned people together. Open Router, Ollama as you mentioned — they're all great partners and friends in the ecosystem — because we're there to understand how everybody else can leverage AI model better and making sure they have a good use of it.

十四、Hugging Face 事件与 Guardrail 的困境

Q: Speaking of leveraging open-weight open source models really well — another thing that was in the news really recently was Hugging Face using a Chinese open source model to help contain a cyber attack carried out by a rogue unsandboxed OpenAI model that was being tested. What can we take away from something like that? Can you walk us through your impressions and understanding of what happened, and what you think the takeaways are?

Simon: Yeah, this goes back to our previous point about control. So for the Hugging Face incident, they broke it down pretty well on their website and blog — so really thanks for their transparency there.

In the end it is about: all the closed proprietary model APIs, their guardrails are a little bit arbitrary but also very difficult to enforce. That means they have so much false positive in the guardrails, that will have legitimate use cases just being blocked. And this is an evergreen problem, even in the social media days — how do you design content filters correctly and be able to do the moderation correctly.

So if moderation is never solved — which is going to be very very hard — then there's always a place where you have a model where you know and trust that you are publishing to and be able to use from. Hugging Face — they had to use open-weight model. But in the future also, for trusted use cases, people will go to open-weight by default, because that is where you know for sure that the guardrail is lessened, or you can control your guardrail for trusted use cases.

Even for us, this actually applies to us today. A lot of the Anthropic models are banning frontier AI research — and when we're studying GPU kernels, even an invalid memory access error triggers the red line. So a lot of our developers within Infact and for VLM are retreating from using Fable 5 — because you have a two-hour job and you trigger the red line, which is false positive, and then you have to lose all of your work.

So a lot of our developers are using like Kimi K2 today, even just making sure — because it's similar quality and it has a guardrail that makes sense to us. There it goes. We're using it.

十五、社交媒体的类比：责任、豁免与 AI 内容治理

Matt: I think your social media analogy is a really apt one. Because in both cases, what's happened is you've taken distributed human activity and centralized it in one place. Before social media, people talked to each other, right? And published articles and messaged each other on message boards. But then you centralize it all under one kind of profit-seeking enterprise, and all of a sudden the incentives change a lot.

And we have a specific carve-out for social media, which is: you're not responsible for what people say on your platform. And that allowed the moderation problem to be tractable. It's like: okay, we're going to do our best to eliminate obviously illegal things, things that are just going to degrade experience on the site in really bad ways — but if it's on the edge, something that's maybe out of fashion to say but not illegal, we just can't police everything. We can't be the world police of all human communications.

I think something similar is happening in AI — where a lot of work, not just talking but work, is being consolidated in one place. If I need to write code or create a spreadsheet or get advice — health advice or anything — it's all happening in one or two sites. And they don't have that carve-out. They don't have that exemption of "hey, we're not responsible for what actually happens on the site."

And some of them, especially Anthropic, is going further than even what would be sort of legally required. They're taking ethical stances on these things, which may be right or maybe not — that's their decisions.

But how do you actually do this? The problem's actually bigger than just communication, because it's actual work and action, and you don't have this exemption, and you have this layer of ethical stuff on top. So I'm just totally with you. It seems like some of these companies have erred on the side of caution, which is probably a reasonable thing to do, but very very frustrating as a user. I saw online, some translation attempts are blocked because they think the particular combination of language and content is somehow triggering politically sensitive topics.

十六、Infact 的路线与 Ion Stoica 的影响

Q: Simon, we're nearing the close of the conversation, and I just wanted to take a step back and ask about Infact and running the company. I know that Ion Stoica of Databricks is an adviser and a co-founder of Infact. What have you learned from him in terms of taking an open source project like VLLM and building a company?

Simon: Yeah. Ion, as a co-founder, he has always been thinking about open source and how do you support open source better — and then now with experience from Databricks and Anyscale, and even Arena, which is a public platform, and now at Infact, his focus really stems from: how do we build in a world where this software is being used by so many people, on such a critical project — how do you make sure they're getting the best quality, and where does the value come from?

If the open source movement and open source inference engine is a starting point, then what are the gaps that we can fill as Infact, and what are the gaps that we can put in? Ion has always been open source first. So for whatever we need to build, we would like to build them in open source. And then for whatever value we can deliver, we want to really close the last mile and make sure that customers and partners are getting the best out of it.

十七、五年之后：开源会追平前沿吗？

Q: Just to close this out — five years from now, do you think open-weight open-source AI models have closed the gap with frontier models completely? Are frontier models always one step ahead? How do you see that shaking out?

Simon: Five years. That's like 500 years.

Q: All right. One year.

Simon: One year, yeah. Five years, we're — who knows?

Matt: We're either all going to be just floating around in our Wall-E pods on our spaceships.

Simon: Exactly.

Matt: Progress, right?

Simon: For me really at this point, there's kind of a point we haven't talked too much about, which is: what really differentiates open-weight model from closed-weight model?

In the end there's not much differentiation. It's more about the distribution strategy and go-to-market strategy. Capability-wise, I don't really see a big gap. Not even today. Because how these models come to being — they're really starting from the first principle. You have a computer cluster, you have training data, and you have brilliant researchers that group together and really to build this amazing artifact — this pre-trained model, and then later RL / post-trained model, that the world can use.

But if you look at the ingredients, one of the most important parts is just the data — who gets what data. And then what are the environments you are building to let the model improve on itself and make better. One of the very useful benchmarks that we have on Arena for K2 has been front-end coding. That means for Moonshot they have built some of the best environments for front-end coding. They have published amazing demos on the ability for this model to code, and then see what the rendered is, and then continue looping — this iterative process.

Now, this is about their environment to improve the model. It's not about just source data. It's not about where they get the data from. It's about who can build the best environment and who can make the most optimization and algorithmic choices to leverage learning from this environment.

So the next year is all going to be about: how open-weight model labs are differentiating and really getting the model to meet the real world, and have this kind of — what people are popular today — recursive self-improvement almost to really improve the model overall. And so really project out in your ear, there's not going to be any difference.

十八、"聪明的研究者遍布全球"

Q: And you've used this term "brilliant researchers" a few times. There are brilliant researchers everywhere in the world clearly. Why do you think in the US all the smart researchers are working on closed models, and in China all the smart researchers are working on open models?

Simon: I mean from my point of view, they are attracted to interesting problems, not necessarily on the open or closed stance. But however, open-weight model does give people a really really good boost on the impact of such models. So that is like a plus.

And I think all the brilliant researchers are attracted to how to improve the model overall.

One interesting point about this — maybe fairly technical — for this Kimi K2 model, is they removed rotary positional embedding. So RoPE has always been there for a lot of the Transformers model, and guess who removed it? The inventor of RoPE. Like — yeah — Jianlin Su, he wrote the first paper introducing RoPE as a concept, and then he now also wrote the explanation of why you don't need it, as part of the technical report in this K2 model.

So like when we read it, is like — really come full circle. You have all these brilliant, humble researchers that are able to really study how this works, and really study the secret of training and pre-training, and share it across the whole world, and recognizing and iterating on their past. So really a miracle, I would say, for this model to come alive.

Matt: It's so interesting — AI is in this funny zone where empirically it works incredibly well, but then you go ask the theorists and they have like no idea what's going on. And so you have these iterative things where when you go read a primer on transformers, you read about positional embeddings and positional encodings and why it's so important, because otherwise you can't understand meaning. And then it turns out once you understand one level deeper — because we've been doing this for a few years and you have all these smart people — oh, actually you don't. It's actually simpler, actually is better.

十九、蒸馏（Distillation）的角色

Matt: We didn't talk about distillation much so far in this conversation, but I think it's very relevant. I have just one question — I'm not going to ask like "is distillation happening?" — I think this is speculation on the part of everybody in the world. But you work a lot with these Chinese labs. Do you think distillation is a critical component of what they do, or are they kind of just doing good work and distillation, if it's done, is sort of an incidental part of it?

Simon: I would lean to the latter part. Specifically as I mentioned previously, environment matters so much today. So these are RL environments. These cannot be distilled — you don't have other people's environment to really distill a copy from. It is about constructing it, understanding the learning process. You cannot distill how the model learns within environment — a lot of these are just not doable today.

There are things potentially you can do with rewriting the datasets — making better pre-training data — but again you can do it with any models. Any models that are going to follow instructions are going to be useful in terms of utility there. So I really don't think, from currently what we're seeing, this is a big cornerstone of what's powering the progress today.

In the end what's powering the progress is still just really smart people with very interesting algorithms, data, environment — and of course compute — they will produce the models.

Matt: I think it has really interesting policy implications. I tend to agree with you, by the way — that we have smart people everywhere working on a bunch of smart things, and it's not about distilling data from any one place.

It has really interesting policy implications, because it's almost tempting if you're in the White House to say "oh sure, we'll just turn off distillation, all our problems will be solved." But I think it's more the case that they're just smart people doing interesting things. And so it's like — how do we adapt to that?

Simon: Yeah. And creative innovations. Like one part in my essay we kind of mentioned that open source and open weight really helps innovation, because it sets out this racetrack where everybody can learn from each other and see where each player is in this racetrack — and then you'll be able to improve, and stand on shoulders of each other, to improve yourself. So that is where everybody can move forward faster.

Matt: And one thing we're looking for a lot from an investment standpoint is people doing more open source model training all over the world — not just in China, not just in the United States. Because you get that sort of magic of collaboration when everybody's doing it.

Simon: And achieve global harmony in all.

结束

Speaker: Well, I think that's a good note to end on. Matt, Simon, thank you so much for joining us. Thanks for tuning in.

Simon / Matt: Thanks so much. Cool. Thanks, Sean.

item.description:
## 一、开源的悖论：越"关键"的东西，越不能被"关闭"
有一个让人意外的观察：**在这场 AI 军备竞赛中，闭源模型看起来在赢，但真正跑在生产系统底层的，反而是开源基础设施。** VLLM 已经在任意时刻运行在 50 万张 GPU 上——这个数字比大多数"闭源"公司的私有部署都要大。Cursor、Decagon、Harvey 这些最锋利的应用层公司，最后都得出同一个结论：**不能只在 OpenAI 之上做壳**。
这里藏着一个反直觉的动力学：**越是被大量真实业务依赖的东西，越会被"引力"拉向开源。** 因为闭源意味着别人可以随时改你的 API、改你的价格、改你的 guardrail——而当你的业务已经跑在上面，这种不可控就是致命的。所以你会看到一个奇妙的分层：**上层越闭，下层越开**。Nvidia、AMD、Google 的新芯片都要拿 VLLM 作为 benchmark——这意味着一个开源项目，反过来成为了万亿美元硬件生态的"验收标准"。
## 二、跨领域连接：AI 模型的经济结构，其实是"制药业 + 社交媒体"的怪异混合体
Simon 自己提到了制药类比：R&D 极贵、

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Could an AI Have Discovered General Relativity? – Adam Brown
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的观察：证明机器的"诅咒"其实是人类数学审美的投影

Adam Brown 提到 Terry Tao 那句"indigestion（消化不良）"——担心 LLM 产出十亿行不可读的 Lean 代码。但这里有个几乎没人指出的悖论：数学家害怕的不是 AI 太笨，而是 AI 太像早期的自己。翻开数学史，欧拉、高斯、拉马努金的原始手稿同样充斥着"结果对但过程离奇"的跳跃，是后人（尤其是布尔巴基学派）花了几十年把它们"重新证明得优雅"。也就是说，"不可理解的证明"从来不是 AI 才带来的问题，而是数学在每个时代都要处理的熵。真正的新变量是：这一次，把熵重新压缩成"洞见"的那个存在，可能不再是人类。

跨领域连接：LLM 的"愿意浪费时间"，其实是进化生物学里的中性漂变

Brown 说 LLM 之所以能推翻"单位距离猜想"，恰恰是因为它们愿意花时间去证伪一个大家默认为真的命题——人类会因先验太强而放弃这条路径。这在生物学里有个精确的对应：Motoo Kimura 的中性演化理论。绝大多数基因突变既非有利也非有害，正是这些"看似浪费"的漂变，让种群偶尔穿越适应度谷底，抵达更高的山峰。人类数学家像自然选择——每一步都要"局部有收益"；LLM 更像中性漂变——它的优势不是更聪明，而是没有羞耻感。你甚至可以说：LLM 是第一个规模化实现"认知中性漂变"的系统，而这可能正是它做原创发现的机制根源，而非"更强的推理"这种表面解释。

隐藏的系统性真相：真正被威胁的不是数学家，而是"数学的社交结构"

如果 LLM 既能超人证明、又能超人解释——那么数学共同体那套"讲座—审稿—学生—学派"的知识传播机器，会突然变成冗余系统。想想 Erdős 猜想的那次事件：机器给出洞见 → 人类论文吸收 → 应用到新定理。这条链条里，AI 扮演的不是"新研究员"，而是新版的 Erdős 本人——一个到处播撒问题和思路的节点。差别是，Erdős 一辈子能走访约 500 位合作者；而一个 LLM 一天可以同时"喝咖啡"于全球每一位数学家的桌边。所以真正被重写的，不是"谁能证明定理"，而是"数学的社会拓扑"——从稀疏的合作网络，变成一个每个节点都直连一个超级中心的星形结构。这种拓扑在网络科学里叫 scale-free 的极端形态，而它历史上出现的每一次（教会、印刷术、搜索引擎），都伴随一次知识权力的重新洗牌。

顺手一个"啊哈"

Brown 说 LLM"有极端的耐心"。但耐心这个词，其实是只有会疲倦的存在才能拥有的美德。对一个不会疲倦的系统来说，它根本不是"有耐心"，而是没有时间概念。我们用人类词汇去形容它，其实每一次都在悄悄误读——就像用"翅膀"去描述潜艇。也许 LLM 数学的真正突破，会发生在我们放弃用人类心理学词汇描述它的那一天。

📝 转录文本

数学家的忧虑：会不会只剩下"证明机器"？

Many mathematicians are worried that these LLM's are just going to turn into proof machines. So, Terry Tao has this phrase — "indigestion" — he uses, in which these LLM's will produce billion-line inscrutable Lean codes that will serve as a certificate that a particular theorem is true, without providing any insight as to why that might be true. And wouldn't you know, wouldn't that be a depressing world, say the mathematicians.

另一种未来：超人级的"解释者"

I think that is a possible future, but I actually don't find that to be a very likely future. Because, as well as being superhuman provers, we also expect these large language models to be superhuman explainers.

And, you know, maybe they'll do the exact opposite of that. Maybe what they'll do is they'll come up with — they'll take proofs that are very hard to understand and, by doggedly trying and trying and trying, they will be able to come up with ways that are human-comprehensible. They will be able to take proofs that are difficult to understand and make them easy to understand.

经验证据：Erdős 问题的案例

And I think the empirical evidence — since early days, but it's pretty supportive of that more positive vision.

So, if you look at — there was an Erdős problem that was proved a few months ago now, and it wasn't just an incomprehensible set of Lean. In fact, it wasn't even proved in Lean; it was proved informally. And then there was a follow-up paper by some human mathematicians that took these new, human-interpretable ideas that the machine had come up with to prove this Erdős conjecture, and used it to prove new theorems that had not been used before.

So, that was — the exact of that case: it came up with a very human [approach], and then humans were able to fully comprehend it, and comprehend it so well they were able to deploy it in a new scenario.

单位距离猜想：跨越"人类偏见"的能力

We've seen that throughout. I mean, the unit distance conjecture, I think, is a good example here for a number of the themes you've been discussing here.

One is that it's totally comprehensible — the disproof of the unit distance conjecture that it came up with. I mean, to mathematicians — I'm not a mathematician.

Perhaps the reason that humans hadn't disproved the unit distance conjecture is 'cuz they erroneously believed the conjecture to be true. And that the good thing about large language models is that they're willing to push through that barrier and just waste their time, as a human would understand it, trying to disprove a presumed-true conjecture, and would reach the other end.

LLM 的"极端耐心"

So that's another, you know, aspect of large language models that makes me pretty optimistic: that they just have extreme patience, even for doing —

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

item.title: [No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups] Chasing Trillion-Dollar Companies, Founder Ambition, Token Budgets, & Regulatory Capture
item.dc:creator: No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"三年造出万亿"其实是一场认知错觉——真正稀缺的不是市场，而是"营收速度"

对话中最反直觉的判断是：未来五年能再诞生一批万亿美元公司的假设，很可能是错的。Elad 把它拆得极其锋利——TAM（市场规模）和"到达速度"被投资人系统性地混为一谈。一个万亿公司需要 500–1000 亿美元的年收入，这样的收入池在全球屈指可数，而"物理世界"的公司（能源、机器人、材料）即便市场足够大，footprint 的搭建速度根本追不上估值曲线。

这里藏着一个更深的"进化生物学式"洞见：技术史不是线性增长，而是间断平衡（Punctuated Equilibrium）——寒武纪爆发之后必然是长期的整合与沉寂。我们正处在爆发的尾声，而不是新一轮爆发的开端。绝大多数今天在"追万亿"的资本，其实是在追上一轮爆发的余波。

二、跨领域连接：Token 预算 = 1990 年代的"内部工具工程师配额" = 医院的病床分诊

Elad 提到 "return on invested tokens (ROIT)"，这是本集最被低估的框架。它表面在讲 AI 算力分配，但本质上是一切稀缺资源的分诊问题（triage）的重演：

  • 1990–2010 的工程组织：内部工具团队永远被饿死，因为同样的工程师去做产品收益更高。
  • 医院急诊室：床位不是给"最需要的人"，而是给"边际收益最高的人"。
  • 顶级实验室的算力分配：不再问"我们要不要多招研究员"，而是问"这个人配得上多少 token"。

这引出一个惊人的推论：AI 时代最重要的岗位不是模型研究员，而是"Token CFO"——决定 token 该往哪流的人。SaaS "已死"论之所以被高估，正是因为大多数企业根本没有把 token 投在 SaaS 场景上的机会成本收益——他们把 token 留给了核心业务的高毛利提升。这不是 SaaS 的失败，而是资源分诊的胜利。

三、"18 个月 RSI"的心理学副作用：整个行业正在集体演练一场"末日的心理排练"

Sarah 讲了一个几乎没人公开谈论的现象：一些顶级实验室的研究员在问她——"我该不该结婚？" 因为他们不知道 18 个月后世界会变成什么样。

这不是关于 AI 时序表的问题，而是一场大规模的"预支性存在主义危机"。它在心理学上与临终病人的行为模式极为相似：极端工作、极端放纵、或者极端的意义追寻。而 Elad 提出了一个尖锐的反问：如果每 18 个月都有人说"RSI 就在 18 个月后"，而这个预言已经连续讲了 5 年——那么这个预言的真正作用不是预测未来，而是重塑现在的工作强度和资本流向。

跨领域连接：这与核末日恐惧塑造 1960 年代反主流文化、以及千禧年 bug 塑造 1999 年 IT 支出激增是同一种机制——未来的不确定性以现在的行为形态被"贴现"出来。所以真正的问题不是"RSI 是否会来"，而是——如果整个精英群体都在按"我只剩两年生产力"的方式生活，这个信念本身会不会先于 RSI 真正到来，摧毁这一代研究者的持续产出能力？

四、一个隐藏的对称性：法国 70% 核电 vs. 加州 AI 监管——同一个剧本在不同介质中重放

Elad 用了一个几乎所有人都没注意的数据锚点：法国 70% 电力来自核能，几十年零重大事故；美国 18%，40 年没建新反应堆。他真正想说的不是核电，而是——一个国家的技术命运，往往由 5–10 年内的一次"安全叙事"决定，之后 40 年都翻不了身。

把这个模式套到今天的加州"亿万富翁税 + 退出税"提案上，你会发现这是同一部戏的第二幕： - 1970 年代的美国：安全游说 → 清洁能源死亡 → 化石燃料锁定 40 年 - 2020 年代的加州：财富再分配叙事 → 生态系统外迁 → 硅谷神话可能锁定终章

这就是本集最令人不安的隐喻——监管俘获的真正代价不是"更慢"，而是"路径依赖锁死"。今天决定 AI 监管强度的每一个字，可能都在为 2060 年的技术版图写下第一行代码。

📝 转录文本

开场：核能的隐喻

70% of France is still nuclear in terms of its power generation. 70%. Where are all the accidents and where are all the curtles and you nothing nothing's happened. US is 18% and we haven't built a reactor in 40 years. We had a safety lobby in the 70s basically kill abundant clean energy for us. There are real outcomes where safety has hurt us. But I think if there's any alternative that was easy to do, a lot of people would even more people would be leaving. I do think a lot of people are leaving. Like I know quite a few are starting to go now or planning to go by you know the fall in the next month or so.

十九、下一个生态：德州与硬件走廊

What is your second choice ecosystem?

I think that there's a few different places that a lot of people are considering and the question is like what does critical mass look like in two years at each one of those spots. So I think a lot of these things kind of self-assemble and people talk about weather and they talk about all these other things but the reality is um you know Boston used to be one of the main startup hubs. It still is for biotech, right? They sort of lost competitively in the early 90s, right? In the 80s, Boston was sort of the counterweight to Silicon Valley. And the weather there is awful, you know. And so I think it's more about where do you have enough smart people aggregated working on common things, and then that's where these renaissances tend to happen.

I think it's been really exciting to see the amount of like great technology migration and innovation in Texas around energy.

Because that is really like a reaction to regulatory environment and demand where I've seen a lot of people either move from Silicon Valley or move from other places because it is a place where you can experiment and the there's actually an ecosystem now that's super exciting.

Energy and hardware — actually there's a really growing hardware corridor there as well which is you know it was originally all around El Segundo because that's where SpaceX was. And then now you know SpaceX and I think part of Tesla and stuff moved to Texas and so there's like this new ecosystem kind of emerging around sort of a part of Texas as well in addition to Austin.

So I do think we are seeing these shifts and these shifts are purely driven by regulation. They're not driven — why is Texas a better or worse place to live? I mean, it impacts things, right? But but it's regulatory shifts driving people out.

二十、架构、算力与信息扩散

You didn't take my bait on architecture and like technology. What do you think about architectures? I think we are going to like as an industry consume all of the compute and power available whatever the underlying architectures. So the idea that you are going to have a lot of pressure to find more memory or power efficient architectures is like more interesting than ever. But catching up to transformers in scale and match for hardware remains pretty tough but I think people make that they will make that bet as they get more desperate in terms of more experimentation. I don't think it changes the direction of the industry.

I think whatever it is gets copied and then the labs do it and they hand all the compute — you know, that's that's the high probability outcome. It's not the only outcome. There could be some lower probability thing where some Neolab comes up with something they keep it super super secret they scale on it and suddenly their model is better than anyone else by far and then they can afford all the extra compute and everything else and everybody rallies around them. You know, you could always imagine a scenario like that. But you could also imagine a scenario where just one person from that team leaves for Anthropic or OpenAI and the knowledge spreads and the next thing you know, everybody has it, which is what's been happening so far in terms of these models.

Do you think if the dominant thing is access to compute then and it's an oligopoly because of it, do you see the labs using that access to compute to control other verticals that they want to be in?

二十一、安全叙事与监管俘获：Jansen 的启示

Or or what is the safety that's really needed that's actually protective of people right? What is the risk, what is the outcome? That's kind of the — you know, Jansen from Jansen Pharmaceuticals, you know, he's considered one of the best drug developers of all times. He has these great videos on YouTube where he's interviewed 30, 40 years ago talking about regulatory capture and pharma.

And the reason things got so expensive and so slow is number one uh regulatory capture, and the second is risk-reward scenarios where the FDA — in his mind, I'm not saying this is correct or incorrect, in his mind — the FDA focuses too much on safety and risk and not enough on benefit. And so there's no risk-reward — there's only risk. So that slows everything down because you're only looking at one side of the equation.

One could imagine a scenario where in the labs a version of that is created as well, right? Where the safety burden is so high even if the outcome is even higher, even if the positive outcome is dramatically higher relative to the risk. And so this is back to if you only focus on one side of the equation, you'll always constrain things. And if you constrain things but then push progress forward internally on an exponent — in a year is worth three or four years in normal time, then you're a year ahead internally. That's a massive advantage.

And so it's this very interesting question of like where do we as a society feel comfortable on the risk-reward spectrum for different things. Like if my email gets hacked, is that so terrible relative to better healthcare through AI models sooner, right? And so that's kind of the trade-off. So yeah, these are all things we'll have to work through from a societal perspective.

二十二、核能对照：安全游说的历史代价

I think part of the challenge here is it's not a comfortable stance for the regulators to for many policy makers to hear from technologists that you have to see what happens with the technology versus control.

We've always said that. This always been a tech thing. It's always been throughout history. Hey, like of course this technology could be used in negative ways, right? Every technology has both positive and negative applications. Biotech, you could create a virus, but you can cure cancer. Nuclear, you could have free, cheap, abundant energy, you can also create weapons.

And if you actually look at it, you know, 70% of France is still nuclear in terms of its power generation, right? 70%. Where are all the accidents and where are all the curls and you nothing nothing's happened. US is 18% and we haven't built a reactor in 40 years. Japan is 25%. Very safe, very abundant. But we had a safety lobby in the 70s basically kill abundant clean energy for us right?

Well, we're making them now. We just need to make a lot of them.

We're not making much. We're not making much.

So, I think we've — there there are real outcomes where safety has hurt us. And that's hurt us in power and energy production. It's hurt us in aspects of medicine. It's hurt us in lots of places. And the question is where do we want the spectrum to be on AI for this stuff? And there's many worlds, many scenarios, many outcomes. And society, we kind of get to choose — where do we want to place that needle on the wheel of safety versus risk versus outcome?

二十三、结语：乐观主义与技术进步

Elad, before we go, what is something that you're just excited about that is on the positive end of that wheel?

I mean, there's so much stuff I'm excited about there. Like I think there's so much we can do from a human productivity perspective, from an education perspective, from a healthcare perspective, from a daily life and benefit to life perspective, self-driving and elderly, everything, you know. Like there's so much good that can come of all this. So, I'm optimistic about a lot of applications. And that's why I'm cautious about where we should end up on that spectrum because I do think it's always good to make sure that we have the proper safeguard society, but I think that historically for big industries, we've gone too far.

And the reason tech has been so successful so quickly and has had so much human impact is because it's been lightly regulated. And I think it's better to keep it that way than not. And we'll lose optimism. We'll lose momentum. We'll lose progress. And that's what happened in biotech. And that's what's happened in a variety of areas over time. That's what happened in energy for a long time.

Call to arms against regulatory capture.

All right, we'll see you guys. Find us on Twitter at @NoPriorsPod. Subscribe to our YouTube channel if you want to see our faces. Follow the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you listen. That way you get a new episode every week. And sign up for emails or find transcripts for every episode at no-priors.com.

## 一、"三年造出万亿"其实是一场认知错觉——真正稀缺的不是市场，而是"营收速度"
对话中最反直觉的判断是：**未来五年能再诞生一批万亿美元公司的假设，很可能是错的**。Elad 把它拆得极其锋利——TAM（市场规模）和"到达速度"被投资人系统性地混为一谈。一个万亿公司需要 500–1000 亿美元的年收入，这样的收入池在全球屈指可数，而"物理世界"的公司（能源、机器人、材料）即便市场足够大，footprint 的搭建速度根本追不上估值曲线。
这里藏着一个更深的**"进化生物学式"洞见**：技术史不是线性增长，而是**间断平衡（Punctuated Equilibrium）**——寒武纪爆发之后必然是长期的整合与沉寂。我们正处在爆发的尾声，而不是新一轮爆发的开端。绝大多数今天在"追万亿"的资本，其实是在追上一轮爆发的余波。
