And so one can be wary of top-down imposition of the sort of a Weberian ethic of ultimate ends, that if you're so convinced of the righteousness of your political cause you might be willing to kind of destroy the world for it — and how dangerous that is. And that cannot be the sole guiding principle of anyone who seeks to affect politics, including — I think even if you see yourself as an intellectual thinker and what you're arguing for, I think you should think that your arguments might have political implications.

But the point I want to make with this is that the risk that we have is that if you don't — what you need to at least do is show that sort of sensitivity to what's wrong with the world, and that in that way, whatever your proposals are, they won't be taken as just an attempt to justify or just an attempt to cool down the temperature, but as one that's much more keen — mean with a "we see things that are wrong, we are just sensitive to the fact that it's so hard to correct them, and in knowing that we're going to be inter—" there's a reflexive process here. Whatever you act and whatever you do in the world will bring forth its own reaction, is important.

英国内战与反动反弹

And to this more moderate side of Smith and why you think he's concerned with injustice, there's something to Nussbaum's points. He talks about that in the chapter that's on the origin of the distinction of ranks and ambition, where he talks heavily in Theory of Moral Sentiments — that material I draw on in terms of how we disdain the poor and admire and trust the rich — he talks about the English civil war, and he talks about the incredible sympathy for the rich will also mean that as civil wars go on, as the monarch is humiliated, that creates its own reactionary backlash.

And so in terms of even if one has — even if one sees that there is grand corruption in the system and it requires an ambitious political vision, if one isn't careful about that, and if one just seeks violent revolution in the way that Smith's describing in that era, that doesn't mean that you're going to get your vision. It could also give the people that you think have an even more troubling vision an advantage. And so you need to be very — this is very much what politics is about, is negotiating these different camps.

冷战阴影下的斯密解读

The other thing — and I don't want to — I'm sure you have stuff you want to say to that, but I wanted to kind of close the loop on why I mentioned the invisible hand thing as a system, and something that liberals have to negotiate is also that — and maybe to some degree the development of Smithian interpretations in the 20th century that were more in economics, although I don't want to paint a discipline I'm not really in with a broad brush — is the impact of the Cold War.

At least members of my generation might assume that there's a lot of this kind of privileging of Smith as being a part of a Cold War championing of the liberal capitalist system and association with that. And I don't think that there's so many jumps that we have to go from Smith's text to American military interventions in South America and all these that sort of American imperialism. But for many people, that's what comes to mind. They think that this capitalist system then became the justification for imperial violence and occupation.

And so that's something that — I think it's quite, when you read Smith, you can see how he's actually quite critical of imperialism, he's critical of military domination in various ways. But if you are coming up in this post-Cold War environment, that's maybe the hangover that you have to deal with in terms of what this gets associated with politically.

1976 与政治风向的转变

You know how I said earlier that we've had this boom because we had the 300th birthday and then the 250th celebration. I think it actually is quite fascinating. I can't remember if Glory in her book — you know — gets this timing, but I know that she gets what Stigler and Friedman and whatnot were trying to do. But there was a particularly interesting timing because the 200th anniversary was right in the middle of 1976, which is right when the political winds are starting to shift because of the stagflation that took place in the UK and the United States. You end up very soon after having Thatcher and Reagan, and it was all connected up in that.

As someone who read Adam Smith more as a process theorist and things like that — we always used to make fun, when I was learning which is in the 80s, we used to make fun of Stigler as, you know, he only read the first five chapters of the Wealth of Nations and then stopped, kind of thing, and didn't read the rest of it.

对 Judith Shklar 的挑战：恐惧的自由主义

But I was just wondering if — I think maybe I'm wrong about this — but it would connect up to what you were just saying with your discussion with Judith Shklar and the liberalism of fear kind of idea. Maybe if you could talk a little bit about that, and then we'll get to Jeremy Bentham.

Yeah. Well, do you have any specifics on that you want to talk about with Shklar that you had in mind? I remember you said that there were two challenges.

Well, the only thing is that she talks a lot about Hayek, and I tend to think that she doesn't always get Hayek right. There's actually some areas of overlap between concerns that she has and what Hayek has, but she doesn't see those. But I know that you've at least given a talk on some of this stuff.

Well, I would say that there's more I would have to do to really do justice to putting Shklar in conversation with Hayek specifically. I do agree — I've been more focused on the fact that she often oversimplifies Smith, although she's not alone in that. So much literature — Charles Taylor also does this. Even though we now take for granted, at least in Smith scholarship — I don't know that everybody outside of specialists appreciate all this myth, especially Theory of Moral Sentiments. But Theory of Moral Sentiments, in terms of interpreting it and bringing it into political theory and philosophy, really took off more after some of the influential texts were written that still people are reading. And then if you don't read Smith, you might get confused anyway.

Not to interrupt you, but I just read a piece the other day that was accusing Smith of atomism.

Yeah.

You know, and all these things. And so you read it and you're kind of like, "I don't know what the hell."

原子化的错位指控

That's a classic one. And honestly, I find it strange because I'm very sympathetic to critiques of modern society in like 20th century, 21st century, and the issues of atomism — maybe more so than some liberals. I'm very interested in that literature. I think liberals are interested, but maybe more sympathetic than some. But I always find it weird to project that onto the 18th century. I don't really think that that's — I mean, he is talking about urbanization, but it's very different.

And I don't — I agree with you, and especially with Theory of Moral Sentiments, such — one of the few thinkers that we read in the canonical political theory canon who just starts from an assumption that people are social and sociable and empathize with each other. Like sociability — that is something to see as very different from what people will tend to assume of the liberals, quote unquote, anyway.

消极自由与法律地位

So let's set that aside. But to the Shklar points — what I'm interested in with Shklar, and what I think is interesting, is that it does strike me a little bit that Hayek is much more antagonistic — or I don't know if that's — it's always a blurred line between: is a thinker antagonistic or critical of or skeptical of a concept, or do they just deprioritize it and not see it as important, particularly given whatever the context that they're in, whatever challenges they see at the moment?

So it seems to me like Hayek is a little bit skeptical of what we would say positive liberty, or the idea of political participation and engagement as being a part of freedom. Because there is this more emphasis on emergence, there's an emphasis on the English common law system, and therefore not so much on actual parliamentary legislation or political parties and those types of actions.

I know there's other ways in which Shklar and Hayek might talk past each other or ways that she criticizes Hayek. But what I'm struck with is that she takes a lot of care in her work to talk about the American context specifically. And in the American context, just how important being able to access legal standing was. Especially if we're also celebrating this year the semiquincentennial of the founding and the Declaration of Independence — the ability for enslaved people, for formerly enslaved people to have legal standing in the judicial system was essential to actually having what we think of as negative freedom, what we think of as negative liberty.

And so that is a little bit distinct from maybe just even the right to vote, although that I think is also really crucial. So this idea of: do we think of freedom from interference and the more positive liberty of ability to be engaged in self-governance or being able to participate in politics — do we see these as completely separate? I understand why analytically we separate them, but if we look at them throughout history, is there a way in which at least in particular contexts for particular cases, they are much more interrelated than we might analytically treat them as?

黑人优雅与被承认的尊严

It's funny, the thing about standing — this is going to sound really weird — but on NPR this morning, because the Tony's are this weekend, they had an interview with André De Shields, who is 80 years old, but now up for his, I guess, second Tony, because he's in the remake of Cats. What's fascinating is they were talking to him and they said, "what do you hope your career—" and he said, "one of the things is that I want to represent black elegance." And then they asked him to talk about that, and he said, "what I mean by that is that I want people who come from an enslaved background to look in the mirror and say that they have dignity, and they can acknowledge themselves that they are here."

So it's quite fascinating to me this notion that you talk about and other people talk about. Because a book that had a big influence on me was Jeremy Waldron. I'm a huge fan of his. He has this one book called Political Political Theory, which I think is really quite good. But then he has another book called One Another's Equals. That's been an influence on me because to me, when I was a student of Jim Buchanan, Jim Buchanan stressed that a big part of his discussion — which is: we are one another's equals, and we must treat equal things equally. And then you go from there in terms of like the calculus of consent or whatever.

But again, just like with Adam Smith, a lot of people don't see that in these thinkers, right? And I think it's your point that you just made, which is that they tend to deemphasize certain aspects which other people elevate, because they themselves are working on something else that has occupied their imagination to some extent. It is a kind of invisible hand process and quite an aspect of how markets can liberate people that previously don't have access — rather than the idea that the power structures keep people from having access. It's like, okay, let's get rid of the power structures and then look what happens with the access. And they want to focus on telling that story.

So anyway, I don't know — that's just a reaction. I don't know if it's an answer to this.

福利国家、社会最低限度与学科视角

No. And well, and I do think, to be fair to the differences with Shklar and Hayek — she was much more enthusiastic about the rise of the welfare state, and also the importance of work, but also the complexity of being able to work and being respected to work. So there is this element of this deep concern with social recognition and dignity. And I don't know that necessarily means that Hayek isn't concerned with those things, but it could be a change of emphasis.

And also, I think it's fair to acknowledge the disagreements, but it is always interesting. One could probably always kind of say, well, there's these elements that maybe — so for example, when it comes to the welfare state, Hayek talking about the idea of there being a kind of minimum, a social minimum, right? And that's something that at the time, because of other political concerns and arguments that are happening, that just wasn't coming to the fore. So was she totally wrong to disagree in those other ways? I'm not sure.

I'm a little blind to this aspect of social history. I really value social history, so I want to be honest about that. But I also think that sometimes it's just a disciplinary emphasis issue. Because in some sense Hayek comes to liberalism from technical economics, because the liberal background was the framework within which the economic process plays out. And then what happened was his fellow economists stopped paying attention to the framework. And so then he has to do an analysis of the framework. Whereas I think a lot of political theorists, the framework is their subject matter, not the operations. And so then it's about the representation of political rights within this framework, and so they just come at it in different ways.

But in both cases, I think what they really want to do is — to go along with Waldron's thing — develop a system of where we begin with the recognition that we're one another's dignified equals, and then what are the rules that allow us to live together in that kind of experience. But anyway, like I said, we're not going to solve that today.

边沁与索蒂米昂：被遗忘的乌托邦

But I wanted to finish up by asking you to talk a little bit about the work that you did on Jeremy Bentham. Because what's fascinating about Bentham is, again, what economists adopt from Bentham is basically utilitarianism, and the thrust of the philosophical radicals of the 19th century. So basically James Mill, Ricardo, Bentham, and then John Stuart Mill kind of idea, that tradition.

And what I was fascinated with — and I have to tell you before I read you, I did not know this — which is this shift of Bentham from the panopticon to this issue having to do with much more on the ground and dealing with these pregnant unmarried women, and how they are — he's solving a problem so that they don't — if I understand you rightly, he's solving a problem so that they can still be connected to society but not suffer society's social shame.

Yes. Yeah.

So maybe you can explain that.

索蒂米昂的构想

No, thank you. And it's funny because this institution — and I am always asked how to pronounce this, and I always worry because I pronounce so many things wrong, that I'm sure I can't possibly be pronouncing it right.

That's why I avoided saying it — because I'm afraid I'll say it.

I also believe in — like, people should be able to say — I don't love — I'm the opposite of a grammar Nazi. I'm like a grammar anti-fascist or anarchist or something. I just feel like everybody should be able to say what they want to say, and we should try to just make sure we can understand each other. Maybe use more words if required.

But anyway, so he had these other designs. And what's so fascinating is he's working on these after the initial panopticon designs, but in the same time period where he's working with the government to try to create what would have been this panopticon prison that then becomes this huge influence on Foucault and still influences the way people talk about surveillance today.

But at the same time, he had these notes on something that he referred to as a sotimion, or we could also say sotimian would be the maybe other way to say it. I like saying sotimion mostly because it rhymes with panopticon — it just seems like we should lean into that kind of what people are already used to saying.

边沁对性道德的批判

What this institution — what's so fascinating about this is he has all these other writings at this time too that we should read these notes in context with. These were writings that were very critical of the criminalization of sodomy, the social censure as well, the Christian aesthetic norms around sexuality. So he's both defending homosexuality, but he's also defending other marginalized sexual practices, including prostitution, including unmarried pregnant women — the idea of illegitimate pregnancies and childbearing outside of marriage.

And in all of these writings, he has such an institutional approach to these questions. So in terms of institutions at the time that were similar to what he ends up designing in the sotimion — which the sotimion never existed. It's all hypothetical. It's all notes. It's all in his archival manuscripts. But it's such a provocative — I mean, it's similar to the panopticon. The panopticon was this project he was really enthusiastic about, but it wasn't created in his time, and by him, not in the way that he was envisioning.

And so, we have less material on the sotimion, but he had these writings about criticizing the way society would stigmatize and socially punish women who had children outside of marriage. And he makes it quite clear that from his point of view, this was really not a problem for people to do this. And often, to the degree that this was happening, it was maybe because of poor marriage laws. Similarly with prostitution itself, or sex work, that it was difficult to have marriage — marriage laws — it was difficult to get divorced.

抹大拉医院与短期婚约

He also talks about the institution that did exist at the time — there were the Magdalene hospitals for penitent prostitutes. If you're familiar with the book Small Things Like These by Claire Keegan, she talks about what is essentially Magdalene laundries in Ireland later. But the Magdalene Hospital for Penitent Prostitutes was an institution to try to reform young women who were sexually promiscuous and potentially prostitutes. And it required this kind of "oh, I repent, I regret what I did." Bentham talks about how some of these women — their fundamental problem here was poverty, was a lack of opportunities.

Also all these hospitals were so focused on the problem of these women, and not the idea that men who were in the armed forces, military, and the navy — they were unable to create the relationships required to have marriages. So you couldn't have people having short-term marriage contracts. What Bentham argues in all that literature is talking about you having short-term marriage contracts, so that you would ensure that a man would be responsible for any offspring, and enabling these more — these couplings — this idea of like, why are we punishing people for these activities when our institutions make it more likely that they will do this?

索蒂米昂的设计细节

So the sotimion is something he designs in — or he imagines — in this period for how do you deal with this problem that women are punished for their pregnancies outside of marriage. And he has this really moving writing in some of these pieces about describing what it's like to be a woman who is punished by society for this. She's essentially opened up to the center of the world. It has this language that we would say panoptic — of the idea of being an object of surveillance, of being judged, and then being encouraged to internalize that public shame and stigma. But it's an isolating experience.

And that is what I think is interesting about surveillance. I mean, talk about atomism. What surveillance can do is force you to be exposed to the public and exposed to total social judgment and observation, while isolating you as well. So he talks about how the women then are isolated from their friends, they're treated as dangerous, right? And so how can you deal with a situation where you want to protect women from that social judgment, maybe give them measures of privacy, but you also don't want to actually isolate them from their friends, their family, because from Bentham's perspective, they didn't do anything wrong. There's no reason for them to be punished for this.

So he imagines this institution called the sotimion, which was not a panopticon in design. The panopticon is this central inspection tower with cells circling around it — or spaces, because it could be applied to various things — but in a prison, all the prisoner cells around it, such that the inspector at the top, hidden by blinds, wouldn't be seen by any of the prisoners at any time, but the prisoners would know and internalize that they could be under surveillance at any moment. So this is this disciplinary — and I think, to say that Bentham has all this other stuff doesn't deny how disturbing and strange this is, although there's more we could say here too where he was attempting to create a system that would actually also protect prisoners from themselves. It would also make the prisons more hygienic, would also subject the inspector, the guards, the management to the public as a whole system of public oversight as well.

But setting that aside, the sotimion was very much not that. It would have been a part of the same — he was imagining as part of the same grounds — he was trying to get the government to set up in the center of London, so it could all be under public oversight to some degree, not be kind of set aside and on the fringes of society.

There would be a bunch of cabins for each woman to live in — very well equipped. A common room that the women would govern themselves. It was basically like a gentleman's club at the time. A blackball system where if they disagreed with each other in terms of their behavior — any kind of offensive behavior or something like that — they might be able to exclude one another at least temporarily, or from various parts of the grounds, from that common room. But it was still managed by the residents themselves, not the management. And it was very much a social environment. He also envisioned all these very fun, nice things. It made it seem very idyllic, almost utopian really.

检查室：可见性的翻转

But all that — so a mix of common spaces, of these private spaces — but then the entrance. This was, I think, the special crowning for me, like such striking element of this design: there would have been an entrance and a porter at the door to welcome any visitors to this space. Again, very unique, very different from the other institutions at the time like the Magdalene hospital. Not only could these women be pregnant and give birth and maintain their privacy, but also they could allow visitors, friends, lovers, family members to come.

But they would have what he called an examination room in this entrance, such that the woman could be hidden and they could observe whoever the visitor was that came. They would give to the porter their name, the visitor would give their own name. The porter would go back, check with the resident: is this the person that they say they are, and do you mind that they know you're here and they want to see you? Is that okay? And they can say yes or no.

They could be actually in total control over the terms of their public appearances. They could conceal the fact that they were pregnant. They could maintain their social reputation, which mattered so much in this time — would help them maintain things like domestic servant roles, various jobs, but also of course a time — I mean, this is the era of Bridgerton really, after all — the ability to get married. All those things. While also still not being isolated, not being atomized.

被咨询的女性novelists

And it is this extremely — he writes about women that he would consult for this project. In fact, it seems like he probably was maybe influenced by Mary Ford, who was his sister-in-law — I have to remember the timing — she, I think, had not quite gotten married yet to his brother. And potentially Maria Gisborne may have been — that's something that Eileen Hunt, who's also one of the guests on my podcast, talks a little bit about this possibility that maybe she was also an influence, although that's very speculative. But in these circles in his life are women like that. And he writes about these novelists, these female novelists, that he thought maybe they would be people he could consult for this project, who were writing sentimental novels.

So this is all to say, it doesn't deny his utilitarian arguments, his conceptions of utility, but there has always been this oversimplification of Bentham as not concerned with individual rights or not concerned with the individual and autonomy, or not concerned with this more emotional, complex social experience that in fact he was very much motivated about.

And again, to go back to what I was saying about Smith, the fact that these thinkers — they were not just envisioning these simplified projects of how to make the world adhere to a system. Like it wasn't just this system thinking of the man of the system or something. It was also a social criticism. It was also a keen sensitivity to the relations of power, the entrenched institutions and interests that shaped the status quo.

被看见：斯密、边沁与尊严

When I was reading your piece and a couple other things that I've read, I kept on thinking to myself: there's this relationship that these people have — Smith and Bentham — to the essentialness of being seen as connected to the cultivation and practice of the moral sentiments. And so that's such a crucial thing for them, to make sure that you spread out who is seen, more and more. I was quite struck by that, and I thought that this example that you gave of this thing that Bentham envisioned, given the time in which he's writing, is pretty amazing.

It's also the case, I see it also when Adam Smith talks about slavery — he refers to the slavers as the refuge of the prisons of Europe, but refers to the slaves as nation of heroes.

Yeah.

He wants you to see them, right, in a way. And so it gets all lost when we just pigeonhole these thinkers in different ways.

无法忽视的可见性欲望

100%. And I want to add to that. Because that is a part of this larger book project that I've been working on. What I think is so striking about this notion of being seen is that there is this pernicious surveillance that we can feel. We can feel as though — especially when we are not in control and we don't have the discretion over how we're observed and judged by other people — we're exposed in this way. There's also a way in which people can subject people to public shame, can bring them out in society in order to humiliate and punish them, and to serve as an example for others, to kind of make others afraid and control them, right?

But the issue with this is that we can't just then avoid visibility entirely. There isn't this way that we could just ignore, or we could say, "well, just don't think about what other people think of you." I mean, that's — I think also to get to the opening stuff we were talking about — even though there is a way in which you could say Smith's answer to us would be something stoic of "don't worry about what the public thinks or what the average person thinks, or this idea of vanity, or all these public performances we have in our lives — just try to cultivate that inner sense of integrity and self-esteem, and imagine that impartial spectator that you're trying to imagine."

I think he's quite so sensitive that this is not something we can just wish away. It's very hard for any one person to form the total security of self absent — you know — validation, but also in the face of such stark social opprobrium or judgment, or even more severe legal prohibitions and punishment as well.

In fact, it is a political and social problem that we must face. And I think we have to acknowledge — to get to the sort of "how do we manage our emotions?" — you don't just suppress the desire to be seen and understood. You figure out a way to find these fulfilling experiences, and how can we create a society, both through more emergent or bottom-up, or what is available to us, where people really do feel seen and acknowledged and recognized on equal terms — as opposed to in that kind of punitive, disciplinary surveillance way.

结语与推广

Well, Kristen, I greatly appreciate you taking the time today. I'm so grateful that you are here as my colleague, because I constantly learn so much from you about the liberal project and how we need to restate it for the current generation and build on it and improve on it. So thank you so much for that as well. And I wish you all the best this summer and be a big hit in Glasgow.

Thank you so much, Pete. No, I'm really grateful. And again, I'm always so grateful when we get to talk. It definitely is one of the privileges of my job that we get to be at so many tables together chatting and thinking and arguing too — but in a way that is always productive and always makes me feel seen and respected. So thank you so much, Pete, for creating that environment, for giving me the opportunity to come on the podcast.

Virtual Sentiments 播客与新书预告

Thanks Pete for having me on the Hayek Program podcast, and to you for listening. If you want to hear more from me, Kristen Collins, check out my podcast, Virtual Sentiments, a series on the ethics and politics of digital technologies today with an eye to the past. I talk to scholars, practitioners, journalists, and other experts in political science, history, philosophy, computer science, and all sorts of other fields, with the aim of bridging the gap between expertise and public discourse. My goal is that you come away from every episode feeling like you learned something new and are more confident to contribute your own voice to the public debates about major technological, political, and economic changes our societies are undergoing today.

Currently releasing our fourth season, we have a truly varied and interdisciplinary slate of guests from over the years that you can choose from. Our latest episode was with AI scientist Katherine Gormley on her work on data privacy and open-source or open-weight large language models. Past guests include international political economist Henry Farrell on AI as a social technology, political theorist Deva Woodly on social movements, journalist Samantha Cole on how sex changed the internet, and political theorist Eileen Hunt on Mary Shelley and the ethics of AI.

If you're interested in my work, I'm currently finishing up my first book, Spectatorship and Surveillance in Liberal Democracies: Seeing and Being Seen. Drawing on canonical figures, including Thomas Hobbes, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Adam Smith, and Jeremy Bentham, I reinterpret the liberal tradition and illustrate its continued relevance for criticizing the impact of surveillance and inequality on freedom and democracy today. I also write a Substack newsletter, Theory of Virtual Sentiments, and my handle is Kristen Rosec on Twitter and Blue Sky. I also share news about my latest research, including my book at my website, kristenrcollins.com.

Thank you for listening to the Hayek Program podcast. To learn more about the research, scholars, and work of the Hayek program, visit hayek.mercatus.org. For more information about graduate student fellowship opportunities for students at Mason as well as at universities across the globe, please visit students.mercatus.org. We hope you recommend students to our programs or consider applying yourself.

item.description:
## 一、被误读的"自我克制"：不是压抑，而是共情的前置条件
大多数读者把 Smith 的 self-command 理解为斯多葛式的情感压抑——一种"男性化的坚忍"。但 Collins 在这场对话里揭示了一个反直觉的结构：**self-command 不是切断情感，而是让情感变得"可翻译"**。你之所以要节制自己被冒犯时的怒火，恰恰是因为你要保留识别他人被冒犯的感官带宽。压抑得太彻底，你就丧失了共情的语法。
这里有个几乎没人指出的隐藏对称：Smith 笔下的"公正旁观者"其实和现代**心理治疗中的 mentalization（心智化）**惊人地同构——都是让主体在情绪高峰时保留一个"可观测的自我"，以便同时看见自己与他者。也就是说，Smith 早在 1759 年就描述了当代依恋理论直到 21 世纪才命名的能力。Nussbaum 批评他冷酷，但被她指为"冷酷"的那个动作，恰恰是"温情得以稳定传导"的必要机械装置。
## 二、正义的起源不在契约，而在"戏剧"：一个被忽视的美学转向
对话中最锋利的一刻，是 Collins 指出：Smith 的正义感不来自"己所不欲勿施于人"这样的规

💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽略的"估值锚点漂移"：市场正在悄悄重写 AI 公司的估值语法

小涛这期最反常识的一点埋在他对比 Oracle、Broadcom、英伟达、AMD 时的一句话里——"现在市场对纯 GPU 公司给了非常低的估值，而对 CPU、ASIC、Inference 相关公司给了溢价"。

这其实是一次估值语法的静默政变。过去两年市场用"训练算力增速"给英伟达定价，但当英伟达 29 财年 forward P/E 只有 13 倍、而博通 28 财年还有 16 倍时，市场实际上已经把英伟达重新分类为"周期性硬件"，而把 ASIC 玩家重新分类为"软件式复利资产"。

这里有一个跨领域的类比：这跟 2010 年代智能手机产业链的估值迁移一模一样——最初市场给高通（芯片王者）最高估值，但当 iPhone 生态成型后，估值溢价迁移到了做"定制化最后一公里"的博通、Skyworks、村田身上。GPU 正在经历它的"高通时刻"：越通用、越强大，反而越像"电力公司"而不是"AI 公司"。

二、马斯克的"数据中心 ROI 一年论"是一次高风险的会计叙事错配

老马说 SpaceX 数据中心回报周期"小于一年"，而亚马逊 Andy Jassy 说的是"两到三年"。小涛敏锐地指出这是长租/短租的差异，但更深一层的洞察是：老马正在用短租 On-Demand 的现金流曲线，去讲一个需要长租折旧节奏的资本开支故事。

这是一种典型的"期限错配叙事"——就像 2007 年前的次贷机构用短期票据滚动融资去持有长期 MBS。逻辑上短期数据都成立，但一旦短租价格下行（而这在 15GW 供给上线后几乎必然发生），估值模型会瞬间从"一年回本的黄金印钞机"翻转成"十年折旧的电力资产"。

一个跨领域的意外连接：这和电影行业首周末票房与长尾流媒体收入的关系高度相似——你可以用《复联4》的首周末数据说服投资人"电影公司回本快"，但你不能用它来给整个片单估值。老马正在做的，就是拿"首周末"给"整个片单"定价。

三、真正的隐藏赢家不是英伟达也不是 SpaceX，而是 HBM 供应链的"隐形税收官"

财报会议里那个关于 HBM 涨价的问答，小涛点到了但没有拆完。AMD 承认 HBM 涨价成本无法加价转嫁，只能通过"减少 HBM 用量的产品重设计"来应对——英伟达的 Rubin 也在做同样的事。

这透露一个惊人的结构性事实：HBM 厂商（SK Hynix、三星、美光）实际上对 GPU 巨头拥有"税收权"——它们的涨价直接吞噬下游毛利，而下游巨头只能通过牺牲产品性能（减少 HBM 数量）来"避税"。

这个模式的跨领域镜像是中世纪的"莱茵河关税城堡"：河流上下游都是大公国，但真正稳定收租的是控制关键渡口的小主教国。在 AI 产业链里，HBM 就是那个渡口。

一个让人意外的推论：如果 SpaceX 真的要在 27 年前上线 15GW（哪怕打对折 8GW），加上英伟达、Meta、谷歌、Oracle 的扩张，HBM 的结构性短缺会持续到 2028 年之后——这意味着市场目前对存储周期股仍在用"周期股 P/E"定价，是一个和"给博通打推理溢价"完全对称的错误。当估值语法在 GPU 端已经改写，它在 memory 端的改写只是时间问题。

四、一个元洞察：小涛的方法论本身正在成为市场信号

值得注意的是——他反复强调"估值是模糊的正确"、"不需要天天看"，但观众"尝到甜头后想天天看"。这实际上暴露了一个反身性陷阱：当越来越多散户用同一套 forward P/E + PEG 框架时，这个框架本身会失效，因为估值折价的窗口会被更快消化。

3 月和 7 月的两次低估值窗口能被抓住，恰恰是因为大多数人还没转向这套思维。方法的普及是方法失效的开始——这是每一个价值投资者最终都要面对的悖论。

在低估值的时候，很多市场里边那些宏观因素也好、技术指标也好，我个人认为都是偏向于噪音，好吗？

那因为我知道部分的观众在估值上面确实尝到了甜头，对吗？诶，估值高的时候我减仓，诶，估值低的时候我去加仓。但是我在这边强调一下：就不需要天天去看估值。这不是因为你在这个标的身上尝到了一个甜头之后，你会发现我天天要去关注这个，没有必要。

估值本身它是一个模糊的正确，我强调过很多次，它没有办法帮助你每天去做这个交易。并且今天即使涨了 2%、涨了 3%，也不代表这个估值就会去到非常高的这个位置，不会。所以估值是一个模糊的正确，且估值我们用来判断高估还是低估，它是要有时间的这个跨度的。没有时间的这个跨度或者涨幅，你短期之内涨了 3%、跌了 3% 再去看估值的话，没有什么意义，好吗？

那今天我就市场的话，我就稍微聊这些，然后主要和大家聊两家公司财报：盘后发布财报的 SpaceX 和 AMD。

一、SpaceX 财报解读

1. 财报数据总览

OK，来来，先来看一下 SpaceX 这次的一个财报。首先先来看一下数据：

  • 营收本身大幅超出市场的这个预期
  • EPS 的这个增速或者体量也大幅超出市场的预期
  • 营收超出了 15%
  • EPS 超出了 62%
  • 如果你去看它的 adjusted operating income，调整之后的一个运营利润超出市场预期 91%

所以是和市场预期去做对比的话是非常好的这个财报。但是因为是刚刚上市，且里边的业务的波动本身非常的大，所以现在其实市场几乎没有办法对于未来 SpaceX 所有的业务去进行一个比较准确的一个预估。经过几次财报之后，包括管理层给出指引之后，市场会有这个更好的一个把握。

2. 市场对 SpaceX 的估值预期

但没办法，即使在这种情况下，我们还是要去先看一下市场对于 SpaceX 的一个估值。先来看一下整个 26 年，你看一下 26 年市场预计运营利润是多少，0 点……就一个 billion 都不到。那从这个角度去看，而且是 forward、是向前去看的嘛，如果你 2026 年一个 billion 都不到的话，现在多少？一个 T 的一个估值、一个 T 的一个市值，你自然就会觉得现在 SpaceX 贵到非常的夸张。

但实际上呢，没有那么的夸张。你看一下 2028 年市场预期多少？Operating Income 运营利润 38 个 billion。三年不到的时间里边，将会从一个 billion 上升到 38 个 billion，翻 38 倍。那么，如果假设现在市场预期是正确的话，那到 2028 年，它的 EV（Enterprise Value）除以 Operating Income 估值是在 44 倍。看起来就没有那么的夸张。

3. 三大业务分部拆解

然后我们来看一下具体它三家业务或者三个业务。那这三个业务我之后再给大家做估值更新的时候，一定要把这三个业务分开去看，对吧。你如果不分开去看的话，就像我前面和大家看的，你一年的 operating income 才一个 billion，你合在一起去看的话，一个 T 的一个估值，你的估值是上天了的嘛。所以没办法这么去看，一定要把三个业务分开去看。

第一个业务：Space（火箭业务）

那市场预计，我这边看的是 26 年、27 年和 28 年整个我看的全年： - 27 年营收增速是 44%，还是比较的高，6.2 个 billion - 28 年营收增速将会放缓，到 7.2 个 billion - 从盈利这一个角度去看，基本上 27 年的话还没有盈利 - 到 28 年才开始出现盈利，Operating Income 27 年的时候是 2000 多万，然后到 28 年的时候是 0.2 个 billion，两亿美金左右

所以我们大致要有个概念：他 Space 这一块的业务，26 年不赚钱，27 年可能刚刚 break even，然后从 28 年开始进行赚钱。这是它第一块业务。

第二个业务：Connectivity / Starlink

然后第二块业务也是它最赚钱的这一块业务，叫做 Connectivity，就是和 Starlink 有关。那这一块的业务市场的预期其实非常的 bullish： - 整个 25 年你看下它的营收是 11 个 billion - 26 年同比增速 50%，来到 17 个 billion - 27 年继续增速 50%，来到 25 个 billion - 28 年增速在提速，增速 61%，来到 41 个 billion

那从它利润这一块，Starlink 是赚钱的： - 26 年的话 6.6 个 billion - 27 年几乎要翻倍，到 11.5 - 28 年几乎再翻一倍，20.2 个 billion

所以 Starlink 这一块的业务是非常的赚钱，而且增速非常的高。如果去按它利润上的这一个增速，26 年是 60%，然后到 27 年和 28 年都是在 70% 以上。这样的一个增速比 Palantir 的增速还要快。这是它第二块业务。

第三个业务：AI

第三块业务：AI。那 AI 这一块的业务也是不确定性最高的这一块业务。你看一下 25 年它的营收才多少？3.2 个 billion。市场预期 28 年到多少？84 个 billion。三年的时间要翻 20 多倍。

而实际上，如果我们听完财报会议的话，你会发现 28 年市场做的这一个预期，如果在财报会议里面老马说的是正确的话，28 年的这个营收非常有可能在 27 年就可以做到。

那我稍微给大家一个概念，就是 84 个 billion 的这个营收、22.3 个 billion 的这个 Operating Income 到底是什么样的一个概念：市场预期 SpaceX 将会在 28 年的时候能够做到，但其实 Oracle 在 27 财年（也就是他们下一个财年）马上就可以做到。市场现在预期 Oracle 27 财年营收正好是 90 个 billion，比 SpaceX 里边的 AI 稍微高一些，然后运营利润这一块 35.8 个 billion、36 个 billion 也比 SpaceX 稍微高一些。

所以这差不多给大家一个概念：27 财年 Oracle 在整个 AI 这一块、数据中心这一块的营收，包括它的利润，和 SpaceX AI 这一块现在市场的这个预期，差不多两年半之后会达到同样的水平。

另外一点我们也需要有一个概念：就现在市场预期 Oracle 他们在 29 年（也就是三年之后了），29 年它的营收将会达到 128 个 billion。就三年之后的营收体量大概有多少。那现在市场给 Oracle 多少的估值？差不多在 400 个 billion 稍微多一些吧。就你可以假设：OK，我三年之后的营收 182 个 billion，然后现在的估值是 400 个 billion，那你往未来去看，三年之后的一个 Price to Sales Ratio 多少？两倍左右。

4. 我的分部估值方法

那带着这样的一个概念，我们来对 SpaceX 的估值去做一个更新。我前面说过了，要把它的业务分开去看，拆成三个业务去看。

火箭业务 → 0.2T（200 billion）

第一个业务就前面说的火箭业务这一块。我给了他 0.2 个 T，就是 200 个 billion。我怎么去算？我是算现在市场里面另外……我们叫大火箭小火箭的那种，起码在社交面上大家喜欢怎么去称：大火箭就是 SpaceX，小火箭就是 Rocket Lab。Rocket Lab，我们如果去看营收的话，SpaceX 的营收差不多是 Rocket Lab 的四倍，但是增速的话其实比 Rocket Lab 要稍微慢一些。所以我现在按照 Rocket Lab 的一个市值 50 个 billion 去算的话，那你可以假设 Rocket Lab 现在是低估的或者高估的都可以，那我只是按照 Rocket Lab 这个估值去算：市值 50 个 billion，4 倍的这个营收，那 SpaceX 火箭业务这一块就是 200 个 billion，或者 0.2 个 T。

Starlink → 1.12T

第二块业务 Starlink。我如果按照它 2026 年上半年的这个运营利润去算的话，把它年化——运营利润上半年是 2.8 个 billion，年化之后是 5.6 个 billion。如果你去看过去 12 个月的话，会比这个数据还低一些，所以这一个算法本身相对是乐观一些的，并不是一个保守的一个算法。

5.6 个 billion，我给它按照 200 倍的这个估值去算。为什么给 200 倍？因为如果市场假设是正确的话，其实它未来的两年 Operating Income 的这个增速还是比较高的，每年平均如果在 70% 以上的话，就像我前面说的比 Palantir 的这个估值还要高。所以你给 200 倍的估值，你说贵吧，一定是贵，但是没有到非常的夸张，对吗？

再说的简单一点：就 200，如果真的是 200 倍的这个估值，然后你平均每年 EPS 的增速可以有 70% 的话，那你 PEG 是多少？PEG 就是 3 倍，好吗？但是还是一个比较慷慨的一个估值啊，200 倍的这个估值。你算下来就是 1.12 个 T。所以这是他们第二块业务。

AI → 0.2T

然后第三块业务就是 AI。那 AI 这一块，现在 SpaceX 他们拥有 1.4 GW 的这个算力。我按照 CoreWeave 现在只有一个算力，CoreWeave 一个算力对上 50 个 billion 的一个市值。那因为基本上 AI 这一块它就是卖算力的。老马在这次财报里边也聊了，因为他看到现在这个市场非常的好，所以会去布局很多数据中心这一块的建造，然后去卖算力这一块的业务。

那 1.4 GW 嘛，他这边是 CoreWeave 一个 GW 对标 50 个 billion 的市值，那 1.4 GW 就是对标 70 个 billion。再加上 Cursor 收购的价格是 60 个 billion，剩下乱七八糟的广告业务全部加在一起，凑一个整数吧，0.2 个 T 或者 200 个 billion。

那很多人说：哎，三年之后 AI 这一块的营收可以达到 80 个 billion 呢，你现在估值只给他 200 个 billion 是不是合理呢？其实一样。我前面为什么带大家看 Oracle 他们在三年之后的营收是多少，包括现在的估值是多少，那么未来三年之后 Price to Sales Ratio 两倍的这个估值呢，你就假设 OK，SpaceX 两三年之后也是 80 个 billion 的一个营收，那两倍的估值 160 个 billion，那你再加上 Cursor 的话就是 220 个 billion，你再加上乱七八糟的业务，可能就是 250 个 billion 左右。那么就是 200 至 250 个 billion，就取决于我们怎么去算。

那如果按照 0.2 个 T 的话，那全部加在一起就三个业务，那么全部加在一起总共是 1.52 个 T。

5. 结论：SpaceX 仍不便宜

就我说了，1.52 个 T 里边包括了给了 200 倍 Starlink 的这个估值。我给了，是因为它的增速比 Palantir 还高嘛，那如果能够做到的话，这个估值也没有非常的夸张了。

那 1.52 个 T 市值啊，对应的就是 113 块钱的这个价格。所以我现在认为——而且我这边是给了一些比较乐观的假设嘛——所以我认为现在的 SpaceX 仍然是不便宜的。

那而且接下去会有非常大的一些解禁。几乎我能够接触到的一些一级市场的投资者，SpaceX 的投资者没有一个不等着解禁之后卖出的。所以接下去 SpaceX 这一块的抛压，我仍然认为会非常非常的强。那所以我的看法是：等解禁全部结束之后，市场找到这个共识、找到这个估值上的一个共识，或者说等 90 以下才开始去考虑 SpaceX 这个股票本身、这家公司本身有没有投资的这个价值，有没有性价比在这边。

完了，最后我想提醒一下的是，估值本身它只是一个模糊正确的，所以没有必要和我去争我是对的还是错的。我只是给大家分享方法本身，包括我自己主观的看法。

6. 财报会议：老马的宏大叙事 vs. 华尔街预期

最后我们聊一下财报会议。如果去听财报会议的话，你会发现前面我们分享的华尔街的一些数据，基本是狗屎了，就是老马所分享的这些数据远远是高于华尔街现在所做的这些预期。但它到底能不能做到呢？不一定。

关于 15GW 数据中心

那么，首先，老马说到他在 27 年之前，他要上线 15 GW 的这个数据中心。15 GW 什么概念？非常非常……体量非常夸张。你不算 GPU，如果你算上 GPU 的话，现在一个 GW 100 个 billion。你算上 GPU 的话，15 个 GW 起码在 1.3 个 T 到 1.5 个 T。也就是说，你一家 SpaceX 在资本开支上的这个花费，抵上了整个全部市场全部加在一起——现在全部市场加在一起才 0.7 个 T。在 0.7T，他一个人要建 15 个 GW。他又说 20 个 GW，他说 20 个 GW 假设其中 1/4 是会被延后的，所以我们就按 15 个 GW 去算。

即使是 15 个 GW 也是非常非常的夸张。我觉得是做不到的。也没有那么大、也没有那么多的钱。如果说 SpaceX 真的要这么去做的话，接下去的融资体量会非常非常的大，他们没有这个现金流去支撑，好吗？

然后行业里边的一些调研机构，比如说方德 AI，最近他们的观点也被 Gavin Baker 所引用了。方德 AI 认为 SpaceX 从今年到 27 年底能够上线 8 个 GW 的算力。如果真能够上线 8 个 GW 的这个算力的话，那他们上线算力的这个速度其实也已经超过了这些 HyperScale——比 HyperScale 都要快了。好吧，所以老马在财报会里面所讲的这些数据，我认为是有待验证的，我这边打一个非常大的一个问号。

因为首先你现在建数据中心的话，最难的点是什么？你本身大多数的成本来自于哪里？来自于 GPU 和 memory 的这个价格。第二点就是你的电到底哪里来？没有那么容易去拿到这个电。

看好 SpaceX = 看好英伟达

然后我们继续看下去。第二点，就如果说我们看好 SpaceX 的话，你必须要看好英伟达。为什么？是因为老马接下去他所要建的这些数据中心全部是和英伟达去合作，起码现在他表达的是全部是和英伟达去合作。并且他说到期待明年英伟达有很大一部分的 GPU 会安排给 SpaceX。

1000 亿美金 ARR 到底可不可能？

第三点，老马说到认为今年年底 ARR 的营收就可以达到 1000 亿美金、100 个 billion。我去算了一下 1000 亿美金，而且他在财报会议里面特别强，他说我们什么事情都不用干，就可以达到 1000 亿美金 ARR。我还是打上一个问号。因为我去算了一笔账：

  • 1000 亿美金的话，代表一个季度的营收达到 25 个 billion，年化就是 1000 亿美金
  • 谷歌：差不多从 10 月份开始每一个月给他们一个 billion，那四季度谷歌可以贡献 3 个 billion 的营收
  • Anthropic：差不多一个季度给 1.25 个 billion，四季度贡献 4 个 billion；再加上最近新签的这个订单——6.7 个 billion 的订单，10 月份开始持续 6 个月，那四季度总共还可以贡献 3 个 billion
  • Cursor：因为现在 6 月份 Cursor 的 ARR 是在 2 个 billion，我假设 Cursor 到年底的 ARR 是 12 个 billion，那就是 12 月份单单一个月的营收就是一个 billion，我把它乘以 3，也就是四季度会贡献 3 个 billion
  • 这些东西全部加在一起 13 个 billion
  • 再加上 Connectivity / Starlink 这一块 5.4 个 billion，Space 这一块 1.5 个 billion
  • 全部加在一起也只有 20 个 billion

和老马所说的 25 个 billion 还差了 50 亿美金，我不知道哪里可以获得。

回报周期 <1 年的疑问

最后另外一点，老马提到了，就包括他们的 CFO 也有提到，他说现在他们整个数据中心的一个回报周期是多少？小于一年。小于一年。

然后你会发现，如果大家有仔细去听的话，在亚马逊的财报里边，Andy 有说到——安迪，亚马逊它的一个回报周期是两到三年，基本上通常是三年，那但是他们可以做到小于三年。但是这边 SpaceX 却告诉我们，他们的回报周期是一年。

为什么会出现这种情况？那这就是取决于你签的这个订单到底是长期订单还是短期订单。长期的这个订单，首先你订单的时间会长，那你的价格一定会低。那这就是现在在租算力的时候，租算力有一个长租价格和一个短租价格。短租价格叫做 On Demand。所以短时间之内，如果市场对于算力的这个需求非常的高，短租的这个价格就会非常的贵。

这也是为什么我们看到了谷歌和 OpenAI 都向 SpaceX 去购买这个算力，然后我们看到了 SpaceX 开始出租这个算力，然后我们看到了 Meta 开始去卖自己的这个算力。之所以他们会选择去卖自己的这个算力，就是因为短期的这个回报 ROI 非常非常的高。

但是像老马这样，如果说我要建 15 个 GW 的数据中心，然后我的期待是每一次的回报都是在一年以内的话，都是非常非常不合理的。为什么？你要建那么大的这个数据中心，不可能所有的数据中心几个 GW 的、10 个 GW 的数据中心全部是用于短租，你不可能这么去做。因为短租的这个价格波动非常的高、非常的大。

两点结论

所以 SpaceX 大举进军 AI 市场或者算力市场，其实是对于 NeoCloud 整个运营模式的一个验证，这是第一点。第二点绝对利好英伟达，因为他们现在 exclusive 这个合作伙伴就是英伟达。

二、AMD 财报解读

1. 财报"没有惊喜"是常态

OK，然后我们来聊一下 AMD 的财报。那首先 AMD 的财报和我昨天视频里面聊的一样：他们财报出来，每一次的财报结果出来，你都很难会发现他们超出市场预期非常的多。

我这边举了他们过去 8 个季度财报出来之后 EPS 好于市场预期的这个幅度。我们可以看到，只有一个季度——2025 年的第四季度超出市场预期 15.62%——其他所有的季度几乎都和市场的预期一样，其中有一个季度还比市场预期稍微低了那么一些。就基本上每一次华尔街的这个摸底，或者说 AMD 给予下一个季度这个指引，都非常的准确，完全不给自己留任何的空间在那边。

所以 AMD 有这样的一个历史。这也是为什么在昨天的视频里面，我会给大家聊到：就你不会发现 AMD 的财报出来之后会给你有非常大的这个冲击，不会的。因为他们历史上的财报出来这个结果就是这样，好吗？

2. 财报会议要点

然后我们来看一下财报会议。那基本面我不用太多聊，AMD 的基本面还是非常的好。

要点 1：27 年服务器 CPU 增速 70%

财报会议里边，27 年服务器 CPU 增速 70%，速度非常的快。那这一块的服务器的一个 CPU，你也可以理解为接下去 27 年英特尔的一个增速。那么我在上一次分析英特尔估值的时候，我说你得把英特尔的 product 和他们的方矩这一块分开去看。product 这一块我假设 27 年是多少？我给了 50% 的这个假设。

很多人问我：你凭什么能够给 50%？如果营收增速在 70%，你的 bottom line、你的 EPS 增速那绝对不止 70%。那如果你有一个运营效率在那边的话——而当时我只给了 50% 的这个增速。所以你会发现，而当时我在下面我说其实我给的这一个预期已经非常的保守了，好吧。

要点 2：GPU 总增速 100%+，一个 GW ≈ 15B 营收

所以 CPU 的这个增速 70%，然后总增速是 100%。为什么？因为他们 GPU 的这一块的增速会非常的快。那主要 GPU 这一块的客户——MI 系列嘛——GPU 这个客户来自于哪里？OpenAI、Meta 和 Anthropic。

那当时分析师问的一个问题是：一个 GW 是不是代表对你来说是 15 个 billion 的营收？然后你们 27 年可以卖 3 个 GW 的这个芯片？这是一个概念性的一个问题，就你起码和"一个 GW 约等于多少营收"可以去画上这个等号。这是第一点。

要点 3：HBM 涨价压力与产品重设计

第二点，分析师有问到，他说你们 GPU 里边 HBM 比你们的这一个竞争者（谁？英伟达嘛）多用了 50%，那你们怎么去管理这一个毛利？因为他们在卖芯片的时候，他们的芯片本身和 HBM 是捆绑在一起去卖的。那如果 HBM memory 这一块的涨价，涨完价之后对你来说是直接的这个成本的一个上涨。而你成本的这个上涨，你是不可能在这个成本上面再去加这个溢价的，不可能的。你就只能把 HBM 的这个成本完全转移到消费者身上。但是你统一的价格绑定在一起，将会因为 HBM 的这个涨价，将会使得一个毛利润出现下降。

所以这个问题问得非常的好。那 Su 妈有聊到，她说我们可以对自己的产品去做出这个调整。如果说模型本身不需要那么多的 HBM，我们可以去减。其实是类似于现在市场里面所聊到的下一代英伟达这个产品——Rubin 有可能会把 HBM 的这一个数量给往下降一半。也就是因为现在市场里边 HBM memory 这一块的一个短缺，从产品端这一块，英伟达和 AMD 正在做一个产品上的一个优化，为了去应对不同的场景，你使用不同的产品，那而这不同的产品对应的是不同数量的 HBM。这是第二点。

要点 4 & 5：CPU 量价齐涨 + GPU 27 年增速远超 100%

第三点，CPU 27 年将会出现一个量价齐涨，就是出货量也会上升，然后价格也会上涨。然后第四点，GPU 在 27 年的这个增速将会远超 100%。

要点 6：EPS 指引"significantly 高于 20 美金"

最后一点，其实在他们上一次这个投资者大会里面有给过这一个指引——他们给出了未来三年之内他们 EPS 的这个体量可以达到 20 美元，就每股收益可以达到 20 美元。然后在这一次财报会里边 CFO 有聊到，这个数据将会 significantly 远远高于 20 美元。那我的一个假设就是 25 美元每股收益。

3. AMD 估值测算

那我们先把这 25 美元放在身后，我们先不聊这个数据，因为这个 25 美元呢是非常的重要，大家先记在那边。

这一个季度数据出来之后，看一下总共过去四个季度（Trailing Twelve Months）静态的一个 EPS 是多少？5.76。一年赚了 5.76。按照盘后的这个价格 472÷5.76，得出来静态市盈率是在 82 倍。

那你看，现在原本在发这一季度财报之前是多少？113 倍。因为这个季度数量体量非常的高，144，同比增速要超多少？246。那所以他们一下子 PE 静态的市盈率的 PE 就从 113 跌到了 82。这就是当财报的增速非常高的时候，你 PE 下降的速度也会非常的快。那所以直接从 113 倍降到了 82 倍。

那未来三年 EPS 这个增速——假设你看现在 78、86 和 37——我假设它平均 60% 的话，那你 82 倍的一个静态市盈率对应的就是 1.4 至 1.5 倍的一个 PEG。那讲到这边 1.4 至 1.5 的话，贵吗？其实不贵。我认为就是在处在一个非常合理的一个阶段，甚至于你可以说它是相对便宜的。

这是我在根据市场预期的这种情况下所得出的这个结论和结果。然后我们回到前面管理层所给的这个指引：25 美金，就 25 美金的一个每股收益。现在市场预期 28 年 EPS 是多少？19 美金。而管理层给的这个指引是在三年之内能够达到 25 美金。那如果我把 25 美金给带进去的话，带入现在 472 块钱的这个价格，得出来 28 年它的 forward P 是多少？19 倍。那现在市场预期是多少？27.34 倍。

也就是说，现在如果管理层给的这个指引完全能够做到——当然他们只给了 20 块钱，那他们给了高于 20 块钱、远远高于 20 块钱，假设 25 块钱——他们如果能够做到的话，28 年的 forward P 19 倍。那这样看起来贵不贵？其实 AMD 现在一点都不贵。

4. 但英伟达更便宜——市场估值语法的错位

但是，对吧，没有对比没有伤害。我们来看一下英伟达的估值。根据现在市场的这个预期，且不算英伟达能够做得比市场还要好，英伟达的预期： - 28 财年（两年不到之后）能够做到多少？16.4 倍 - 这个 forward P 远远低于 AMD 的这个 forward P - 29 年差不多三年之后的话是多少？13 倍，非常的低

再来看一家公司 Broadcom 博通： - 27 年一年半之后是多少？21.7 倍，明显比英伟达要高 - 28 年的话是多少？16 倍

那博通和英伟达，它的增速也都非常的高。所以其实如果我们把这三家公司放在一起去看的话，我们可以得出一个结论：现在市场其实对于纯 GPU 这类的公司，像英伟达这类的公司，给了一个非常低的这个估值。而相反，对于未来在 ASIC 这一块、定制 ASIC 这一块，包括 CPU 这一块，都给了一个相对比较高的这个估值。 为什么？是因为现在市场给了 Inference（推理）这一块的一些公司——就只要和推理相关的一些公司——给了一个估值上的一个溢价。

5. 综合结论

所以听完 AMD 的财报之后，我认为 AMD 的估值非常的合理，且 AMD 的估值是便宜的。

然后你听完 SpaceX 的一个财报之后，如果你看好 SpaceX 接下去在数据中心这一块建造非常大的体量的话，你应该是看好英伟达，因为英伟达接下去将会非常获益于 SpaceX 数据中心这一块的上线。

那最终可能很多人会问我，他说："Topc，那我到底应该是去买英伟达，还是应该去买 AMD？" 我觉得这是见仁见智的，就取决于你：

  • 从估值本身去看：英伟达绝对是便宜的，比 AMD 的话还便宜
  • 从故事线这个角度去看：似乎英伟达现在缺少了一个故事线，就是你缺少了一个现在市场聊的比较多的 Inference 这一块、推理这一块，CPU 这一块或者定制 ASIC 这一块

两家公司都是好公司，基本面也都非常的好，估值来说都便宜的。你从一个绝对的 risk reward 这个角度去看，两家公司都可以去布局。你从一个相对的 risk reward 两家公司去做对比的话，英伟达会比 AMD 要稍微好一些，因为毕竟相对便宜些嘛。而如果我们从故事线的这个角度去看，AMD 的这个故事线会比英伟达暂时来说会比英伟达要稍微好一些，好吧。

结尾：活动信息

那最后是今天的活动。富途牛牛美国市场这边，开户且入金，最高可以获得价值 1000 美金英伟达的赠股和闲置资金最高年化 8.1% 的回报。加拿大这边现在有一个我们这个频道的独家福利，通过开户且入金，最高可以获得 100 只免费股票的一个抽取，直接抽到手软，闲置资金最高年化 6% 的这个回报，和前 30 天零佣金交易。那大家感兴趣的话，可以在置顶的留言里面找到开户的链接。

那今天这期内容就到这边，我们下期见。

## 一、被忽略的"估值锚点漂移"：市场正在悄悄重写 AI 公司的估值语法
小涛这期最反常识的一点埋在他对比 Oracle、Broadcom、英伟达、AMD 时的一句话里——**"现在市场对纯 GPU 公司给了非常低的估值，而对 CPU、ASIC、Inference 相关公司给了溢价"**。
这其实是一次**估值语法的静默政变**。过去两年市场用"训练算力增速"给英伟达定价，但当英伟达 29 财年 forward P/E 只有 13 倍、而博通 28 财年还有 16 倍时，市场实际上已经**把英伟达重新分类为"周期性硬件"，而把 ASIC 玩家重新分类为"软件式复利资产"**。
这里有一个跨领域的类比：这跟 2010 年代智能手机产业链的估值迁移一模一样——最初市场给高通（芯片王者）最高估值，但当 iPhone 生态成型后，估值溢价迁移到了做"定制化最后一公里"的博通、Skyworks、村田身上。**GPU 正在经历它的"高通时刻"**：越通用、越强大，反而越像"电力公司"而不是"AI 公司"。

item.title: [Bits + Bips] Coldcard's Firmware Flaw Let Hackers Steal $100 Million. Is Your Cold Storage Safe?
item.dc:creator: Bits + Bips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：Cold Card 事件与 Leopold 爆仓，其实是同一种"熵坍缩"

表面上，一个是硬件钱包的密码学漏洞，一个是 24 岁天才的 AI 基金爆仓，风马牛不相及。但把两者叠在一张图上，会发现它们共享同一个致命机制——"熵源退化"。

Cold Card 的 bug 是：本应流经真随机数发生器的密钥生成，因为一根"线接错了"，静默地退回到低熵源，于是数十亿种可能坍缩成攻击者可暴力枚举的空间。Leopold 的组合是：本应分散在多个不相关因子上的风险，因为都押在 AI 叙事这一个"变量"上，同样静默地退回到单一熵源——一个 Micron 财报的坏消息就足以让整个组合坍缩。

真正的教训不是"要用好钱包"或"要做风控"，而是：任何声称"我很随机 / 我很分散"的系统，都要问一句——你的熵到底从哪里来？谁在审计这个熵源？ 五年没人发现 Cold Card 的问题，因为大家假设"它当然是随机的"；LPs 五个月里给 Leopold 加杠杆，因为大家假设"这些股票当然是不同的赌注"。假设，就是熵的敌人。

二、跨领域连接：Ken Griffin 是 21 世纪的"最后贷款人"，而这重塑了金融的物理学

节目里 Rahm 顺口讲了一件被低估的事：1998 年 LTCM 爆掉时，是纽约联储把投行召集起来"传帽子"接盘；2026 年 Leopold 爆掉时，接盘的电话直接打给了 Citadel、Jane Street 和 Millennium。

这不是"华尔街换了个门牌"，这是最后贷款人角色的私有化。在物理学上，这类似于把一个由政府维持的公共"引力场"，替换成了几个由私人做市商维持的"局部势能井"。后果是深远的：

  • 危机不再走"银行 → 央行 → 财政"这条监管链，而是走"基金 → 私人做市商 → 市场"这条不透明的链。
  • 信息不对称被制度化：Citadel 不仅是接盘者，还是做市商、还是数据的第一手观察者。它在几乎无摩擦地把危机转化为利润。
  • 反脆弱性集中化：整个市场的抗震能力，正在寄生于三四家私人机构的资产负债表和风险胃口。

有意思的联想：这跟 Cold Card 事件里"self-custody 的信任最终又流回 Coinbase / Fidelity"是同一种拓扑塌陷——去中心化的理想在压力下会自发收敛到少数节点，因为"可以起诉的对手"本身就是一种流动性。Austin 引用的那句话堪称本集金句："I want a throat to choke."——机构不是在买托管服务，是在买"可诉性"这种衍生品。

三、隐藏的系统真相：AI 安全的"防御-进攻不对称"，正被美国自己的护栏放大

这一段最值得停下来的信号是 Alex 的一句抱怨：负责审计 Bitcoin 硬件钱包代码库的美国红队工程师，不得不使用中国开源模型 Kimi 和 GLM，因为 Claude、GPT 的安全护栏会拒绝这类"看起来像攻击"的任务。

这里面藏着一个反常识但很严重的系统性事实：

当前 AI 安全策略在无意间创造了一个"防御者征税、进攻者免税"的市场结构。

  • 攻击者本来就在灰色地带，用越狱模型、开源模型、自训模型毫无心理负担。
  • 防御者反而被合规、TOS、护栏三重征税，甚至连"分析自己本地数据库"都要被 refuse。
  • 结果：护栏越强，边际上受影响最大的是善意使用者，而不是恶意使用者。

跨领域连接一下：这跟 1990 年代美国的加密出口管制（Crypto Wars）几乎是同一个错误的第二季。当时限制强加密出口，结果是全世界的加密标准反而绕开美国发展，最终美国不得不放开。今天限制 frontier 模型的攻防用途，很可能重演——中国开源模型正在成为全球网络安全的默认工具链，这不是意识形态问题，是纯粹的可用性梯度决定的。

再往深走一层：Cold Card 的漏洞五年没被发现，可能不是因为没人有能力，而是因为有能力的人被护栏拦在门外。 如果这个假设成立，那么"AI 安全护栏"本身就正在成为一种系统性金融风险来源——一个几乎没有人在讨论的、隐藏在合规叙事之下的负外部性。

一个留给你思考的问题：如果熵源退化（观察一）、最后贷款人私有化（观察二）、防御者被护栏征税（观察三）都是同一个更大结构的三个切面——那这个结构是什么？我的猜测是："信任的重新集中化"正在以三种伪装出现——技术假象里的分散、监管缺席下的私人兜底、合规叙事下的能力垄断。 这三条线，可能在未来 5 年会汇合成一次我们尚未命名的危机。

They likely are dormant for a while in general because again, these are long-term holders. They're fully swept. They're swept with a fee that typically most of these patterns um have dramatically exceeded the medium fee rate, right? Attackers, they'll overpay for fees to get the coins and they have other transaction fingerprints. I saw all of that at the chain tip last night. Um, and in the mempool, and that's why I flagged that. You know, there definitely are some false positives in there. Um, we need some victim reports to really help us confirm.

其他"footprints"与整体规模

The last thing I'll say, which I haven't yet really reported, but I will um on X sometime tonight — there are like 14 other identifiable patterns that we have found that do not appear related to any of those waves, but do have verifiable victims identified because victims have come forth and then I've looked at the patterns and behavior of their attackers and found several others or at least one other, right? So more than one instance. You know, those are literally footprints A through L that I'm calling them at the moment. I think N actually now — those have crept up the count. While we may not be able to yet extrapolate like a giant amount to each of them, they are confirmed victims.

And so um you know, we've been saying I think the last numbers we put out were near 1,400 Bitcoin yesterday at the end of wave three. If you add the amount, um, you know, we're saying maybe two or three, I think three or four hundred in wave four, but I'm not adding that yet. I really do need confirmation. And I encourage victims to DM me on X. I've been diligently helping people for several days now, not just cataloging it for us, but providing back basically wholesome Chainalysis-style reports that they can use to report uh to authorities.

Um, but I have it now at, you know, if we include wave four, we're almost at 2,000 Bitcoin. So, we're well over a hundred million dollars of self-custodied Bitcoin. Um, even without wave four, we're over $100 million. I would place it more in the 1,600 BTC range. Again, for a distributed self custody storage hack, that's unprecedented as far as I'm aware. Um, quite devastating.

信任与量子先兆

Chris: That's awful. Um, the thing that jumps out at me is that, you know, we operate in this trustless, permissionless environment. And the problem was is that as as trustless and permissionless as you try to be, you have to have trust somewhere. And they trusted Cold Card to do the right thing. And that's where everything broke down. And so, it's really, really hard.

Um, hopefully, you know, there's some good things that come out of this, which you hate to even emphasize right now because it's so terrible. But you know, Alex, you're very much in the Bitcoin world. If a high level of compute allowed people to derive seed phrases, to me, this is a precursor to what Quantum could do, not only in Bitcoin, but across, you know, all of financial services and beyond. So maybe this is a wakeup call um you know for the community to really focus on these high compute threats. Um, you agree with that?

Alex: Um, I do. Of course the threats are a little different. Um, yeah, but you know, they're not really that different, right? I mean, if you had substantially, you know, um industry standard entropy, you're not affected here, but you could be, you know, because the world's GPUs combined probably couldn't break it. But that, you know, you're talking about multiple step function increases in the case of quantum. They might be able to derive uh seeds across that whole space. That's the fear.

Um, I think this — you could call it a trial run perhaps if quantum does emerge. It wouldn't look that different, right? Because the attacker — this is one thing that's going to be tough with the recovery if it can happen.

受害者如何证明所有权？

Austin: How does the victim prove their ownership, right? Like —

Alex: Um, the attackers have their keys, right? So it can't be solely via cryptographic proof. Um, that's why we're encouraging people to make um you know wholesome formal victim response filings and reports to FBI's IC3, their local police, to establish their victimhood and keep the Cold Card device. Don't use it necessarily. Don't use it, but keep it because it could be evidence that shows that you actually were the one that first had the keys.

AI 红队 vs 美国护栏

Um, you know, I think another point worth raising is that it's not just the cryptography or the generation of the keys that's an issue. Um, AI is of course across other domains as well are finding substantial codebase issues all over the world right now. There's a red team uh of Bitcoin security engineers working as we speak and for days um unfortunately forced to use like Kimi and GLM and not Frontier US models which won't allow this type of cyber work — um literally going over every hardware wallet codebase, every open-source library that's used in crypto and in Bitcoin fulsomely to try to uh patch and you know fight back against what is becoming an increasingly dangerous threat environment. Um, that work is ongoing.

I think you may also see that some of the coins that I've labeled as stolen may end up having actually been rescued in a white hat effort. Um, again because the vulnerability is so well known uh at least since Thursday and there are quite a lot of people with compute these days at their fingertips. Um, I hope that's the case. It's going to be messy.

对自托管叙事的伤害

Um, but you know, I think the other one last part here, Chris, sort of goes to your question is like — but I know the whole group here has probably thought about this. Um, and I will say that red team has looked at the codebases for all the other major hardware wallets. None of them have this vulnerability. It doesn't mean, you know, I can't tell you they're all 100% safe, but they are not affected here.

Um, the damage to self-custody though — because these are some of the most principled self-custody coiners. Um, you know, they chose Cold Card — some of them chose Cold Card over Ledger or Trezor because those two support altcoins and they don't want those.

I think one thing to know about is that Cold Card ultimately was relatively niche hardware and firmware. And if you're building cool niche hardware, like you better be using widely adopted open-source software for the firmware. I think that this is where the bug was introduced — was when Coinkite basically rejected some of the open-source software and started building their own.

So I think this can damage the narrative at a minimum for self-custody uh for at least you know among the most ardent people, um, and push more into ETFs and on exchanges. You know, you've seen one of the largest flows of you know off-exchange bitcoin back into exchange — uh, I saw 22,000 Bitcoin uh Sani from Time Chain Index uh posted since Friday, and CryptoQuant said the largest influx of sub-1 BTC transfers into exchange over I don't know how many years, right? People are fleeing. It's the opposite of FTX. They're fleeing from self-custody into exchange. Um, so that's going to have repercussions over the long term as well.

AI 是长期利好安全吗？

Chris: Yeah, I even saw Muneeb, founder of Stacks, talking about, "hey, diversify your custody. You go into ETFs." It feels to me like we're in this max period of AI threat, but I don't know about you guys, I think AI over the medium term is going to be actually very very good for security once we get through this little hump because once these vulnerabilities are solved, they're solved.

And I feel like, you know, I was watching Face the Nation today — like big political show obviously — and they had the the founder of Hugging Face on and he made this point, you know, despite the fact that that rogue agent started going nuts, he's like, "AI is going to be the biggest asset for DeFi long term. We just got to get over this hump" is my take.

防御者 vs 攻击者：AI 到底站在谁那边？

Austin: So, let me ask — I know Alex you have some views on this. I suspect Rahm will have some views on this as well. In the current state of AI, is it being more or less helpful for attackers versus defenders? Because one thing I've been observing and had a few people talking to me about today is ironically some of the guardrail training on some of the US LLMs are actually frustrating the efforts of defenders in this case. Alex, what can you see in there?

Alex: That's absolutely right. Right. I can tell you the red teams that are literally objectively evaluating these codebases — they're not trying to create exploits, right? But they're doing, you know, I understand how uh, you know, an objective robot, uh, clanker mind might think that it is. Like, I get that.

They're all using Kimi and GLM, literally open-source Chinese models. The frontier models are not available to them. Even when I traverse my own Bitcoin analytics stack, I'm not going out onto the web, right? I have a 3.7 billion row 1.7 terabyte Postgres database of every coin's movement in the history of Bitcoin, every change to the entire state, and I ask you know Claude Fable 5 to go and you know pull some data for me — half the time I get cyber-safeguarded, right? Just to look at my own data on my local machine, right?

So um, and this is to your point about the Hugging Face CEO — is exactly the same thing that they faced when the OpenAI lab leak happened. So I don't have a great policy answer to this at the moment. I just know that on its face it's absurd that American, you know, companies and victims are having to rely on Chinese AI models. That's insane.

Chris: Yes. Well, just on your policy point, I think the line between defender and attacker needs to change as well. Like I've been pushing this for how many years now? We need to go on offense. And the thing about clarity, which is making me crazy right now, is that there is a Rewards for Justice program. Finally, we can permission white hackers to go on an attack. Going back to the early days of our constitution and privateering, you know, we have to have a much better policy response.

Like people cannot — this is illegal. This is like no different than someone going to your house and stealing your car or robbing your house. And like just because it's crypto doesn't make it any better. So we do need a much better policy response across the board.

Rahm：技术史上，进攻永远占优

Rahm: I like — Austin, the way you posed that question is super interesting. Like, does technology favor the attack or the defense? Most of the history of technology is that it favors the attacker. You know, you've seen this with Stuxnet and Neuron. You've seen this with the development of uh, you know, aircraft. Um, so many forms of technology favored the attacker. The defense that you have to cover is simply too broad. The fact that the United States has two oceans on both sides has been an incredible benefit. There's just too much to protect and defend and insulate and inoculate. So, it goes towards the offense.

Um, it is a shame that we don't have an open-source American model yet. You know, China's got several and they're impressive and the VCs don't want to fund an American open-source model, which I also can't blame them. I can't blame them for that. Where's the value capture around open source?

Austin: I mean, this is one of those — what's the right way to say — this is a public-private coordination problem. Open-source models are in many ways like a public good, a little bit like a park. Everybody benefits from them, but nobody individually has much incentive to fund one unless it's purely charitable giving.

I think China having to play from behind on the hardware and original development front took a very different approach here because now you're playing like a call it multipolar competitive threat game which is very different than just looking inward and figuring out what you'd fund. I feel like an open-weight model is the sort of thing the government should be looking at. You know, Department of Defense — this seems like a pretty mainstream DARPA sort of thing. There are definitely levers that we could have to pull, but we are just not doing it in the United States. And like even today, as I wanted to get up to speed just to have this discussion with Alex for our segment, Claude is guardrailing me and I end up using Qwen. What does that really say? Like I'm an American citizen here, guys, right? Is this not the circularity?

自托管的未来 vs 机构托管的口碑

So, Alex, I want to come all the way back around to a point you made at the start because for me, this is probably the hardest part of where this goes. And I'm curious about everybody's views here.

I don't have a good answer on the self-custody thing right now. Like, if my mother, if my father, if my friends are asking me — what does this mean, how could I have protected myself? My answer is: I don't have an answer for you. And I think demonstrably, especially after this hack — I agree with your commentary on Eric talking about tokenized stocks — but as of yet, the track record of things in MPC institutional custody at regulated places is significantly better than self-custody funds. So, what does that say going forward for Bitcoin with where we are?

Alex: Uh, yeah, I mean most of the time that people uh lose self-custodied funds, it's because of phishing attacks on them or their own mistakes. And I do think, you know, there's that old, you know, "would you have your grandma use a hardware wallet or just tell her to open a Coinbase account?" I think most people really truly would have them open the Coinbase account, uh for, you know, or get the Bit Key, which I've actually — I think was the first hardware wallet I ever even considered suggesting to like, you know, older family members.

I will say that multi-sig collaborative custody in Bitcoin — like provided by Casa, Unchained, Nunchuk, Liana Wallet, AnchorWatch, others — uh remains incredibly secure and there is support uh to help you use it. Um, you know, because it diversifies among many hardware wallets. Not really that complicated. Still probably too complicated for grandma.

Um, but I think, you know, so it is possible. It still is possible. I'm, you know, I'm like, uh, Jordan Belfort — like we're not effing leaving yet from the self-custody trade. I know I'm not. Um, but it is very problematic and I think, you know, you've already seen an enormous amount of coins flow into the ETFs and, you know, let alone MSTR and people getting exposure through centralized means.

And that's fine. You know, I think there's been a wing of the Bitcoin community that has, you know, looked down upon those people like with a purist mindset as if they're not, you know, true Bitcoiners. And, you know, they might not be as much a Bitcoiner as you if you're rolling a hundred dice to introduce your own entropy into your Cold Card, you know, MK5. Um, but that's okay. That is okay. You know, this is your money. If you don't feel strong that you have the uh education and training to do self-custody, um don't and don't feel bad about that.

I think it's totally fine. You know, I use River.com all the time as a Bitcoin uh exchange. It's a great Bitcoin brokerage. Um, I've got accounts at most of the big exchanges and custodians. I bought and held Bitcoin at Fidelity Digital Assets. You know, I own ETFs, right? So, like, all of that is fine.

I think in the near and medium term you absolutely are going to continue to see uh people move towards those, and I agree. Look, they have a checkered history — crypto exchanges — of catastrophic failure. Um, but again, it's sort of like the nuclear uh power plant thing. You know, was Chernobyl a nuclear power plant thing or was that Soviet mismanagement? Was FTX fundamentally like a crypto exchange thing or was that a criminal named Sam Bankman-Fried? Right. I do think with strong regulation and oversight and industry standards, centralized intermediaries can be very safe and are demonstrably very safe.

监管过的中介 vs 无中介理想

Rahm: I have to pile in on the regulated front — the one area where FTX had a truly regulated subsidiary, which is FTX Japan, they didn't lose any money, right?

Chris: US2 or LedgerX. Do you name any US?

Rahm: Yeah, LedgerX. That's a great call. And by the way, on the ETF front, like Chris, I'm just shooting from the hip here, but EZBC, do you know anything about that thing? But I was going to make the point — like, have you lost any Bitcoin to this hack?

Chris: Personally, no.

Rahm: No. Well, no. Franklin, right? Like, no. No. No. So, like I think the point is, and I think Eric Balchunas has made it, um, look, we've said this over and over again, um, you shouldn't be forced to use an intermediary. I think we all agree on that.

Alex: Yes.

Chris: But I think we also agree that intermediaries do deliver certain value and there's going to continue to be a desire to use intermediaries by certain parts — probably the preponderance of the population — because you get value added services. Um, and so like you know DeFi maxis can be DeFi maxis but remember, like, what did we learn? You're still placing trust in something or somebody even if you're trying to be, you know, self-custody. You're trusting that software. You're trusting that provider. You know, I tend to hope that Alex is right and these MPC players are secure, but you're trusting them.

So, um, you know, you have to choose at the end of the day: who do you want to trust? Do you want to trust an intermediary that's well capitalized? Do you want to choose an intermediary that's insured or not? And I think we all agree on this, you know, because we've been in this space for so long — the government shouldn't tell you what to do. You should make that choice and it should be an informed choice.

多重签名与信任分层

Alex: Yeah, I totally agree. And it's not just like the random number generator in this hardware wallet. Like you are trusting — making different trust assumptions depending on how and where you store your coins, right? Like it's true that at a centralized intermediary, they could have a catastrophic failure. It's also true that even if the random number generation and key generation in a hardware wallet's great, they could have a different error, right?

So, I mean, this is one reason why — if you — one reason why me personally, I'm not in the business of recommending uh ways to store Bitcoin, but um I like the multi-sig collaborative custody where I hold some keys, a vendor that I pay uh holds some other keys and that gives me some peace of mind. I can lose a key or two of mine or they can go away and I can restore — they can't. Right? To me, and by the way this is I think as we know, this uh fundamentally is the way that regulated custodians basically also store, which is with multi-distributed multi-sig setups. Um, that they — those are available to individuals — they still may be too difficult for you, and that's okay.

机构心态：想要"一个可以起诉的人"

Rahm: Yeah, last point if I just make one more point. So we're in this institutional age of crypto. And when you unpack the institutional mindset, it really comes down to one thing. I want a throat to choke. I want to be able to sue somebody. That's what they'll tell you over and over again. "I don't care. Like I need somebody who's capitalized that I can sue." And I think there's value in that for many institutions. Um, so that's my last point about this segment.

Austin: Yeah. There are not institutions that are single-sig Cold Card. Well, that is not a thing. We hope.

Alex: And very few — I would say Fidelity and Coinbase I think are the — and maybe uh I guess Bitco doesn't have an ETF. Fidelity and Coinbase I think are the only two ETF uh — because well, Coinbase doesn't have one either.

Austin: Gemini —

Alex: Well, they don't have an ETF though. I guess Fidelity is I think maybe the only ETF that is self-custodying, but of course they themselves are an institutional custodian using all the sort of same principles as Coin. So most are — and I think at this point many if not most of the major Bitcoin ETFs in the US are using multiple custodians um for this reason again. So everyone's sort of making that same point.

And I think you know again, we — I typically do not go to you know defined contribution or defined benefit plans or high-net-worth individuals or liquid funds or family offices and suggest even that they self custody coins. Right? We're all suggesting qualified institutional custodians.

Austin：多元化是唯一的免费午餐

Austin: So another point that I would like to make here — because I've given this advice to my students actually about US regular way bank accounts — is the only free lunch in finance is diversification. And what I mean by that is always have multiply redundant options. Don't leave your stuff in one place because things that have nothing to do with you can break your [ __ ] if you do that.

If you only have one bank account and your bank goes bankrupt or something gets hacked or there's some sort of fraud that you had nothing to do with, which totally happens due to things like account compromise, all your money can get bricked until that gets fixed. You should always have a backup plan.

It's probably not a bad idea to extend that thinking into crypto, right? Like everybody, you're going to need to decide on your own personal situation, but I do not have all my Bitcoin in like one single ETF. I have it spread out amongst — for exactly this reason.

Alex: Yeah, I think Giannis — uh not going to try his last name — the NBA superstar Giannis from Greece, right?

Austin: Thank you.

Alex: Uh, he said in an interview once that he has his literal cash in American banks spread across like 50 banks. Yeah. He comes from a unique, you know — Greece has a unique history with banking and haircuts, right? Like, you know, the Cypress haircuts are literally why like the Winklevoss twins got excited about Bitcoin. Um, so I mean that's an extreme example, right? But I agree. I think it's great advice, Austin.

第三段：FOMC 与利率环境

会议结果与市场反应

All right, so final point on something that requires trust before we run out of time. The Fed.

So FOMC kept rates at 3.5 to 3.75. The vote was 9 to 3 uh with three people dissenting. Um, Kashkari spoke publicly about his — saying data center investments have added a new demand element to inflation. "I would rather tighten policy incrementally as we gather more data."

Uh, the long end's not thrilled here. It's pushed up into the 4.7s at the 10-year point as I talked about. We're going to pretend the 30-year is not looking even worse.

Um, and Lyn Alden said "bond bulls don't make arguments for why deflation is coming anymore. They just look at WSH like this now" and included the amazing meme from The Whale.

Alex：不确定的利率环境，没有 Fed put

So, Alex, while we've got you here — I know you talked to your friends at Galaxy about this frequently on your own podcast — but what are you making of the rates environment?

Alex: Oh man, it's the market. They're letting the market uh try to do it for them. Um, I think that's — there is no more Fed put, right? I mean, that's sort of the obvious empirical consensus. And are we in an era now of — I mean I'm starting to feel like this is a parliament at the Fed voting uh you know with many different ideas.

I think it's a very uncertain rate environment um is the simplest way to say it. You know, I declined not just for this reason at the end of last year — I said I was refusing to make a Bitcoin price call for this year. I'm quite happy I did refuse. I have to say I said it was a very uncertain investing environment. Not just because of AI or macro or the Bitcoin drawdown and the crypto bear market, but also because of rates. And to me, you know, I'm an observer but a relatively novice one, but um I don't know what to say here exactly.

And did you see um Scott Bessent's photo of the uh buying JPY — and Trump said on Air Force One that "why are we doing — we really love the Japanese, they've been really great to us except for that one time about Pearl Harbor-y." How to throw —

Austin: Yeah. And we're selling the euro, too, right?

Alex: Yeah. Yeah. I mean, I think it's a very tricky environment and so far uh it looks like we're kind of getting less information from Powell as now is pretty clearly expected um than what we're used to and so the market has to react on its own.

Chris：市场自主定价可能是健康的

Chris: It may be healthy. I mean, it ultimately that may be a healthy option here. You know, I tend to lean free market and you know, I am a Bitcoiner. I am — I would say my sort of base position is to be a critic of the Federal Reserve.

Um, I think that this is in some ways although not necessarily the ones that matter to your pocketbook right now, you know, a little bit healthy to have the market sort of drive the rates a little bit more than the Fed. But um again, I'm not an expert in that. That's just my sort of sense.

And for years, the yen carry trade like really was one of the foundational parts of markets. We saw it, you know, we saw it get shocked um some months back. We saw markets puke because of it. I'm just hopeful now that traders are realizing that that's not here to stay forever. Uh and that they'll adjust.

That said, the Secretary of the Treasury wants to keep rates low. It's very much on his mind. We're also seeing more power move from the Fed to the Treasury. We've known this. And um look, if there's anyone who understands currency markets and uh it's our current Secretary of the Treasury. Um, you know, he was on board when they broke Bank of England. So I think he knows what he's doing.

Let's see how he plays it out. But um yeah, it's — how do you keep rates low? How do you stabilize and not shock markets through an abrupt uh unwind of the carry trade? And uh how do we stay uh onwards and upwards?

Rahm：Fed 问责、前瞻指引与"茶叶叙事"回归

Rahm: I like Kevin's message creating accountability for the Fed. He's right to point out that the Fed has missed its aim. We've been well above 2% for over five years. So, he's saying the right — but he's not really cutting rates. The bond market is doing the work itself on the long end of the curve.

Um, on forward guidance, we'll have to see how this plays out. This element, I'm not sure, right? Because you may have other Fed members that do in — if Kevin Warsh uh provide less feedback, right? The market's going to make a reaction function for the Fed anyway, even if it's imperfect.

What used to happen before forward guidance — I remember this distinctly — go to these conferences, there'd be some connected party that knows someone at the Fed or in the FOMC, and everyone would gather around the fireplace and they would tell the story about how they're reading the tea leaves. It's kind of similar to the world before Reg FD — buy-side investors who have access to sell-side analysts and could front run research and exploit — take advantage. The is that people have privileged access have an advantage over other investors.

收尾

Austin: All right, so Rahm thank you for closing us out. I've got to stop us here because we have a couple of hard halts at 5:30 today.

So, for everybody listening, remember to subscribe to the new channels. Thanks for joining us for this episode of Bits and Bips. Special thanks to Alex for joining us to discuss these topics today. We appreciate it, man. And for everybody else, we'll be back in one week to discuss more about how the worlds of crypto and macro are colliding.

Until then, thank you for watching and hope you enjoyed this episode of Bits and Bips. Just remember, nothing we say here is investment advice. And please check unchainedcrypto.com/bitsandbips for more disclosures.

Hey, hey,

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：Cold Card 事件与 Leopold 爆仓，其实是同一种"熵坍缩"
表面上，一个是硬件钱包的密码学漏洞，一个是 24 岁天才的 AI 基金爆仓，风马牛不相及。但把两者叠在一张图上，会发现它们共享同一个致命机制——**"熵源退化"**。
Cold Card 的 bug 是：本应流经真随机数发生器的密钥生成，因为一根"线接错了"，静默地退回到低熵源，于是数十亿种可能坍缩成攻击者可暴力枚举的空间。Leopold 的组合是：本应分散在多个不相关因子上的风险，因为都押在 AI 叙事这一个"变量"上，同样静默地退回到单一熵源——一个 Micron 财报的坏消息就足以让整个组合坍缩。
**真正的教训不是"要用好钱包"或"要做风控"，而是：任何声称"我很随机 / 我很分散"的系统，都要问一句——你的熵到底从哪里来？谁在审计这个熵源？** 五年没人发现 Cold Card 的问题，因为大家假设"它当然是随机的"；LPs 五个月里给 Leopold 加杠杆，因为大家假设"这些股票当然是不同的赌注"。假设，就是熵的敌人。
## 二、跨领域连接：Ken Griffin
