item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、真正结束战争的不是军事胜利，而是一个"谢林点"

请注意转录里一个被轻描淡写、但极其反常的事实：李将军投降时，南方仍有数万人处于武装状态。按纯军事逻辑，战争根本没结束。但"virtually on both sides"都认定它结束了。

这不是军事事件，而是博弈论里最经典的焦点均衡（Schelling point）：当所有参与者都在寻找一个"大家都会认为对方也会认同"的信号来停止行动，李的投降就成了那个共同注视的坐标。Jefferson Davis 是唯一没读懂这个信号的人——不是因为他更有战斗力，而是因为他在协调博弈中掉队了。

这里藏着一个反直觉的教训：战争的物理终结和心理终结从来不是同一件事。同样的模式在软件系统崩溃、婚姻破裂、公司倒闭中反复出现——真正的"死亡时刻"是所有相关方在心里同时勾选的那个瞬间，而不是最后一行代码 / 最后一份文件 / 最后一颗子弹。

二、Grant 让南军带马回家——这其实是 19 世纪版的"马歇尔计划"

大多数人记住 Appomattox 会想到剑、旗、正式仪式。但 Gallagher 反复强调的那个细节——让骑兵带马回家去春耕——才是这场谈判的真正天才之处。

跨领域连接：这在经济学上是一个生产要素保全（factor preservation）决策。Grant 直觉性地明白：如果你彻底剥夺战败者的资本存量（马 = 当时最重要的农业资本），你就制造了一个结构性绝望阶级，而结构性绝望是叛乱的种子。80 年后马歇尔计划做的是完全一样的事，只不过资本变成了工厂和港口。

更妙的是，这个决定在逻辑上违反了"无条件投降"的字面含义——你怎么能"无条件投降"却带走战争资产？Grant 用一个非常小的动作，把"惩罚性和平"重新定义成了"重建性和平"，而且他做得如此低调，以至于连宪法级的原则冲突都被绕过了。

这是一堂关于"制度性妥协的艺术"的大师课：真正会协商的人不改变规则的名字，只重写规则的内容。

三、被埋没的第三方主角：抗拒"胜利者的自然冲动"的那个人

转录后半段真正炸裂的部分不是 Grant 对 Lee 的宽容，而是——Grant 事后威胁辞职，来阻止自己的总统（Andrew Johnson）追杀 Lee。

想想这个画面：一个刚刚赢得战争的将军，把辞呈当作武器对准自己国家的最高领袖，只为保护昨天的敌人。

这里有一个让人意外的心理学观察：胜利后 6-12 个月，才是复仇冲动的高峰，不是战争期间。战争进行时，你忙着活下来；战争结束后，多巴胺退潮、代价开始清算、幸存者内疚翻涌成愤怒——Thaddeus Stevens 和激进共和党人的"惩罚还不够"叙事，就是这种时间差的完美症状。

跨领域连接：这和离婚后的诉讼周期、政权更替后的清算浪潮、创业公司被收购后的"胜利者内战"是同一个曲线。人类系统在从"战斗模式"切换到"共处模式"时，会经历一个反常的愤怒延迟爆发窗口。

所以 Appomattox 真正的英雄不是握手的两个人，而是那个愿意用自己的职业生涯去对冲"胜利者延迟愤怒"的中间制度。Lincoln 死后 Grant 单人扛住了这个窗口——如果他动摇一次，整个 Reconstruction 的可能性就会不同。

一个悖论：南北战争没有变成永久性的种族/地区宿仇，靠的不是伟大的和平条约，而是几个人在几个关键早晨拒绝做人性告诉他们做的事。这比任何宪法修正案都更脆弱，也更值得敬畏。

📝 转录文本

战争的终局：Atlanta、大选与不可逆的推进

Lex： How does the war end?

Gary： So clearly there's the turning point with Atlanta and Sherman's March, and the election of '64 is the — that drives the dagger in. I mean, there's no question but that the war will be pushed to the end, because Lincoln and Grant are in charge and they are not going to take their foot off the pedal. They're going to push it. So it's a question of time.

It drags on — still drags on another six months. Lee surrenders on April 9th. They lay down their arms on April 12th. There are still tens of thousands of Confederate soldiers under arms in different places. But it's a measure of how important Lee and his army were, that for everybody virtually on both sides, that's the end of the war.

Lee surrendered. There's no reason to push this any farther. And other surrenders came pretty quickly. Jefferson Davis was one of the few people who didn't figure that out. He thought something was still possible, but it wasn't. That was the end of the war. The final surrenders are over in June, and that's it. And everybody gets the same terms that Grant offered to Lee. His friend Sherman tried to do more, and they had to rein Sherman in and say, "You can't. No, you're a general, not a politician. You can't do this."

4月9日：Grant 如何对待战败的对手

Lex： So, can we talk about April 9th? I mean, this is a really important moment — of what Grant did in terms of how he treated the opposing army.

Gary： As I said earlier, he treated him the way that he knew that Lincoln wanted them treated. And it may be that Grant thought exactly the same thing. But I think this is a measure of how Grant was — a very — he's a soldier who knew his place. He has civilian superiors. Other generals didn't act that way. I know I'm beating up on McClellan — he's one. Joseph Johnston on the Confederate side is one. They didn't really defer to their civilian superiors. US Grant did.

And in this — this is one of those cases — he sent the rations. He didn't know that Confederates supplied their own horses. If you're a Confederate cavalryman, the government didn't buy a horse for you. You had to supply your horse. And if a horse got killed, you had to buy another one, or they'd make you an infantryman. When Grant found that out, he let them take their horses home with them. He said they'll need them for the planting and so forth.

He did everything in a generous way that you could reasonably think might happen in a situation like — it's still an unconditional surrender. You are surrendering. You're going home. You're not an army anymore. But nobody's going to prisoner-of-war camps. Nobody's doing those things. You lay your arms down. You lay your flags down. You lay your ammunition down. But that's it.

象征性举动与长期和平的地基

Lex： Yeah. But there's certain symbolic actions like this that can lay the groundwork for long-term peace.

Gary： Yes. He didn't demand that Lee give him his sword. He didn't do that. None of those kinds of things that you could have done.

Lex： Sorry to linger on it, but there's certain elements of humiliation that prevent long-term peace. I have to go back to Hitler and what Germany experienced at the end of World War I.

Gary： You mean Versailles — the terms from Versailles. No question about it.

Lex： Some of it is economics, some of it is geopolitics, but some of it is just on a basic human level — humiliation. And people are just not good with humiliation. They remember.

Gary： No. And they can turn that around into something you don't want it to be, to get back national pride.

But Lincoln's bottom line was: the point is to put the nation back together. And the good way to start that is not by imprisoning tens of thousands of Confederate soldiers. That's not the way to do it. Send them home. Make them accept the terms, but then send them home and leave them alone.

Grant 捍卫投降条款：宁愿辞职

The president wanted to go — after Lincoln's death, Andrew Johnson wanted to go after Lee — and Grant said, "I'll resign if you —" because his term — we extended the terms. He's abiding by the terms. You can't change the rules here.

But — like, it should be said — that's not easy to do. You have just fought an extremely bloody battle. There's hatred. There were lots of people who wanted Davis to swing and Lee to swing. Kill them. Execute the rebels. They're rebels and traitors who almost destroyed the nation. "Why are you being so easy on them?"

Thaddeus Stevens was on board that train. Lots of radical Republicans — "you need to punish them." "For what? You haven't punished them enough. You're not punishing them. Yes, you took slavery away from them, but that's not enough. They should be punished more for what they did."

Lex： Confiscate their lands. Take their wealth away from them.

item.description:
## 一、真正结束战争的不是军事胜利，而是一个"谢林点"
请注意转录里一个被轻描淡写、但极其反常的事实：李将军投降时，南方仍有**数万人处于武装状态**。按纯军事逻辑，战争根本没结束。但"virtually on both sides"都认定它结束了。
这不是军事事件，而是博弈论里最经典的**焦点均衡（Schelling point）**：当所有参与者都在寻找一个"大家都会认为对方也会认同"的信号来停止行动，李的投降就成了那个共同注视的坐标。Jefferson Davis 是唯一没读懂这个信号的人——不是因为他更有战斗力，而是因为他**在协调博弈中掉队了**。
这里藏着一个反直觉的教训：**战争的物理终结和心理终结从来不是同一件事**。同样的模式在软件系统崩溃、婚姻破裂、公司倒闭中反复出现——真正的"死亡时刻"是所有相关方在心里同时勾选的那个瞬间，而不是最后一行代码 / 最后一份文件 / 最后一颗子弹。
## 二、Grant 让南军带马回家——这其实是 19 世纪版的"马歇尔计划"
大多数人记住 Appomattox 会想到剑、旗、正式仪式。但 Gallagher 反复强调的

item.title: [Business of Sport] “The Next 50m fans will come from outside the US” | Brett Gosper
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、隐藏在“扩张”背后的悖论：NFL不是在出海，而是在“出口稀缺性”

大多数人以为NFL国际化是在把美国产品卖给世界——错了。仔细看Brett的话：一年只在一个市场投一场“大石头入水”的比赛。这不是扩张，这是刻意的稀缺工程。

有意思的对照——奢侈品行业的爱马仕从不打折、限量发售铂金包，反而拉高品牌溢价。NFL在做同样的事：用地理上的稀缺替代时间上的稀缺。橄榄球本身17场常规赛已经是"稀缺产品"，现在他们把这种稀缺切成地理切片，让墨尔本、马德里、慕尼黑各自成为"一年一度的圣殿时刻"。

真正让我震惊的是：NFL宁可放弃在伦敦设立第五队的机会（那意味着立即增加大量收入），也要保住这种"一年一次的仪式感"。因为他们算得清——一场稀缺的比赛，创造的品牌溢价大于50场常规供应。这是极少数敢于"不最大化短期收入"的体育联盟。

二、意外发现：NFL其实是在偷偷学Formula One，而不是相反

Brett自己提了一句"Formula One is in that model in many ways"——这句话被访谈匆匆带过，但它揭示了一个惊人的方向颠倒。

传统叙事里，F1一直被视为在向美国体育（尤其NFL）取经，学习娱乐化包装、学习Netflix《Drive to Survive》式的叙事经济。但仔细看NFL的国际战略——每年一站、每站变成城市级事件、大石头入水的涟漪效应、把比赛变成"一整个周末的城市庆典"——这不就是F1大奖赛的模板吗？

跨领域连接：这其实是"巡回赛制"（tour circuit）逻辑对"主客场制"（home-and-away league）逻辑的悄然入侵。歌剧、马戏团、TED大会、Coachella音乐节——所有这些"稀缺-巡回-仪式化"的商业模型，在数字时代反而击败了"密集-常规-流量化"的模型。NFL国际化的深层含义是：当供给可以无限复制时，稀缺+在场感成了唯一的护城河。

三、最反直觉的洞察：他们改造的不是市场，是浴室

这个访谈里最耐人寻味的细节，藏在一段几乎被当作笑话的对话里——为了让NFL球队打客场，他们要拆掉伯纳乌和安联球场的更衣室重新布管、加淋浴、砸墙。

这看起来是段趣闻。但停下来想想它的符号学意义：世界上最伟大的足球圣殿——皇马的伯纳乌、拜仁的主场——为了迎接一场一年一度的NFL比赛，愿意让美国人重新给他们的球队更衣室通水管。

这不是租赁，这是基础设施殖民的软性版本。而且是被邀请的殖民。

跨领域连接：这和苹果早期做零售店时的策略惊人相似——乔布斯坚持苹果店必须自建，因为"店铺本身就是产品的延伸"。NFL发现了一个类似真理——体育产品不止是场上90分钟，而是从更衣室水管到观众席infinity screen的整个物理空间。他们不是把"比赛"运到欧洲，而是把"NFL体验"这个物理系统整体空投过来。

更深的隐藏系统真相：Brett说的"我们不设神圣不可侵犯的传统"（fewer sacred cows），配上"欧洲球迷更保守更纯粹主义"的评论，其实指向一个体育产业的根本裂变——欧洲卖的是历史，美国卖的是体验。而在一个注意力越来越稀缺的时代，可复制、可升级、可娱乐化的"体验"，正在慢慢吞噬不可复制、不可扩容的"历史"。

那些愿意让NFL来砸墙加淋浴的欧洲豪门，其实已经在无意识中承认了这一点。

📝 转录文本

开场：NFL国际化的核心命题

The opportunity is to grow your fan base outside of the United States, where we have quite a dominant position, and the belief is that the next 50 million fans will come outside of the States.

One big game in a market each year — you can create that big rock-in-the-pond ripple effect and then build off it all around the rest of the year. Formula One is in that model in many ways.

The players tend to be interested in globalization of the sport. I think there might be some envy around the way that the footballers have that global footprint. We have that global footprint that maybe some of the American players don't.

We're given a license that's broader than the traditional European sports to do something which is not as traditional. And people come for that. Have you turned up to an NFL game in London or Paris and it wasn't like an NFL game in nature like the US? You'd feel, "I've missed out. This is not what I came for."

欢迎与背景

Thank you so much for joining us today. It is so great to have you in the studio.

It's great to be here, thank you for having me.

Brett, this is our first venture into NFL. I think I said that to you when we spoke — 130 in, which is quite frightening. What does that mean? You've never had a conversation about NFL on this podcast?

We had this thing at the beginning which was: when you're talking about sport, how broad do you go? And the NFL has come up in so many conversations — particularly now when we look at things like scarcity of games and the value of the product, creating it, centralized governance — but we've never actually properly sat down and had the conversation. And when we had the chance to do it with you, I thought actually it was the perfect introduction to the sport because of what you're doing there and because of some of the experiences that you've had before.

So I'd like to say an easy break-in for those that need it, but also more than enough of an interesting angle for all of those that already love it, of which there are plenty in the audience. Having said that, you should probably explain a little bit about what you do with the NFL, because it is probably one of the most exciting times for it, in your category in particular.

Brett 的角色

Yeah, it's a great time to be at the NFL. I've been lucky to turn up at the right time.

My role is I look after geography. So I look after Europe and Asia Pacific, essentially the big markets in Europe being UK, Germany, France, Spain and some others — because they're the places where we play games. Where we play games tends to be a priority market, of which we've got 12 in the world. And I'll look after some of the markets where we have offices and planning a greater activity as we globalise a bit more, like China, like Japan, like Australia and so on.

国际扩张的目标与逻辑

International expansion is a huge priority, or it seems to be a huge priority from the outside of it. And what we're really talking about here is a sport that has built the strongest brand, business, property in sport in a very focused market. Now the aim is to take it abroad. So what are the great opportunities that come with that, and what are some of the challenges that you face?

Well, the opportunity is to grow your fan base outside of the United States, where we have quite a dominant position in America — whether it be from broadcast, sponsorship, fan engagement and so on. And the belief is that the next 50 million fans will come outside of the States.

And that coincides with the globalization of the media platforms that are no longer just looking at what the US market can do for them, but they're very interested in having a global footprint. And these are the streamers that we all know.

When you join, do they say the objective is: we want to become one of the dominant sports? We want to have X million viewers? How does success look in your job?

We'd like to be in the top three non-endemic — that usually takes football, or Aussie rules if you're in Australia, or the most popular sport in the country — out of the picture broadcast-wise. Because we've done our analytics and our sums, and we know that if you're in the top three or four you get payback on broadcast revenues over a long period of time. You have to be patient — not going to happen overnight.

Fortunately, we're a private company owned by high net worth individuals that can play the long game, and that helps a lot in what we're doing. We work out what those future revenues might be, but it's all around acquiring fans — either turning casual fans into avid fans or acquiring more casual fans at the base, which feeds that process.

国际比赛的历史演变

Because the first international game, if I'm correct, was played in 2005.

2007 actually — 20 years ago. Regular season game, which was Wembley.

So it's not a brand new concept, right? This has been an objective for a while. But it does seem like it's been ramping up, and this year we're going to have the most games played outside of America.

It's ramped up because there's been a few pivots there. There was obviously "let's play some international games." Then there was, earlier than that, "let's set up a European league" in the 90s. That European league mostly had German teams in it, wasn't successful financially, so the plug was pulled on it at one point.

In the early 2000s, I think the objective then changed from: okay, that second-tier league is not working, what do we do now? Let's set ourselves up maybe for a franchise in a foreign market, which kind of reeks of globalness and "we're more international." And so let's set up probably the UK, because that's an easy lift for an American company — easier lift.

So it was all about: let's work the media market, let's work the fan market, let's ensure that there's stadia that can host NFL games and an NFL team eventually. And that was kind of where I arrived. There was this feeling that a team was going to fall from the United States — probably the Jags, because you'd put your money on that. They were playing at Wembley each year as well outside of the league's own rotational games.

为何没有真正“搬迁”一支球队

And that didn't happen in the end. They pivoted to renovating their stadium, they've set up their shop significantly in that market for the future. And so it's unlikely. And it's complicated bringing one team to the UK, and all of the complications that has in equalizing the fairness of the proposition is quite difficult.

There were even conversations — it could be much easier to pull a division into Europe. You pull a division into Europe, you need four teams, they play off, and then you probably relocate to Florida at the end of that season and so on. But that's an incredible lift. And expansion means adding mouths to feed to the revenue model, which means you've obviously got to be bringing some revenue on board very quickly for the current owners to be willing to do that. Too big a lift.

And then I think the feeling was, as we did the analysis around broadcast values and future values and so on, and fan growth possibilities — that actually one big game in a market each year (and more in some cases like London), you can create that big rock-in-the-pond ripple effect and then build off it all around the rest of the year. Formula One is in that model in many ways. Therefore you can expand broadly much faster and engage with those markets in different ways.

It doesn't mean one day we might not come back to a franchise-in-another-market model, but this is a great way of preparing a more global market in a more significant way.

产品质量与基层生态

I think it's probably the first step though, isn't it? Because while it makes a lot of sense of course to say "hey, if we've got all this interest and want to grow the sport, we can set up a new league" and do all that — it sounds lovely if you just sit and have a conversation about it. But the reality is: this is a sport that doesn't have a grassroots ecosystem, an infrastructure ecosystem. You need that to happen, to be in place, to be able to properly run that. Because the product — the most important thing I imagine about the NFL is the quality of the product. You cannot have something that is NFL-driven if the quality of the actual product isn't top level. And I don't think fans want to see a second-division version of a major brand — they want to see the best of the best of regular season games.

And I think you're right as well: the base of the participation of the sport outside of America is not as strong as it could be in order to generate the athlete quality that you'd want, spread across Europe. Does that mean then we will always have US NFL teams coming to Europe to play, not domestic American football teams and leagues set up in Europe?

I think you'll have those set up in Europe, and they are there. I'm just not sure the NFL will invest in that so much. Maybe they'll invest as an investor, but not as a driver.

Flag Football 与参与度增长

And there is a growth in participation because there's a sport called flag football now, which is the non-contact version of American football, which is an Olympic sport in Los Angeles, and which is growing at a clip around the world — men and women. And that is feeding a kind of assembly line of players that both will have a career in flag, whether they go to the Olympics or play pro league (which we've invested in in the States), or whether a lot of those say "I'm now going to play tackle football."

So we're in the early days of that growth, but eventually that might provide the participation infrastructure that you need to have a much stronger local or European or regional American football league.

国内球迷的“保护主义”

So the flip side of that — while it makes a huge amount of sense — is I would imagine the protectionism needed to put in place to not corrupt what's actually made the NFL so successful in its really core market. And while that makes sense internationally, you will of course have fan bases domestically that will then look at this as going, "well, why are our games moving abroad?"

That's sport, right? And you see what happens the minute it's mentioned in football. I mean, everyone goes completely — whether it be Spain, Germany, the UK — it is delicate with the fans, because the fans are owners of sorts of those leagues. So they get very sensitive.

We've been fortunate in the sense that where we've increased the number of games internationally, it's coincided with sliding a game that's in the practice season into the real season. So we went from 16 regular-season non-playoff games to 17 when we moved to eight games a year internationally. And if we move further, then the conversation — and we've seen the commissioner talk about this — is the possibility of moving to 18 games. So the fans, in a way, don't feel they're losing a game. It's incremental.

球员的态度

The players want this. We see a lot of debate in football about the congestion of calendars — too much in terms of pure activity and also travel times. The players want it because the toll on them is real too.

Well, again, if we move to 18 games, that would be the max. So it's not congestive — still a rarefied season versus other leagues and so on. The players tend to be interested in the globalisation of the sport and the growth of revenue in the sport as well, because they're directly related to that growth in revenue — a fixed percentage of revenues go to the players each year.

They also like to further their possibilities as global superstars at the high end of that player area. I think there might be some envy around the way the footballers have that global footprint that maybe some of the American players don't. But generally speaking, they like the experience of playing internationally. I'm not sure they think about it a huge amount, but when they actually get on the plane, come across, play the games and experience a different atmosphere and so on, they tend to be very positive in how they talk about it after it happens.

时区、时段与全球观赛习惯

Yeah. On the fan side, it was interesting because I actually just, from my own interest, had a look at some of the comments. And obviously you're always careful where people do post comments. The majority of fans that were struggling with games moving internationally — it came down to timing. So the timing of matches, rather than taking away from maybe being able to attend.

That got me thinking about just the different markets that we're talking about, because the American sports market is still very very different to how we operate a lot of our sports here. We think about a lot of our sports purely fandom-driven, whereas in America there's always an understanding I think a little bit more of the commercial element, the business element of it. And therefore the challenge maybe is making sure — "hey, if we can at least consume the game, I'm not overly concerned about where it is," because of the broader geography of America being far less receptive to just being able to turn up to your local game and go and watch it. It's still on their time zone, it's still on their viewing period.

And we're driven by the viewing habits of Americans because of the revenue that's generated by the broadcast deals in the United States. We don't have European-zoned or Asian-zoned games for those local markets when we play. We'll play in Melbourne in September at 10:30am in the morning, Melbourne time, on a weekday.

Is that a bit weird? For who? For everyone?

从 World Rugby 到 NFL

In what way, just for people?

A federation is very oriented towards participation, because a lot of their local federations get funding from governments because of how many people are competing in or participating in that sport in their country. It's very regulatory. Almost most of these federations began as legal entities to regulate the game. So they don't really think about the fan aspect or the fan engagement aspect. And I think World Rugby transitioned during the period I was there — not saying I was the only one driving it, but very much transitioned from regulation as a priority to inspiration a lot more.

It's a much more fragmented sport, because you've got different entities managing — you've got Six Nations, you've got leagues, you've got — so you can't do everything that you want to do. Whereas the NFL is a hermetically sealed business operation, laser-focused on fan growth.

And to be fair, in all the meetings, there's rarely conversations about money. It's all about fans. What can we do to please them? What can we do to engage them? What can we do to bring them in? And people know that that's going to show up as revenue at some point.

It's a very different environment. And I said to you before: in many ways, I'd have done a better job, I think, as CEO of World Rugby had I done this job before. Because I think the understanding and the sophistication with which they go about fan acquisition and pleasing their fans is second to none. And it's been a great school for me, even at my late age.

Because, hey, at the moment sports teams on the whole, whether rightly or wrongly, and a lot of people have opinions on this, are generally valued on multiples of revenue. So the Cowboys — I think the Cowboys generate the most of any sports team, just ahead of Real Madrid, revenue-wise. But it's interesting on that side — I mean, I always think on sport it's fascinating because you have these massive global brands, but as revenue businesses they're actually nowhere near the size of their brand. I mean, the Cowboys did just over a billion last year, Real Madrid the same. But you think about the brand — the brand seems like it's much more influential.

It's incredible. Scarcity value has to keep coming back into it. Now you get a chance to own part of an NFL franchise — it's part of the attraction.

快问快答

Quick fire.

Yeah, go for it.

What's the single best experience you've had in the stadium?

I think the opening/closing — you know I'm going back in time here — opening and closing ceremony of the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics.

Wow. There you go. Why?

Just because it was creative, directed by Steven Spielberg for a start, so you know it's going to be good. But it was just the most incredibly creative and entertaining opening and closing of Olympic Games I've seen — quite a few of those.

Sporting?

I think — I'm going to entertainment more than sporting here — but the London opening ceremony was fabulous too. The London Olympic ceremony in 2012 was extraordinary.

如何向欧洲初学者介绍 NFL

So you're taking NFL, you're talking about NFL to someone in Europe that's never seen it before, that doesn't know what it is. If you're trying to say the reason why someone should watch it or be engaged with it, what would you say?

I think the athletes mainly. I don't think there are better athletes in the world — every aspect of athleticism you're going to see in a game of American football that you might not see in other sports is the first thing I'd say.

I'd also say it is an acquired taste, and you have to understand a certain amount. So if you're not allowing yourself to understand the mere basic of it, you're never going to get fully into it. But just allow yourself to get into that first step: you've got four attempts to get 10 metres — it's yards in America, 10 yards.

But yeah, so I wouldn't lead with a halftime show, because I think that's the cherry on the cake.

Did the NFL, with expansion in mind, put any like additional budget or whatever to creating a content series — like YouTube videos etc — around explaining the NFL?

We do all of that. Whether it be on the big screen in those games that are played internationally, whether it be on YouTube, there are all sorts of — not titled the Dummies Guide, but the Beginners Guide or whatever — to getting into America. We do a lot of that, and it's important. And flag football is going to help that a lot too, because that's going to become far more ubiquitous, and that will help people just see, "oh I see — every time they throw it and they gain yards, they get another chance to do that," and so on. It's very simple in that sense. Once you get past that gate, everything else becomes interesting learning.

橄榄球 vs NFL：谁能跨界？

Who would do better: an American football player playing rugby, or a rugby player playing American football?

Probably the American footballer playing rugby is my view, because we've seen a lot of rugby players try to break into the NFL and have not succeeded in doing that. It's very difficult. It's very technical. It doesn't look it maybe to the outside of it.

No, it doesn't.

It's very complicated. Christian Wade, lots of these players who are magnificent athletes — they did well, but they didn't break into it at the level that they did with rugby. You don't see it happening the other way so much because the money's too big. Which schmuck's leaving there? The river flows more that way — that's your daily salary, yearly. Oh my god. So your changing room's so small.

You can see so many American athletes, whether it be wide receivers, running backs, offensive linemen, whatever. They all find their spot in rugby in a significant way, I think.

So do you think those core skills — a Louis Rees-Zammit, let's say, for the technical, physically incredible speed, obviously has to have the strength to play certain positions — but if you're looking at that technicality piece, it's very hard —

You never say impossible. It's very hard to pick up that technicality if you haven't grown up with it. Exactly. These kids are baked through high school, through college, and then into the NFL. And just turn up — and we've got an international player pathway, we're trying to create these athletes, and some of them do make it through. They tend to be the less technical positions and they do break through, and they spike interest in the countries where those people come from, and so on — which is why we do it.

And we have an academy in the UK for European young athletes to become European NFL players. Which over time some of them will. But generally it's not an easy task for that transfer to happen. And as a former rugby player and as a guy out of the rugby community, I thought it would be a much easier thing of "he's good, he'll do well there." It's not as easy as that.

Is having more international players come into the NFL a metric of success?

Yes, for us it is. We're trying to create more international — like the Premier League, like the NBA — it breeds interest in those markets those players come from. We've got a player, Jordan Mailata, who's with the Eagles, won Super Bowl a couple of years ago. He's one of the biggest stars in Australian sport. Everywhere he goes — we were with him in Australia a little while back — signing autographs, people coming to him in the street. He's huge as well, you can't miss him. But the effect he's had on fandom in Australia has been phenomenal.

So yes, we're looking for those international athletes, and not just to spike interest in those countries, because the NFL wants the best athletes in the world to be at the NFL. And so whether they come from the African region, the European region, Asia, whatever, we're on the lookout for those top athletes.

五年后的展望

Five years' time, what are going to be the top three countries for the NFL outside of US? And I say excluding Canada.

Germany for sure. Germany is on a huge growth spurt. We have incredible partners, media partners. Our office there is high-performing. But that market is quite obsessive about American football.

I think the UK will be the other market. And I think in European terms, probably France. It could be France or Spain, but I think France will embrace American football a lot more. They love their NBA, they love American sports. I think the rugby will probably on balance help them get into American football — to look at it and be interested by it. So I think that'll be the third market.

It tends to help when those markets are on time zones. Asia's more challenging for us because it's on a far more challenging time zone to watch American sport from American broadcast. The day will come, I think, when international is significant enough that we can move some of those windows in America to more favorable viewing times for other markets. That'll be the sign that international is really really growing in terms of its interest and revenue.

But as you said, for now, I mean, the power of just having the NFL means people will hopefully turn up, whether you put it on at 10:30am or 8pm.

Certainly in Australia, that's the case.

Well, to be honest, Australia lives on such strange time zones for most of their sport anyway that they're used to it, aren't they?

结束语

Brett, I've absolutely loved it. Thank you so much for giving us some of that insight into this world. It is amazing to actually have a proper chat about this rather than just referencing it all the time. So thank you for coming in.

Thanks for having me. Thank you.

item.description:
## 一、隐藏在“扩张”背后的悖论：NFL不是在出海，而是在“出口稀缺性”
大多数人以为NFL国际化是在把美国产品卖给世界——错了。仔细看Brett的话：一年只在一个市场投一场“大石头入水”的比赛。这不是扩张，这是**刻意的稀缺工程**。
有意思的对照——奢侈品行业的爱马仕从不打折、限量发售铂金包，反而拉高品牌溢价。NFL在做同样的事：**用地理上的稀缺替代时间上的稀缺**。橄榄球本身17场常规赛已经是"稀缺产品"，现在他们把这种稀缺切成地理切片，让墨尔本、马德里、慕尼黑各自成为"一年一度的圣殿时刻"。
真正让我震惊的是：NFL宁可放弃在伦敦设立第五队的机会（那意味着立即增加大量收入），也要保住这种"一年一次的仪式感"。因为他们算得清——**一场稀缺的比赛，创造的品牌溢价大于50场常规供应**。这是极少数敢于"不最大化短期收入"的体育联盟。
## 二、意外发现：NFL其实是在偷偷学Formula One，而不是相反
Brett自己提了一句"Formula One is in that model in many ways"——这句话被访谈匆匆带过，但它揭示了一个惊人的**方向

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被颠倒的"最惠国"：美国其实是全球处方药价格最低的国家

大多数人以为美国被制药公司"宰"得最狠，但Phillipsson教授揭示了一个被政策辩论系统性掩盖的事实：93%的美国处方是仿制药，而美国仿制药的价格只有欧洲的一半。当你把处方按"份数"加权平均，Medicare和Medicaid支付的价格实际上比欧洲低18%。

这里藏着一个反直觉的统计错觉：正因为美国的仿制药太便宜，品牌药才在总支出中"看起来"占比高得吓人（80%）。如果仿制药完全免费，那么100%的支出都会集中在品牌药——但患者显然过得更好。这是一种典型的"分母消失谬误"：当一个类别价格趋近于零，它在支出结构中就"隐身"了，而剩下的类别看起来就异常突出。

跨领域连接：这与云计算行业的"存储成本白菜价，但计算账单看起来吓人"是同构的现象；也和公共交通里"通勤补贴让票价便宜，反而让偶尔的长途出行显得贵得离谱"是同一种认知陷阱。政策辩论几乎从不校正这种"结构性偏见"。

二、价格管制的"时间套利悖论"：省了三年，涨了二十年

这是整段访谈中最出人意料的洞察：《通胀削减法案》可能让某些药物的"终身价格"反而上升。

逻辑链条极其精妙： - IRA只在专利到期前的最后3-4年强制"谈判"品牌药价格 - 但这打乱了仿制药厂商的进入策略——他们不知道哪些药会被政府"提前狙击"，投资的靶子变得模糊 - 更关键的是：政府提前压低了品牌药收入，等于削弱了仿制药进入市场的动力（首个仿制药享有的180天独占期变得不那么诱人了） - 结果：品牌药便宜3年，但仿制药市场竞争减弱、价格居高不下20年

这里有一个惊人的"熵增"式的系统真相：任何试图在价值链某一点"锁定"低价的干预，都会在其他环节释放出更大的价格弹性。这和交通管理中"某条路限速反而让整体拥堵加剧"、金融监管中"堵住一个套利漏洞反而催生更大的影子银行"是同一个模式——局部最优往往是全局最劣。

三、被忽视的"跨系统会计"：药物是医院成本的隐形对冲工具

CBO（国会预算办公室）的会计规则说：每多花1美元在药物上，只能省下20美分的其他医疗支出。但真实的经济学文献显示：很多药物类别（SSRI、GLP-1、他汀、Sovaldi）的下游节省远超药物本身的支出。

这里有一个被政策圈完全低估的"跨部门套利"现象： - SSRI替代了心理咨询师的人力成本 - GLP-1可能对冲糖尿病和心脏病的手术支出 - Sovaldi治愈丙肝，直接消灭了未来数十亿美元的肝移植账单 - 而住院费用占联邦医疗预算的30%——是药物支出的3倍以上

跨领域惊人连接：这与"预防性维护 vs 事后维修"在制造业的经典权衡完全同构；也和软件工程里"重构成本 vs 技术债利息"的博弈异形同构。药物本质上是一种"生物学重构"——在低成本阶段解决问题，避免高成本的紧急干预。

而最讽刺的是：肿瘤药物的"后续创新"（follow-on innovation）——把治疗从4期癌症前移到1-2期癌症——正是价值最大的部分，却恰恰被IRA的"独占期时钟不重置新适应症"规则扼杀了。这就好比只允许工程师修复bug、却禁止他们在下一个版本做架构升级。系统性地惩罚了最有价值的那类创新。

四、一个隐藏的"公地悲剧"反转

最后一个不易察觉的洞察：全球75%的生物制药利润来自美国市场。这意味着丹麦的诺和诺德不是为500万丹麦胖子研发的，而是为Medicare研发的。

一旦美国用MFN（最惠国价）把自己的价格拉到加拿大水平，结果不是"外国被迫涨价"，而是外国干脆"等你专利过期"或"强制许可"——美国从"最大买单者"变成"唯一买单者"，free-rider问题不但没解决，反而恶化到极致。

这是博弈论中"承诺的悖论"：当A威胁"要么你也涨价、要么我也降价"时，如果B知道A降价意味着A自己毁灭研发生态，那么这个威胁就不可信——最终A只能自己承受降价的后果。这和核威慑中"相互确保毁灭"的失效条件是同一个数学结构。

📝 转录文本

开场：药价争议的双面性

Greetings everyone and welcome.

Cost of living and affordability are high on most Americans' list of concerns. Prescription drugs are no exception. Americans are rightly frustrated and confused about why we pay two to three times the price for the same patented drugs that citizens of other developed nations pay.

But what's missing from this conversation is the reality that it takes billions of dollars in upfront investment to discover, research, develop, and bring new drugs to the market. And the ability to recoup that revenue through a temporary period of monopoly over the drug is a high-powered incentive needed for that investment.

It's no surprise then that less expected future revenue means less investment in R&D — and the high sunk cost of failed projects and trials before a blockbuster drug is discovered mean the companies must make a 60% profit on their commercially successful drugs to get just a 4% return on their overall assets.

美国市场的独特角色

According to the Congressional Budget Office, Americans might pay more for patented drugs, with prescription drugs accounting for 9% of the federal health budget. But being the source of a disproportionate amount of global revenue means that we can access the most and newest drugs before citizens of other countries.

America also witnesses faster entry of generic drugs than other countries, and this puts downward pressure on prices. But there would be nothing for generic manufacturers to replicate if it wasn't for the commercial incentive to discover and bring new drugs out in the first place.

两届政府的价格管制尝试

Despite all this, Democratic and Republican administrations alike have tried to replicate some of the tactics that other governments and their single-payer healthcare systems use to keep prices low.

Under the Biden administration's Inflation Reduction Act, makers of some patented drugs must enter into negotiations with the government to set a so-called "maximum fair price" for their drugs. And failure to sell at that price means incurring financial penalties. This effectively reduces the exclusivity period for a small molecule drug to just 8 years after FDA approval, and a biologic to about 13 years — shifting incentives to fund research between projects based on things other than what is most useful and valued by the public.

More recently, the second Trump administration introduced an executive order on Most Favored Nation drug prices that threatens manufacturers who don't lower their prices to the prices they charge in other countries with targeted lawsuits, antitrust investigations, tariffs, and even revocation of the approval for their drugs if they don't comply.

The legal authority of the administration to do this is questionable and it will likely be challenged, as the first administration was when it tried doing something similar. However, a number of companies have still entered into voluntary agreements with the government to lower their prices, most notably makers of the GLP-1 drugs.

This might seem like a great win right now, but it remains to be seen how this will affect research and development for such new drugs in the future — especially considering that many of these cures help keep Americans out of the hospital, and hospitalizations remain one of the biggest costs that our public healthcare system incurs.

To unpack all of this, I'm joined by Professor Thomas Phillipsson of Chicago, who was also a senior economic adviser of the first Trump administration.

Welcome Thomas.

Morning.

反直觉的真相：美国其实是"最惠国"

All right, so help set the scene for us. Why are American patented medicines so much cheaper in other countries and why can't we just do what they do? Why do we pay so much more?

Yeah. So the first thing I want to argue is that essentially US is paying less than other countries for prescription drugs. And that sounds strange to many people who are in the policy circle. So let me explain where I'm coming from on that argument, which I think is definitely true.

The reason is that about 93% of prescription drugs in the US are generic — for generics, off-patent drugs essentially — and US is roughly benchmarked paying half the price of generics relative to other countries, particularly in Europe. So more than nine out of 10 times you go to the pharmacy, you're paying half of what other countries pay in the US essentially.

Obviously, we're paying more for brand-name drugs, on-patent drugs, and essentially that order of magnitude is roughly 3x relative to other countries, and it varies a lot across those countries. But if you look at the average prescription price therefore — which we usually weigh by volume when we take average prices — our prices are actually for the government, Medicaid and Medicare, about 18% below the average price of a prescription abroad in Europe.

So I think that's very important for several reasons, and this is all on our center webpage by the way, if you're interested, for this exact sources. They're all on the Initiative for Choice and Competition in Healthcare, which is at the University of Chicago Department of Economics.

支出比例的统计错觉

The reason why this is important is that essentially people will argue, "But wait a minute Thomas, spending is much higher on brand-name drugs — in fact 80% of spending roughly is on brand-name drugs compared to generics."

And the way that's misleading is because the reason spending is so high on brand-name drugs in the US is because generics are so cheap. So if generics were free, then we would have 100% of spending being on brand-name drugs essentially, and presumably all the patients would be better who got 93% of their prescriptions for free, even though 100% in that case would be spent on brand-name drugs.

So the fact that we have this system in the US where we have a 90%-plus generic market share — relative to Europe, which has many times 70 or 75% market share of generics, and also in addition they pay more for generics, so they have lower penetration or lower volume potentially due to that (they pay essentially more for generics) — it's not surprising that they therefore potentially have lower volumes relative to the US. But because they have lower volume and pay more, essentially their spending on generics as a share of spending is much much higher.

So I think that's important to recognize. We have the Hatch-Waxman system in the US which has fierce competition for generics, and generics is by far the most common form. Nine out of 10 prescriptions are generics. So we're actually living in a world where we're the most favored nation for prescription drug prices in the US.

私营部门的价格数据

Great. You know, I think that's something that a lot of people end up missing out on. The fact that we are such a huge market for drugs means that we do get access even to generics a lot faster than other countries do. And also as you pointed out, we have those regulatory settings including the Hatch-Waxman Act that foster generic entry.

So you mentioned your study which found that US public sector prices for prescription drugs are 18% lower than comparable peer nations like France, Germany, Canada and Japan. What does the data then say about private sector prices — what our insurance plans pay?

Yeah, we have actually replicated — we're in the process of trying to extend the study to commercial plans. Obviously, commercial plans pay above Medicare and particularly Medicaid, who has a 23% discount relative to commercial plans.

But it's still true because of the high penetration of generics in commercial plans, because they are obviously into the cost savings of generics. So many states therefore mandated even for both public and private payers essentially have generic penetration that is very high.

So even though the numbers are not as stark, it's still true that average prescription drug prices — even when you include the commercial sector in the US — is lower in the US relative to abroad.

品牌药定价争论的盲点

Great. Cool. I'm definitely looking forward to seeing that study. So why does the media and policy debate almost exclusively focus on brand-name list prices, and what are the consequences of policymakers designing price controls based on this sort of incomplete data that doesn't look at what people actually pay?

Yeah, there's a very important point here that we are also in the process of analyzing, and this will come out in a couple weeks, which is: if you only focus on brand-name prices, you will basically have very adverse effect many times on price controls on those brand-name drugs essentially.

So if you take IRA, the Inflation Reduction Act, which controls prices at the last 3 or 4 years of your exclusivity period, they only come in at the end of the exclusivity period with the negotiations. The problem with that is that you basically are interfering with generic entry after the patent expires.

So generic manufacturers — the Association of Affordable Medicine — raised this issue very quickly after the IRA was implemented, that you're now basically limiting competition in the generic market after the molecule expires. So that's a major issue.

双重不确定性

There's two issues there. The generic manufacturers don't know exactly what drugs are going to be negotiated. So they don't know — it takes a year or two to prepare to hit a target that is expiring, but if the public sector through negotiations come in first, all their investments are in vain. So there's a lot of uncertainty for them: which is the target that we're actually going to attack with price competition when the patent expires? That's one issue.

But even if you had that being clear, the fact that the government lowers the revenue of these companies dramatically with negotiations make them less of a useful target for generics. They want to come in and get the first-guy 180 days where they're alone, and then get more and more entrants coming in. That whole process, the manufacturing association of generics have now been upended according to them, and therefore competition is not as fierce after the patent expired — meaning prices are not going down as much as they otherwise would when a big brand-name drug goes off patent.

Remember, IRA goes after the highest spending brand-name drugs. So those are the ones where the generics have the most fierce competition coming in after the patent essentially.

终身价格可能反而更高

So here's the bottom line of this which is very important. You may lower brand-name prices at the last end of the exclusivity period, but if you raise prices after that exclusivity period, it may turn out that that's more important — because the 3 or 4 years of reductions may be dominated by, you know, 20 years of generic prices being higher than they should be essentially after the patent expires.

So it may be essentially that for some drugs, we're finding that these price controls essentially increases the lifetime price of the molecule as opposed to decreases it. Because you don't make up the brand savings with generic — or you basically have offsetting generic effects after the patent expires that dominate the savings of the brands once before the exclusivity runs out.

R&D投入减少的连锁反应

That's really interesting. You know, we all know that in theory price controls lead to shortages, but they also create this sort of significant uncertainty. It clearly seems like that's a huge issue in these sectors which are characterized by huge upfront investments and expectations about future revenue.

So you've established that for every 1% cut to pharmaceutical revenue there would be a roughly 1.5% drop in pharma R&D. So how would this decline affect other costs in the healthcare system in the long run?

Well, that actually is not our finding. We have used that finding to study the effects of — you know, if IRA reduces revenue, how much does R&D get cut, and therefore how many fewer drugs get introduced. But that number comes actually from an average of the entire economic literature on this which is studied quite extensively. There's about 15 papers in that literature on estimating the elasticity of R&D to revenues essentially. So just to make clear that that's not our number, that comes from the broader economic literature. So that's an important caveat.

药物支出的"抵消效应"（Cost Offsets）

But how does drugs essentially affect the rest of healthcare? It depends on the drug class. So in certain drug classes, certainly drug spending raises total healthcare spending, but in many drug classes the increase in drug spending is more than offset in future reductions of other forms of spending. So other forms of spending goes down more than drug spending goes up.

So think of SSRIs replacing the manual labor cost of shrinks. Think of GLP-1s having offsetting effects on diabetic care or heart disease care, etc. And think of similar with statins and heart disease having offsetting effects on surgical expenditure at hospital.

These are usually called cost offsets, and many times it is the case that the increased drug spending — even for the big sort of poster child when people thought drug spending was getting too high, which was Sovaldi for Gilead of hepatitis C — it turned out that Sovaldi spending, the increase on Sovaldi spending for curing hepatitis C, was dominated by the reduction in future cost of liver transplants etc that were saved from people not having more severe liver disease.

So it's many times the case that future healthcare spending more than offsets drug spending. Now, the CBO doesn't score it that way when they do federal impact analysis, because they basically take a very biased stand on the literature. So they only say for every $1 increase in drug spending, you only save 20 cents. But that's a very strange take on the literature that we have summarized in other papers.

肿瘤药物：后续创新的巨大价值

Great. And I think that's just so important, right? Because hospitalizations alone account for about 30% of federal healthcare budget, and that's more than three times what the federal budget is spending on drugs.

So this year you pointed out that nearly 60% of cancer drug improvements between 2000 and 2024 focus on treating the disease earlier in its course. So why are price controls uniquely destructive for these earlier-stage innovations, and what does a patient lose when we disincentivize drugs that prevent long-term complications rather than just treating the late-stage symptoms?

Yeah, the oncology case is a very important case, because about half the pipeline — almost half, not fully — of FDA drugs is oncology. So it's a very very large drug class, the largest drug class.

If you look at oncology, how it was impacted from IRA, particularly in small molecules, the problem is that essentially when you have new indications — so if you have an oncology drug that works for breast cancer, but you want to extend it to liver cancer or what have you, another new indication — they don't let you get a new extension in exclusivity on the IRA. So you're still under the 9-year or 13-year time clock during IRA essentially.

早期干预的巨大治疗效应

So what that means is that many times these new drugs that come out after the first drug — that are follow-on drugs on the initial innovation — are much more productive because they hit lower, earlier stages of the cancer. So instead of treating a metastatic stage 4 cancer, the next drug, follow-on drug to the same molecule, is treating it in stage 2 or stage 1 ideally.

So what we found is essentially that follow-on innovation hits much earlier stages of cancer, and therefore when you hit much earlier stages of cancer, you're basically getting much larger treatment effects of these drugs, because you're not at the last step of the cancer where it's gone metastatic across the several organs.

So I think that's very important, because many times the follow-on innovations are the real valuable ones relative to the initial molecule. So it's essentially saying that once you get a new cancer drug approved, that's just the start of a set of new drugs that can actually be even more beneficial than the initial one. And that's what's being limited by these time clocks not adjusting to new indications.

Yeah, I think that's a really important point. And I've also heard that it's leading to great delays, even if this follow-on innovation eventually happens — delays in them being introduced to the population, because these exclusivity periods kick in a certain number of years after the initial approval. So that's another important thing.

CBO估算的巨大差距

So the Congressional Budget Office — and you mentioned some of the issues that they have with how they score costs — they projected that the IRA would only result in a tiny handful of lost drugs, whereas your research shows that it will likely result in 135 fewer new approvals. So could you elaborate a little bit more on why there is such a big gap between your economic modeling and the government's projections?

That's a very good question. So let me start why we got our numbers, and then I can speculate what CBO is doing.

So again, this was not really our analysis. We basically took the CBO's number on revenue reductions from IRA, which they said would be 12%. We then took that to the economic literature and just said: what is the R&D reduction associated with a 12% revenue reduction according to this literature I mentioned before, that measures how much R&D gets reduced when revenue gets reduced. We took an average of that literature and said here's how much less R&D is done. And then we have also an existing literature: what does that mean for new number of drugs coming on the market essentially. So we are basically taking several literatures and just putting them to CBO's revenue reductions and coming up with those numbers.

上市公司的电话会议提供了佐证

Now, CBO said that we will lose five drugs in 30 years or some incredibly low number, which has already been rejected — if you look at earnings calls of public companies who have to report what they're doing to their investors and also can go to jail if they do lie to their investors on these earnings calls. So it's pretty disciplined discussions in those earnings calls. There was much more pulling of drugs in the pipeline due to IRA than we estimated.

So we are basically too low relative to the flow of new drugs being pulled by the companies. Now, that's an underestimate of the total effect, because some drugs will never be started because of IRA and we certainly don't see those on the earnings calls. So I think we essentially have underestimated the total effect, and CBO has drastically underestimated.

They then released a call — sort of a request for information — on how they want to revise their estimates of drug introductions in responding to price controls, which is a positive sign. On their side though is that this is not really their business. CBO is set up to just score budget effects. Implicit though in that effort, they must score essentially future spending which is also dependent on innovation obviously. So they're kind of forced to take a stand on this, but they certainly did not successfully take a stand on the IRA.

You know, Thomas Sowell once said that you shouldn't trust people who have nothing to lose by what they say, and you can probably better trust people who have a lot to lose. So I think that's also quite important.

MFN行政令：能行得通吗？

So I want to move on to the MFN executive order. It seems to me that the rationale behind that proposal — and a similar one by Senator Josh Hawley from Missouri — is that if we try to force drug makers to sell their drugs at the same price they sell the same drugs overseas to foreign governments that use their monopsony power or price controls to keep the prices low, in theory that would result in these companies simply raising the price they charge in those countries, maybe achieving some kind of parity, and in theory leading to those countries paying whatever the alleged fair market value is for those drugs. Is this likely to be the actual result, and who if anyone is likely to step in to fund the sort of R&D if the US contributions decline?

Well, it is true, I believe, that if you have to have the same price in the US and many other countries who have price controls, you will eventually — if the US price comes... let's say we take Canada just for the sake of argument, Canada is about 5% of our sales in drugs. If you were to lower the US price to Canadian levels, you would most likely face a shareholder lawsuit, I would assume, because that's basically suicidal.

美国承担了全球75%的生物制药回报

About 75% of global earnings in biopharma occur in the US, because the US is the largest market and the richest market, but also because we don't have price controls. So it's an enormous disproportionate share of funding R&D returns across the world.

So you know, Novo Nordisk is a Danish company. They don't innovate for 5 million potentially obese Danes. They innovate for Medicare and the US market essentially. So the whole world R&D spending depends on the 75% of earnings coming from the US market essentially.

So if you were to threaten that by trying to mimic the lower price in a smaller country or in Europe, there's a strong case that your shareholders would do something to you essentially.

逼迫外国涨价的可行性

So the question then becomes: if then you go and try to have upward pressure on foreign countries' pricing, they will tell you thank you very much but we can't afford your prices. That is actually not true in general, because of the argument I gave in the beginning — that it turns out, like I said, that we have cheaper prescription drugs than abroad.

So if they reallocated their generic spending to innovative spending, they could actually do two things at once. One is have our prices for brand-name drugs. Second, spend less in total on drugs, because they're basically offsetting that by lower generic spending essentially if they mimicked our Hatch-Waxman pricing of generic and brand-name drugs.

Obviously that's not going to take place overnight, but it is a case that can be made that Europeans can essentially spend less in total on drugs and stimulate innovation more like the US essentially. But that's not going to happen in the near term obviously.

短期风险：搭便车加剧

So in the near term, they will say thank you very much, we can't afford your prices, and therefore may potentially either walk (not buy the drug at all) or compulsory license the drug in their country, because the manufacturer refuses to lower the US price to accommodate the price in the foreign country essentially.

And if that's the case, then MFN leads to more free-riding as opposed to less — because then US in the extreme case is paying for 100% of the return to innovation if the foreign country either steals the patent or doesn't buy the drug essentially, just waits it out to become generic.

双边贸易协议才是正道

So I think the tying prices across countries is not a good idea to attack this. I think the president was right what he did in the UK-US trade deal, which is have bilateral deals where US have a lot more power in bilateral deals than multilateral deals to force these countries up in their pricing, which they did with the UK essentially.

So if they can do that with the five largest countries — Germany, they're now have a 301 investigation of Germany, they can do... that's obviously the largest European country — they can do it with France and Italy and Japan. They're well on their way of getting something through trade negotiations, which I think is a much more productive way than tying prices across countries.

为何欧洲不采用Hatch-Waxman式改革？

Yeah, absolutely. I'm also weighing on the side of this being more of a trade issue certainly than it is an issue for some kind of technocratic pricing. And there's been plenty of good research from Professor Lichtenberg and others looking into how price discrimination between geographic markets promotes actually better outcomes, and preventing it or constraining it will probably result in shortages across the board because you can't allocate those resources efficiently.

So I'm a bit curious about why there's maybe this reluctance in — I mean I can understand why foreign developed countries don't want to shoulder their citizens with higher taxes or higher prices in the short term because of the political incentive there — but why have they not decided to go for something like the Hatch-Waxman Act, the settings on making generic entry more fast and easy?

Well, I think some of the countries like Spain or Canada, they have very strong generic manufacturers also. So they are very reluctant to go after their own industries in that regard. But also, we have much more fierce private competition in those countries in general — it's not just for generics, but it's true across many many industries.

But I've been in discussions with several European countries and there is some potential momentum of getting them to move in this direction. Essentially they realize that: why are we spending money on the copycats as opposed to the guys who came up with this stuff? And if they did, they could potentially lower their total bill for prescription drugs on average.

And so if that becomes clear, and if that actually has some momentum which I hope it will, it will still take a lot of time for those reforms. Maybe one country will do it and then other countries see the value of it, but it's still a very long time away, put it that way.

结语：政策失败的双重代价

Cool. And you know, maybe we could use our trade leverage to nudge them perhaps in the right direction.

Well thanks so much for that. You know, it seems to me that a big takeaway from all this is that we often hear about the trade-off between incentives to innovate and make new drugs and then paying lower prices. But clearly what the evidence is showing is that these policies, these price control policies, will also likely fail to achieve the very thing that they want to achieve — which is lower prices, lower taxpayer spending — while depriving tons of people of potentially new cures by limiting that competition.

So thank you so much for joining us, Professor Phillipsson, and look forward to seeing and reading more of your research as it comes out.

Great. Thanks for having me. Appreciate it.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、被颠倒的"最惠国"：美国其实是全球处方药价格最低的国家
大多数人以为美国被制药公司"宰"得最狠，但Phillipsson教授揭示了一个被政策辩论系统性掩盖的事实：**93%的美国处方是仿制药，而美国仿制药的价格只有欧洲的一半**。当你把处方按"份数"加权平均，Medicare和Medicaid支付的价格实际上比欧洲低18%。
这里藏着一个反直觉的统计错觉：**正因为美国的仿制药太便宜，品牌药才在总支出中"看起来"占比高得吓人（80%）**。如果仿制药完全免费，那么100%的支出都会集中在品牌药——但患者显然过得更好。这是一种典型的"分母消失谬误"：当一个类别价格趋近于零，它在支出结构中就"隐身"了，而剩下的类别看起来就异常突出。
**跨领域连接**：这与云计算行业的"存储成本白菜价，但计算账单看起来吓人"是同构的现象；也和公共交通里"通勤补贴让票价便宜，反而让偶尔的长途出行显得贵得离谱"是同一种认知陷阱。政策辩论几乎从不校正这种"结构性偏见"。
## 二、价格管制的"时间套利悖论"：省了三年，涨了二十年
这是整段访谈中最出人意料的洞察：**《通胀削减法案》可能让某些

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] The WWI Soldier Who Discovered Black Holes – Adam Brown
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

弹道学与时空曲率的隐秘同构

最令人震撼的画面不是史瓦西在战壕里推导方程，而是他同时在做两件表面完全无关的事——计算炮弹的抛物线轨迹、以及求解光在极端引力场中的测地线。但仔细想，这两件事在数学上是同一个问题的两个极端：炮弹沿着地球弱引力场中的时空测地线运动，光沿着无穷曲率下的测地线运动。史瓦西之所以是"第一个"求解者，可能恰恰因为他每天面对"物体在引力场中如何运动"这个非常具体的问题——一线炮兵的手感，比学院里的抽象推演更接近广义相对论的物理直觉。战争把他放在了一个稀有的认知位置上。

"错误理论给出正确答案"的深层暗示

真正诡异的不是米歇尔和拉普拉斯在 18 世纪就"预言"了黑洞，而是他们用彻头彻尾错误的牛顿力学，居然连 2GM/c² 里的因子 2 都算对了。Adam Brown 轻描淡写地说这是"完全巧合"——但科学史上这种"巧合"密度高得可疑：玻尔用错误的电子轨道算对了氢光谱、开普勒用错误的柏拉图立体信念找到了行星轨道定律、托勒密的本轮模型能预测日食。

这暗示一个反直觉的方法论真相：量纲分析 + 守恒律，往往比理论框架本身更接近真理。当一个"错误"理论持续给出正确数字时，它多半不是幸运，而是在偷偷调用某个更深层的对称性——牛顿引力与广义相对论共享的、尚未被明确命名的那部分骨架。这可能也是为什么今天很多 AI scaling law 的经验公式"莫名其妙地"成立：它们踩到了信息论的骨架，而我们还不知道那副骨架长什么样。

创造者看不懂自己创造物的普遍模式

爱因斯坦在自己方程的精确解面前困惑了半个世纪——反复写下"物体会从视界弹回"之类今天看来幼稚的判断。这个细节比"发现黑洞"本身更值得玩味：发明者往往是自己发明物最差的理解者。孟德尔的遗传学被埋没 35 年、图灵没预见通用计算的社会形态、香农对信息论的哲学意涵极为保守、Vinton Cerf 到 90 年代才意识到 TCP/IP 会长成什么样。

为什么？因为创造需要"如何构造"的能力，理解需要"从外部观察构造物"的能力——这两种认知模式几乎相互排斥。爱因斯坦被困在"我知道我写了什么"这个内部视角里，反而看不见方程在坐标变换下呈现的物理图像。这一模式对当下 AI 的启发很直接：LLM 的训练者可能是这个系统最差的解读者，真正理解它的会是那些从外部反复"探测视界"的人——就像半个世纪后重新解读史瓦西解的钱德拉塞卡和惠勒。

意外的隐喻：视界的社会学对应

视界不是一堵墙，而是一个坐标系的失效点。爱因斯坦之所以困惑，是因为他站在远处观察者的坐标系里看——那里一切在视界处"冻结"；而从掉入者的视角看，视界处什么也没发生。

这个几何事实有一个惊人的社会学映射：任何系统性危机都存在一个"外部观察者看得见、内部当事人体验不到"的临界面——组织崩溃前的静默期、抑郁症患者的自我隔离、经济泡沫顶点的普遍乐观、成瘾者的"我随时能停"。视界的数学教会我们的其实不是"信息不可逃逸"，而是"观察者的位置决定了什么被看见"。这也是为什么外部教练、旁观者、审计师存在的价值不可替代——他们占据的是当事人几何上无法占据的坐标系。

📝 转录文本

The Question

I would love to get more insight than the high school version of "light falls into it and can't get out" of why black holes work the way they do.

Einstein's Field Equations and an Unexpected Solver

Yeah, so black holes are fascinating objects in general relativity, and really the quintessential object in general relativity that doesn't really exist in the same way in Newtonian physics. And the story is kind of wild.

So, Einstein wrote down his field equations — the field equations we wrote on the board — describing the relationship between curvature and the amount of energy in the system. And he thought, you know, that those equations are so complicated no one would ever come up with exact solutions to them, and we just always be having to do approximations. And that turned out not to be correct.

But Schwarzschild, who was a Prussian artillery officer in the First World War, in between writing — you know, calculating the trajectories of artillery that they were lobbing over in the direction of their enemy — he figured out that in fact Einstein's equations, pretty much immediately after Einstein had written them down, within a matter of months, in fact have an exact solution.

An exact solution, a solution now known as the Schwarzschild equation, and that we now understand describes a black hole. It is a solution in which there is no matter except possibly at the very very center in a way we will not describe. It's a central point-like amount of matter, and it describes what the space-time around that looks like. It's called the Schwarzschild solution, and it describes a black hole.

Half a Century of Confusion — Including Einstein's

They were not called a black hole at the time. In fact, people were extremely confused about what this solution even meant. People wrote down wrong things for about half a century about what this meant. And perhaps the worst offender was Einstein, who got extremely confused about it — particularly confused about what I would describe as the event horizon — and wrote all sorts of wrong things about how objects would maybe bounce off the event horizon, just totally confused from a modern perspective.

It's extremely simple to understand what's going on. So, let me tell you what a black hole is.

The Collision Between Gravity and the Finite Speed of Light

General relativity, as we set it up, is about the collision between gravity and the finite speed of light. And the simplest collision you could do is actually noticed by people even in the 18th century, before we had special relativity or anything like that. And they just asked a very simple question.

If you want to shoot something off the Earth, you need to shoot it with a certain velocity — the escape velocity. You need to shoot it fast enough if you want to escape far away from the Earth so that the kinetic energy of the object you're shooting is equal to the gravitational binding energy of the Earth's surface. M is the mass of the Earth and R is the surface of the Earth.

And for Earth, that turns out — it's about 11 km per second is the escape velocity. But for objects that are heavier or more compact, the escape velocity is larger. So, for example, Jupiter would be hundreds of kilometers a second you need to shoot it off off the Earth.

The 18th-Century Prediction

And you can imagine objects that are so heavy or so compact that in fact the escape velocity becomes equal to the speed of light. And so, people ideally wondered what would happen then. They didn't have the tools to address it, but in the 18th century they wondered what would happen.

And you can calculate what the critical value of velocity is. Just put in the velocity equal to the speed of light. This gives a critical radius of 2GM — the mass of the object cancels — divided by c². And so, that's somewhat suggestive that if you had an object that was this compact and had this mass, the escape velocity would be given by C, the speed of light.

Michell, Laplace, and a "Coincidental" Factor of Two

The connection you're pointing out is a Newtonian one. Did anybody make this connection before?

Absolutely. So, people in the late 18th century wrote this formula down. I think both Michell and Laplace had this in the 18th century, and they said that if you had an object that was that massive and compact, light would not be able to escape.

That reasoning is not particularly compelling by modern standards, but it does turn out to be exactly correct — even, crazily, including this factor of two is even correct, for completely coincidental reasons.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

观看原视频 →
