An off-the-shelf model might nudge you both to concentrate into one of those names. And if you propagate that view across the entire quant ecosystem or all the competitors, everyone ends up concentrating in the same name. That name becomes potentially a lot riskier than it looks. Obviously, for all the crowding dynamics, I think that may have arguably been a factor related to like August 2007 quant quake or whatever we're calling it nowadays. Can you talk me a little bit about how PGIM went through that period with its own in-house risk model? How things played out for you and how market dynamics looked.

It was definitely an advantage. With the quant quake, you start with some unwinding of a quant hedge fund and then it snowballed into something that was a broader deleveraging event. It really did highlight the connectedness of the quant strategies and did bring to light this idea of crowding.

For our strategies, we did much better than we would have done if we were using one of those off-the-shelf models — because of exactly what you described. Something that looks risky because of historical data, that doesn't mean you can extrapolate that into the future. That means it'll be less risky going forward.

So, what our risk model did at the time would be more of a diversification engine — and have us diversify that idiosyncratic risk instead of trying to predict which stock was less risky. By using a different risk model, we were naturally just a little bit different than others. So, clearly an event like that affected us as well, but it did give us even more confidence that moving in the direction of our own risk model was definitely worth it.

GFC 之后：不只是 quant，要做 different quant

You described the GFC period as driving a realization for you and the team that in a crowded factor world, quote, "it's not enough to be a quant, we need to be a different quant." So, you have the risk model working on one axis. Maybe we can talk a little bit about the alpha model for a second as being another axis of differentiation. What did different really come to mean for the research agenda going forward coming out of that period?

I think anytime there's a market event like the GFC, you always have to kind of go back to the drawing board and see how your model did and dissect what needs to be different. This was also a period of time where smart beta was becoming a bigger thing. Investors can go out and buy these simple exposures in an ETF form at a very low cost. So, if they were going to allow us to manage their money, we really needed to do something bigger than what was simple.

We took that opportunity to really focus on how to be differentiated using alternative data sources, looking beyond the simple factors that look at the biases like momentum or PE. We invested a lot in determining what a quality of a company looked like — so not just ROE, but looking at the company from different angles to understand whether this company could achieve the growth that it was planning to achieve, or whether it was a real good value company, or whether it was a value trap.

We spent a lot of time looking at more quality factors, but I think what was more important is how our research agenda evolved. We were really looking at things not just probable alpha sources, but also things that were very differentiated and that were scalable and feasible.

The Research Shark Tank

What we have today is actually an event that we have every year in December. We call it our research shark tank where we all get in a room and our researchers get up and they pitch three or four ideas, and kind of like a shark tank situation we all get a chance to ask questions, to poke holes, to challenge them. That's how our research agenda comes together.

What we're really trying to do there is look for things that align with our philosophy, are scalable, are feasible, are differentiated, are relevant. An environment like that where you're getting input from everyone in the team to come up with those different ideas is really important — the most senior to the most junior researcher along with the portfolio management team all chimes in. That's how you get some really good ideas that will ultimately make you different from other quant strategies.

什么叫 "fundamental quant"

I want to drill down into that philosophy idea for a second, because PGIM describes itself as a fundamental quant shop. There's a lot of firms that might claim that label, something like quantamental. And so, I really want to get an understanding of when you say fundamental quant versus just quant, where is the real distinction lie to you? Is it in the types of signals you'll use? The process of validating those signals versus a fundamental story? Or the time frame you're targeting? What does that really mean to you?

What we're trying to do is find companies that are just good companies that anybody would want to invest in. They have good growth prospects, they're high quality, they're reasonably priced. It's very much trying to replicate what a traditional stock picker manager would do.

In doing that, we're really looking for every factor in our model to have a really solid theoretical underpinning. And the reason for that is because if we find a signal that works that we want to add to our model, we want to understand why it works. That will solidify that we think that this is a good factor. We understand why it works, we understand when it works in different market cycles, and it gives us confidence that that factor will work in the future as well.

Space in our model is very valuable. If you've got a lot of good factors and you're looking to add something, you're taking away space from something else. You want your model components to all work in harmony with each other and balance each other well in different market conditions.

Being a fundamental manager keeps us away from some of these ideas that maybe backtest well — you're not quite sure why they work, you put them in the model, they're taking space away from something else, and then maybe they may not work in the future. So, we have a very carefully curated list of factors that have true rationale to them — that if I explain to you exactly what it was, you'd say, "Oh, that makes sense." And I think that gives us comfort that we're building a resilient model that makes sense, and in periods of stress, you know the companies in your portfolio are good companies and that they should be resilient.

案例：Financing 因子

Maybe we can ground this idea with an example. In our pre-call, you mentioned one of these factors is the financing factor. This was sort of unique — one of the first times I've heard anyone talk about this particular idea. I was hoping maybe you could walk through what that factor is and how it might illustrate the distinction between being a fundamental quant and a generic quant, dare I say, and how that actually looks in practice.

This was one of the additions to the model after the GFC and trying to look at a quality of a company — and instead of just looking at some basic quality metrics, we were interested in the concept of how a company finances its growth.

If you've got a group of growth companies in an industry, and you've got companies that finance their growth through organic cash flow, what our research showed is that those companies tend to outperform ones that consistently tap the markets to get more capital.

The rationale behind that was that companies typically have opportunities with diminishing marginal returns. A company that has abundant access to external financing might be tempted to fund increasingly lower-quality projects. Whereas a firm that is bound by its internal cash flow will really have to face the decisions on what do we really want to invest in, what really makes sense for this company.

It was an interesting concept, and when we tested it statistically, it worked very well. This is a good example, too, of a factor that's evolved over time. We started with a very simple approach to this, and over the years we still have that concept in the portfolio, but the factor has evolved quite a lot as there's more information and better techniques to use to get at that concept.

因子分类学：Growth / Linkages / Quality / Value

One of my favorite questions to ask equity quants is about the taxonomy of their characteristics or the factors they use in their portfolios. When you talk to your typical equity quant, you're going to end up with sort of a hierarchy of value and quality and momentum, and maybe defensive — whether that's statistical or more fundamental quality. But you do have a cohort of what are more statistical or price-based properties often. Not necessarily the case when you talk to a fundamental quant. So, I'm curious: how do you think about organizing your factors internally? What's the taxonomy that you use and what's each group really meant to capture?

We're looking for those companies that at a high level have good growth prospects, are high quality, and reasonably priced. So, we do have categories. What's interesting is when we talk about these categories, they sound kind of simple. But the model itself is really complex. And there's so much interaction between these individual pieces that the taxonomy sometimes is really just used for a sort of organization to talk about our strategy and to share information with clients — performance-wise, attribution-wise.

The groups that we use are:

  • Growth — we're looking to find companies that have good growth potential and take advantage of investors that are under-reacting to new information, or take advantage of slow information diffusion.
  • Linkages — for us, another way of looking at the growth of a company and trying to understand how information is flowing from one company to another, and how a shock to one company might affect other companies, whether it's positive or negative.
  • Quality — how well is a company run? Does it have solid management? Is it a competitive threat to other companies? Is there something in the options market that's signaling something is concerning here that maybe our models aren't picking up elsewhere? So, getting information from other informed investors.
  • Valuation — looking to make sure that companies are reasonably valued, or maybe they look undervalued, under-appreciated.

An important part of these groups is that we use them dynamically based on the kind of company we're evaluating. For companies that are much faster-growing, younger companies, we're going to tilt more towards those growthier factors. Whereas, if you're a mature, stable company, we're really going to focus more on those valuation factors — because there you're not paying for some future growth. Your return is going to come from the realization of a mature income stream and getting that income stream at a discount.

深入 Linkages 因子

I would suspect that our listeners likely have pretty strongly established mental models for generally what growth and value and quality mean. Linkages is one which doesn't get spoken about very often and likely is a novel factor category for a lot of folks to think about. I was hoping you could spend a little time there discussing: what does this idea of linkages capture, and why does it earn a place among these more classical factor groupings?

If you look at our growth factors and our insights there, we're really looking at the company directly and we're saying: what are signals that are telling us something about this company, about its growth prospects. What linkages is doing is just trying to come at that from a different angle. So it's saying: how is this company connected to other companies in the marketplace, and how can that give us an informational advantage — meaning there's a shock somewhere in the market and that shock is going to trickle through.

A simple example of this is like an industry. If something's happening in an industry, you're going to see this whole industry move together. And there are shocks that happen within an industry that truly do affect every company in that industry.

This is a more sophisticated way of doing that because these days everything is so interconnected across industries, across countries. You're finding other linkages to other companies that are not as obvious. One example is customer–supplier relationship. If you've got company A and a shock happens to company A — say something really positive — you would expect the suppliers to company A to benefit from that. That can go several layers down. The suppliers to the suppliers of that company A should do really well.

You can map out different relationships even beyond customer–supplier relationships. You can measure the strength of those relationships so that you can measure how impactful that new information may be across different companies. We found that this is kind of another layer of mapping information and how it's affecting different companies around the market.

为什么不做 Price Momentum

Now, in your taxonomy, you notably did not include momentum. Maybe isn't a surprise being a fundamental quant shop — momentum being arguably a non-fundamental measure — but it is unusual for a quant shop. And you do often see that even fundamental quant firms do find a way to introduce momentum in some way or another, even if it's just in trading and execution. Curious as to your thinking: is there anything lost in leaving momentum out, or is it captured through some of these other fundamental factors you look at?

It is captured through a lot of the other fundamental factors. But one of the reasons that we did not automatically include price momentum in our models is because, as a fundamental quant, price momentum has a lot of elements to it that are related to the company that you're evaluating, but there are a lot of elements to it that are not related to the company. It could be an industry shock that may or may not affect that company. It could be speculation — let's just call it noise. So, you've got the price movements of a company, some of it is relevant to that company, and some of it is just noise.

What we do is we pull out that relevant piece by looking at things that are actually happening to those companies. So, key events for that company, and how is the price moving around that event? How are investors reacting to that event that's specific to that company? — and then ignore all of the other price movements that are less relevant.

By calling out that informational piece from price momentum, and leaving the noise out of it, you get a much richer signal. We find that our measure, we call it information momentum, is as effective over time as price momentum, but it has a lot less of the crash risk — about half the downside.

When we are building factors, not only are we focusing on the fundamentals, but we're also looking at making that factor as attractive as we can from a risk-and-return trade-off. So, we have an element of risk control built right into the alpha model. Trying to find the adjustments that we can make, looking at all the detail to get the best factor we can from both a risk and return perspective.

到底有多少真正正交的信号？

You mentioned that this strategy first went live in 1996. So, we're talking 30 years of live performance, and 30 years of doing research. And surely, you've looked at some of the same individual names that have been in that basket. It must be 8,000, 10,000 different ways. Realistically, how many truly orthogonal signals do you think exist for things that ultimately move company fundamentals?

It's probably less than you would think. Our models, depending on the region, have maybe 25 to 40 signals — or I would call them concepts, because a lot of them have a lot of components to them. Each one, as I mentioned, is carefully designed and are in the model for a real reason, because they have a benefit alongside each other and through different markets.

We want to make sure all of the signals in our model are there and have an impact. If you have a model with 400 signals in it, how much is each one really contributing? And how can you really dissect what is driving your performance? That's something that's important to us as well. Having a meaningful weight being tied to an economic underpinning — for us, the number is more in the 40s as opposed to the 400s.

Alpha 的来源：数据、特征还是预测？

I want to talk about some areas which you've been leaning into for recent research. One of those areas has been how information flows through the market — trying to get a read on a company before it actually shows up in those traditional income statement, balance sheet type numbers. Given that goal and objective, I'm curious to ask you a question I've been asking a number of guests lately: where do you think the largest source of alpha signal is living today? Is it in accessing unique data that maybe no one else has access to? Is it engineering unique features from that data — getting a different look at the data or looking at it in a unique way? Or is it in actually forecasting more accurately or developing more complex or more complete forecasting models from the same sort of data and features everyone else has?

I think it used to be the data. I think it used to be people getting that unique access, but these days, I think the data is pretty much available. Data's expensive though, so being part of PGIM, which is a very large organization, being able to get that data at scale is important. That's an advantage that we have, but today I think the data alone isn't enough.

You have to be able to take that data, number one, sort through what's really relevant and what isn't. Decades ago, it was hard to find data sources. Now, people are emailing me every day with a new data source they have, but you really have to ferret out what is very valuable and what isn't.

But what matters more is what you do with that data. How do you turn this into a factor that is going to be a complement to your model? You've got to figure out what kind of tools you're going to use in order to analyze this data. You have to figure out how you're going to transform the data. Are you going to normalize it? What time horizon are you going to consider? Are you going to time weight the data? How do you deal with missing data? To us, all of those little decisions make a difference. You've got to take the time to go through and make those decisions thoughtfully, not just try a bunch of different versions and see what looks the best.

It's also how you use those factors. I mentioned before that one of our original concepts for our strategies was using factors where they're most effective. For us, we make that decision at the company level. Faster growing companies who are earlier in their life cycle, we're going to weight those growth factors more. For more mature companies, we're going to weight those valuation factors more. That's really at the company level, and it really increases the power of our factors.

Nuances like that and thoughtful approaches like that, that are pretty intuitive when you think about just investing 101, really do make a difference. So, I think it's not just the data you have, but how you use the data, and then where you use those factors in your decision-making for different stocks in the market.

动态因子加权：像 growth manager 一样看待成长股，像 value manager 一样看待价值股

Can you dive a little bit into that idea of weighting those factor scores on different companies differently a little bit? I'm curious how much of that process is discretionary versus purely systematic, and where you derive the evidence from that that's the appropriate approach to take.

It is all systematic, not discretionary at all. The concept comes from the idea of just evaluating a stock. The price of a stock is going to be driven by mainly two components. You buy a company because of the future growth of the company — and if the company has strong growth, that price is going to go up; you'll get future earnings. The second part of the equation is the existing earnings, and is the company priced appropriately for the existing earnings, or is it a value stock and a discount stock?

If you're looking at a fast-growing company, you want to pay attention to future growth prospects much more than whether that stock is expensive. You can think of a lot of stocks in the industry right now where they might look horribly expensive relative to their current earnings, but their growth potential is huge, and that is why you're buying that stock. Our models want to act more like a growth manager when we're looking at that stock and not really worried too much about how expensive it is.

On the other hand, when you're looking at a more mature company, even if you're hearing hype from management that maybe there's some super wow growth coming around the corner, that can really trick investors to bumping up prices artificially, or discounting historical bad news for a company and it's really beaten down and it's more of a value stock. For those more mature companies, we want to be more price sensitive. We want to look for bargains. Quality is still important, but this future growth piece is not as important. In that end of the spectrum, we want to act more like a value manager.

When we're going to pull our portfolio together of stocks, we're having stocks we like because — even though they were expensive — they're good growth prospects. So, those are the growthier names in our core portfolio. On the value side, maybe they're not great on the growth side, but they're good bargains. That's why they're there. It's taking a basic economic concept and applying it down at the stock level.

In practice, what happens is we evaluate a company's growth rate relative to the universe that we're looking at, and then we adjust the weights on the growth and value factors based on where they fall along that spectrum. That's happening every day at the stock level. When we put the stocks in the portfolio and aggregate it up, you'll have a nice balance between your growth and your value factors, but they're coming from different types of stocks in your portfolio.

应对突发冲击：COVID、Meme、AI

In the last couple of years, we've had these examples of emergent fundamental shocks. We had COVID. Not sure whether we'll call meme stock mania a fundamental shock, but meme stock mania more recently — I think AI is a good example of an emergent fundamental shock. These are kind of a regime change that's arguably difficult to capture with a standard static set of risk factors. In our pre-call, you talked about trying to figure out how to make your strategy more resilient to when shocks hit the market — figuring out which parts of the market are most vulnerable, and building custom factors that get at things like how innovative or cutting-edge a company is or how resilient they can be to these different sort of market shocks. Can you speak a little bit about how you go into building models that can help assess emergent shocks in real time?

The goal of our model is to produce as consistent of a stream of alphas we can in different market conditions. When we're building the model, we're really focusing on resiliency — using different sources of alpha and different types of factors that work different in different market conditions. You can do this by using a variety of data sources, different types of tools that you can use to evaluate the adaptive weighting scheme that we talked about. But the key is looking at companies from different angles and trying to understand those information shocks before they really show up in the numbers for that company.

As far as a larger shock to the market — I guess by definition, it's hard to predict a shock because it's a shock. It's not something anybody can predict. But I think what's important for a manager is what you do during that shock. Having a solid investment philosophy and sticking with it is important.

I think about when COVID hit and everything was turned on its head and only certain types of stocks were doing well. The key is to stick to your investment philosophy, not to throw your model out the window. You had mentioned before about manager discretion — I think manager discretion needs to be pretty limited, because we've all built these models together. We believe in these models. We built them to be resilient over time. We know that there are times in the market when these models don't work, and we know that they will recover. So, don't go in there and kind of throw the baby off with the bathwater or do something with your human biases to mess this up. We're prepared for these situations. We own good companies. They'll hang in there.

That being said, there are times where portfolio managers need to intervene, and that's where experience of a portfolio management team is really important. Example there was when Russia invaded Ukraine. Our models were like, "Wow, Russia's really cheap." Well, that's the kind of situation where the experience of the portfolio management team all working together need to step in and say, "You know what? Maybe we need to make some adjustments here."

The third thing about these shocks is learning from them. Sometimes you go back and you're like, "Well, there's nothing we could have done about that because this is how we manage money and this is our philosophy." But other times, usually, there's some really good insights that you can then work into your model, find ways to adjust it so that you're more resilient the next time the next shock comes — because the next shock is always different. That's an important part of the research process.

回测的悖论：太漂亮反而危险

I want to talk about some of those learnings, and I specifically want to use COVID as an example, because I've heard you say that COVID compressed everything — that long-horizon factors collapsed into short windows, and that a backtest that looks really great through 2020 might actually be more of a red flag than a feature. I think that's an interesting perspective. How did that period change the bar for factor acceptance for you?

Looking for factors and using backtests is such a valuable tool in the quantitative space. The fact that we can take an idea and test how it worked back in time is incredible. Backtesting is an art as much as it is a science, and I'm sure you've heard the phrase like, "I never saw a backtest that wasn't good." But I think that that is a powerful tool that we need to continue to evaluate as if we were actually managing these strategies back in time.

COVID was such a market shock that when we're evaluating something that is based on our philosophy that is fundamentally driven, I would expect that it wouldn't necessarily work in 2020 — because if it does, then it's not in concert with our philosophy, because it was such an interesting period.

I like to see a backtest in time that does have periods of weaknesses, so that I can understand what those weaknesses are and I'm more prepared for the future when there are market events — that I understand what the weaknesses of this model is. The scariest thing is a backtest that does well every year back in time, because that can't possibly be. So, what's really going on with this backtest?

One thing that's happened that we had to kind of accept was that we have shorter histories for some of these new factors or new data sets. It used to be we wanted to see 20 years of data so that we can see how a factor did through time, peaks and valleys, but now we might have information that maybe only goes back five or six or seven years, and we just really need to understand that factor better and understand again the theoretical underpinning to get comfortable with it — and maybe we use that factor at a lower weight for a while to get more comfortable with it. But that's definitely something that's changed in our evaluation, too, is that we need to be comfortable with shorter data sets than we did back in the day.

LLMs 是"火箭筒"

Top of mind for most quants that I talk to today is the role of large language models in the quant process. You've called large language models bazookas — tools of enormous capability with a real chance of blowing up what already works. What do you think the right discipline is for working with these tools? How are you thinking about integrating these tools into your research process?

We like to start with a concept, a data set, or a concept that we want to add to the portfolios or to the models, and then evaluate the best tool to use. Typically, the simplest approach is really the best approach. We want to start with something more basic and then get increasingly more complex to understand where the sweet spot is.

Don't just jump in and use LLMs through your whole model — there are risks there that you want to manage. And the best place to manage those risks is during the research process and really taking the time to understand what the tool is doing for you and how that should be integrated into the rest of your models. How you evaluate new factors with those tools is really the important piece of the puzzle.

把定性变成定量：董事会构成与创新度

I know one of the areas that you've begun applying large language models and even small language models is to these non-financial quality metrics. This is an area you're leaning into — things like board composition and ideas like innovation, things that are squishier and harder to measure and don't necessarily come with a hard numerical value for you to easily plug into your standard quant process. Can you talk a little bit about how you turn something that is more qualitative into a systematic signal, especially taking into account that you don't necessarily always get the breadth and level playing field across industry sectors and geographies that your typical traditional quant process would want and need?

One of the advantages of using these language models — or even natural language processing, which is something that we've been using for decades — is that there is a lot of availability of text data on companies around the world. So, you actually have more data available consistently for companies. Most companies have some sort of earnings transcripts or there's some news about them in the world, so you can get text information.

The challenge is: how do you extract information that's valuable from all of this text, and then how can you compare it across different companies? There's a lot of attention to detail around extracting the right information and making sure that you are comparing apples to apples with the information that you've gathered. Once you've done that, turning it into a score that's comparable to other companies in your investment universe is much easier — but it's that middle step that's pretty difficult.

The more sophisticated our models get, the more insights we can pull, and the more important that intermediate step is to make sure that the information that you're working with is really what you're thinking you're getting — and then that's able to really be that apples-to-apples comparison so you can make that investment decision.

案例：董事会作为信息网络

Maybe we can explore that with a specific example — something like board composition. Or maybe we can start with: what is the fundamental thesis behind why board composition would matter? What are you looking at with board composition, and how this is sort of working through the pipeline?

We want to think beyond just board credentials. We want to understand how boards are connected to one another — so this kind of gets back to that linkages idea. If you've got a really valuable board member — somebody who's really good, really talented — they're going to be in demand amongst different companies, and so they likely sit on a couple of different boards.

In looking at that, we can understand how these companies are connected to each other and how information flow may happen among those companies. What we find is especially for companies who are struggling, if they do have boards that are well connected, they tend to have more resiliency than their peers.

That's an example of trying to look at that both in a qualitative and quantitative way and understand that board quality, and also that board connection, to understand how information can flow among these companies.

LLM 的风险管理：幻觉、前视偏差、记忆化

One of the common concerns among quants that I talked to when talking about using large language models is that they bring their own unique risks — whether it's explicit hallucinations, there's this black box of not knowing exactly what's happening in the version of the large language model you're using, the risk of a look-ahead bias, having the model trained on data that you're trying to not incorporate at any given point in time. I was hoping you could expand on how you are thinking about incorporating large language models into the research process, given the lengthy list of potential risks that go along with using them.

Hallucination and the look-ahead bias, memorization is definitely a challenge. There are some funny examples where you're trying to ask an LLM a question and keep blind what that actual stock is, and the LLM will figure out what stock you're talking about even though you didn't tell it — and then come back with supporting evidence because it knows whether that stock did well or not.

Being able to control the data that you're working with is important. During testing, we tightly control what data we're looking at so that we can dissect the output better.

Model selection is really important. We need to choose models that have been published recently enough that they incorporate the modern LLM techniques, but that they were long ago enough that there's some period of out-of-sample testing that we can do.

We also use multiple models, so we can ask those models similar questions and see if they're coming up with similar answers. That's really part of validating the response of the model. We'll also look at asking the same model the same question and see if we get the same answer back. Also, if you change the question a little bit, do you get a hardly different answer, or do you get something that kind of reflects the degree of the change in the question?

There are a lot of nuances like that or additional levels of review that you need to do to get comfortable with the models — but I think what's most important here ties back to again us being a fundamental quant, that we want to make sure that the insights we're extracting with these LLMs tie back to the company's sales or the company's earnings. Being able to make that connection is important, and again it makes us more comfortable that the information we're extracting is valuable and the way we're extracting it will be beneficial going forward.

收尾：工作之外的痴迷

All right, Stacy, we have come to the end of the episode, and I want to finish with the same question I've been asking all of my guests to finish the episodes this season, which is: what is something outside of work that you are currently obsessed with? This could be an idea, it could be an activity, it could be a book, a show, music — just something that has you completely enraptured at the moment.

This might be a corny answer, but my kids are in their 20s now and they're adults, and we are starting to have fun with them as adults. We go out to dinner and we were just on a vacation together and we play games together — much different from when they were little. I'm really thinking about: how does that relationship evolve, and how do I keep it robust while still being their parent. That's honestly taking up a lot of time and it's a lot of fun. My kids live in the city. We're in New York City all the time. That's something I'm obsessed with at the moment.

I think any parent will agree that that's probably an obsession throughout the whole cycle. As someone at the very beginning of the phase with very young kids at home, I'm thinking about the same things — just a very different part of the age cycle. So, I love that answer. Stacy, thank you so much for joining me. This has been great.

Thank you for having me.

观看原视频 →

## 一、最反直觉的观察：一个"漂亮"的回测其实是危险信号
Stacy 提出了一个几乎所有量化人都不敢承认的悖论——**如果你的模型在 2020 年 COVID 期间表现良好，那反而说明它偏离了你的哲学**。因为 COVID 是一次基本面完全被撕裂的极端事件，一个真正基于公司基本面的模型"理应"在那段时间失效。她甚至进一步说："最可怕的回测，是那种每一年都表现好的回测——那不可能是真的。"
这颠覆了行业里"回测越平滑越好"的默认审美。它意味着 PGIM 在筛选因子时，采用的是一种**反向的可证伪性标准**：一个因子必须有可解释的失败窗口，才配进入模型。这与 Popper 的科学哲学（一个理论必须可被证伪才有科学地位）异曲同工——**量化研究的成熟标志，不是"永不失手"，而是"知道什么时候会失手"**。
## 二、跨领域连接：董事会作为"社会网络传染路径"
PGIM 把董事会成员当作一种**跨公司信息传导网络**来建模——一个稀缺、有能力的董事往往同时坐在多家公司的董事会上，这些公司因此在信息、危机应对、治理弹性上高度耦合。这其实是把**流行病学中的"超级传播者"模型**移植到了

item.title: [Lex Clips] How guerrilla warfare terrorized Missouri during the Civil War | Gary Gallagher and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

海拔与暴力的隐藏方程式

Gallagher 顺口提到的一个细节值得被放大：游击战强度与地形海拔高度相关——山地越多，游击队越活跃。东田纳西、西北卡罗来纳、西南弗吉尼亚、密苏里、肯塔基，全都符合。这不是美国内战独有的现象，而是一个跨越时空的地理暴力常数：从阿富汗的兴都库什山、越南的长山山脉、车臣的高加索、哥伦比亚 FARC 的安第斯山区，到中国革命时期的井冈山——只要一个国家想要垄断暴力，山就会成为它的对手。地形不只是背景，它本身就是一种"政治制度"，决定了国家权力能否投射到最后一公里。密苏里的恐怖，从某种意义上说，是地质学写给政治学的一封信。

规则的诞生，往往来自规则失灵的地方

一个真正反直觉的细节：现代战争法（Lieber Code 的前身）之所以被编纂，是因为 Halleck 在密苏里被游击战逼疯了。也就是说——文明战争的成文规则，不是从"正规战"的秩序中自然生长出来的，而是从最混乱、最不正规的边缘地带倒逼出来的。这是一种系统性的悖论：规则往往由异常事件催生，而不是由常态。这个模式在别处反复出现——GDPR 因剑桥分析事件而加速、航空安全手册几乎每一条都对应一次坠机、金融监管的每一次跃迁都紧跟一次崩盘。秩序是灾难的沉积岩。当你看到一部厚重的规则手册，你其实是在看一部匿名的灾难史。

"总体战"是一个视角问题，而非定义问题

Gallagher 那句被轻轻带过的话其实是全场最锋利的一刀："对那个被军队路过、牲畜被杀光、庄稼被烧掉的农民来说，这就是总体战——即使他们没杀他。" 这是一种尺度相对论：宏观史学家争论"这算不算 total war"，是在国家层面看统计；但对个体而言，总体性不是一个定义问题，而是你自己被卷入的深度。这个洞见跨领域适用——一次经济衰退在 GDP 图上是-2%，但对失业者是 100%；一次瘟疫的"温和"死亡率对失去父母的孩子是无限大。任何试图用聚合数字度量苦难的努力，都在系统性地低估底层节点的经验。50,000 名游击队员在 300 万参战者中只占 1.6%，但他们制造的恐怖占据了整个密苏里的日常心理带宽——这就是边缘节点的非线性影响力，也是今天理解恐怖主义、网络暴力、乃至算法极化的同一把钥匙。

📝 转录文本

什么是游击战？

Lex: As you mentioned Missouri, you talked about how that was the most brutal guerrilla warfare of the conflict. And maybe can you speak to what do you mean by guerrilla warfare? What kind of war was that? And then contrast with the structure, the dynamics of battles elsewhere in the war.

Gallagher: Guerrilla war is more of what I think most Americans can sort of imagine what guerrilla war is. It involves small — much, much smaller numbers of actors, obviously, on both sides. Guerrilla bands might have a few dozen members. They might have a few hundred at different times.

There are no real battles between guerrillas. There is a lot of bushwhacking — which is what they called it — ambushing people, terrorizing civilians, killing livestock, killing some civilians, killing prisoners after you've captured them, hanging some people.

半大规模的暴行与地理规律

There are a few semi-large scale ones. There's a Confederate guerrilla named Quantrill led a raid against Lawrence, Kansas, where they burned parts of the town, executed more than 150 men in the town, and terrorized the place.

There's a relationship in many places between elevation and guerrilla activity. The more mountainous or hilly, the more likely there'll be guerrillas operating. They operate in the mountains — East Tennessee, Western North Carolina, Southwestern Virginia, central... there's even some activity in parts of Texas. But Missouri and Kentucky have the worst guerrilla warfare.

It's present through the whole war. Probably involves maybe 50,000 men out of the 3 million who were in action during the war, and was very nasty — no rules.

战争法的起源

One reason that rules of war were codified was because Henry Halleck, who was a Union general in Missouri dealing with this guerrilla activity, said: we need to get some rules about who's a civilian, who's not a civilian. How do you deal with this kind of situation and that kind of situation?

Lex: What should we take away from the fact that most of the fighting had the rules of war behind it? So it is more structured.

Gallagher: I think what we take away from that supports my argument that this is a war between two mid-19th century nation states that have a sense of how you fight a war. You fight a war with national armies who are led by professional soldiers and who understand that there are limits to what you do in a war.

The war's limits expand as it goes on, but it doesn't reach the point where you have indiscriminate killing of civilians and so forth. You just don't. I mean, there's an argument whether it's a total war or not — it all depends on how you define total war.

什么才算"总体战"？

Lex: As you mentioned, in terms of how encompassing it was — as total war as it gets, because the entirety of the society was involved in it.

Gallagher: When there's wide-scale targeting of the economic infrastructure of your opponent that can be used to support the war effort — which is what you get increasingly as the war goes on, and officially when Grant is in charge as general-in-chief — then certainly that's...

If you're the farmer who experiences an army coming by and they take or kill all your livestock and destroy your crops, that's pretty much like a total war, even if they don't kill you.

战争的升级

Lex: So the war escalates.

Gallagher: Yes, the war does escalate. '62 — it takes a quantum leap in the spring and early summer of 1862. The signals are clear: this is something that we had not counted on before. And the armies are much... they're going to be much bigger. The Army of the Potomac is more than 100,000 men. There's never been an army like that in US history — nothing like that.

Lex: Mhm.

item.title: [Lex Clips] Extreme political division in US - Are we on the verge of a Civil War? | Gary Gallagher
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的观察：内战真正的门槛不是"仇恨"，而是"程序"

Gallagher 给出的判别标准出乎意料地冷静——他不看情绪温度，而看制度动作：德州和加州都"谈过"独立，但没有一个真的召开过 secession convention。1860 年的南方却是"召集了、投票了、离开了"。

这里藏着一个反直觉的洞见：内战的临界点不是言辞的激烈程度，而是"程序性动词"是否被激活。愤怒可以无限扩张而不越界，但一旦有人把动词从"威胁"换成"召集"，系统的相变就发生了。今天的美国充满了"名词化的愤怒"（政治极化、文化战争、身份对立），却几乎没有"动词化的分裂"。这也解释了一个悖论：社交媒体让分裂看起来更近，实际上可能让分裂更远——因为情绪在语言层被过度释放，反而降低了制度层被激活的概率。这有点像地震学里的"蠕滑（creep）"——持续的小滑动反而释放了应力，防止大地震。

跨领域连接：林肯、奥巴马与"生态位继承"

Gallagher 想象林肯出席奥巴马演讲的画面，看似浪漫，但里面藏着一个生态学式的结构。他描述美国是"马赛克"——新来的人嵌进去，然后成为"老马赛克"，去接纳下一批新人。

这几乎是生态学里 succession（生态演替） 的完美类比：先锋物种改造环境，为后来者创造生存条件，自己则被重新定义为"本地物种"。美国的身份政治之所以永远吵，不是因为它失败，而是因为它处于永久演替状态——没有气候顶极群落（climax community），没有终点。

这里的意外之处在于："我们是谁"这个问题无法回答，恰恰是这个国家运作的必要条件。一个能回答"我是谁"的国家（比如高度同质化的民族国家），反而丧失了容纳下一波移民的生态位。林肯时代问的是这个问题，今天还在问——问题的持续性本身就是答案。

隐藏的系统性真相：Gallagher 是"悲观的乐观主义者"

注意 Gallagher 自我描述的方式——"我是个爱抱怨、不乐观的人"，但紧接着给出的是深度的乐观。这不是矛盾，而是一种认知结构：长期研究灾难的人反而更难被当下的噪音吓到。

这与创伤研究里的一个反常规发现相呼应：急诊科医生和战地记者的焦虑水平往往低于普通白领。为什么？因为他们的"参照系被拉长了"。当你日常工作是研究 60 万人死亡的战争，Twitter 上的骂战就无法激活你的威胁探测系统。

这提示一个更普遍的模式：判断"当下是否危险"的能力，与你掌握的历史深度成反比关系的噪音敏感度。今天大量的"内战预言"来自那些参照系只有 10-20 年的观察者。而一个研究了 50 年 19 世纪的人告诉你"没那么严重"——这句话的信号价值，远高于任何实时民调。

一个隐藏的推论：如果你想校准自己对时代的判断，最有效的方法不是读更多新闻，而是读更远的历史。近视和远视，在时间维度上同样存在。

📝 转录文本

我们是否处于新内战的边缘？

Lex： People in the modern day, I have to ask you about this, kind of casually talk about the new Civil War in America.

Gary： Yes.

Lex： As somebody who studied the Civil War, do you think our country today is divided to a degree that's on the verge of something like the Civil War of the 19th century?

Gary： No, I really don't. And I don't mean to play down the degree to which we are divided. We are divided. We do resemble the 1850s now in that I think the first impulse on the part of people on either side of the political spectrum is to attribute the worst to the other side, and to not acknowledge any good on the other side — to attribute the worst possible characteristics to the other side, and to have inflammatory rhetoric coming from various directions that really seeks to sort of stir up as much unhappiness and controversy as possible. I think we're like the 1850s in that way.

But in terms of whether we're really at the point where the kind of actions that I've dealt with in my study of the Civil War — I don't think we're anywhere near that. And I mean, I really don't. If we get there, that will be heartbreaking. But I just don't see it.

I don't see physical assaults against members of Congress on the floor of the Congress. States talk about seceding if things don't go their way. Texas talked about seceding when Obama was elected. California talked about seceding when Trump was elected. But you know what? Neither one of them called a secession convention and had delegates go to it. When Lincoln was elected, they called conventions. They voted to secede, and they left the nation. So that's different to me than talking about it, and threatening it, and posing different scenarios.

结构性平行与联邦的韧性

Lex： Are there genuine structural parallels between that time and now? If you can linger on that.

Gary： Well, structurally a state can call a convention if it wants to, to talk about whatever it wants to talk about. So I suppose that structure is still in place. But I haven't seen any serious movement toward doing something like that.

And I think there's a real cohesion and resilience to the union, as we've talked about. I think people, despite the discourse and the bickering — [snorts] — there's a real love of nation that maybe is not often expressed explicitly. But there is a sense that we're all in this kind of together.

Lex： And then we're yelling at each other kind of like you have a family at Thanksgiving dinner where there's very passionate yelling and arguing, but there's a kind of assumption that we're still a family.

Gary： At least that's the hope.

什么是美国？马赛克与磁石

Lex： You know, one of the questions that the Civil War asked is — what is America? So I have to ask you, from over 50 years of studying the Civil War: what do you think? What is this country? What is this union? What is the core that makes us who we are?

Gary： Well, I think in a lot of ways it's much of what it was in the mid-19th century. I still think it's a magnet. I mean, people come from everywhere here now. They literally come from everywhere here now. And everybody doesn't find a nice easy road here, by any means. And there are lots of things wrong with the United States. But I still think the United States has a role in the world that's unlike — I won't say any other place, but I can't think of a place that's quite like it — that has so many people coming from so many places who somehow manage to fit into this mosaic.

And then I think most people do have a way to fit into the mosaic, and then they become part of the old mosaic when the next group of people who are not like them come in, and those are the ones who are the new ones fitting in.

想象林肯遇见奥巴马

Sometimes I think about — and sorry to romanticize it — but because I do think that Barack Obama is one of the great speech makers of my lifetime. And I sometimes imagine what Lincoln would have thought if he could attend an Obama speech, if he saw that Obama became president — that an African-American became president of the United States of America. It seems like such a trivial thing to say. But I think it's not trivial at all. It's one of the great accomplishments of our country.

I think one of Lincoln's great attributes was his humanity — it comes through so many things that he wrote. His real appreciation for people who faced long odds, worked against the odds, didn't begin with advantages in their favor, and so forth. I think he — and his ability to grow — I think he would have handled that actually pretty well, much better than many other people I can think of from the mid-19th century. I think he had genuine humanity. I don't think you can read all the things he wrote and not come to that conclusion.

Does he check all our boxes now? Of course he doesn't. Was he prejudiced by our standards in some ways? Of course he was. But I think he would have handled that pretty well, and he would have still been really tall. Even in our time, he'd be way taller than most people. [laughter]

250 周年之际的希望

Lex： 250th birthday — what gives you hope about the future of America?

Gary： What gives me hope — and I'm a grouchy, not optimistic person in a lot of ways.

Lex： You had some moments of optimism today.

Gary： I was just going to say — I do have moments of optimism, and one of them I have is in the resiliency of this republic. I really do — and it's genuine optimism, I'm not just… and I know a lot of people will think that it's naive, but I really — because I see what it's been through, and it's emerged, and it's gone forward. And the trajectory — this is something that Obama has commented on, as have many others — the trajectory is in the right direction. With lots of things you wish were different, but the overall trajectory is in the right direction. I really do believe that, and that's why I tend to be in that regard optimistic.

Lex 的结语：一个繁荣中的国度

Lex： I think there's a few folks on the interwebs that talk about the decline of the American empire. Even using the word "empire" — I'm one of the folks who thinks that America's flourishing. It is a beacon of hope and freedom in the world. And there's a lot to criticize — the militarism, and a lot of different aspects that are hypocritical, and it is not always living up to the great ideals that it supposedly represents. But at least it is striving towards that, and it is still a home for the great diversity of humans, as you've mentioned, that I think is one of the great beautiful aspects about this country.

And the full mess of it — the drama, the arguments, the heated passion, the chaos, the thing that feels like chaos, but I think ultimately will lead to progress — I love all of it. I think it is the greatest nation on earth. So on this 250th birthday, I hope there's 250 years more. And I'm truly grateful that there's somebody like you studying our great history. And I'm grateful for this wonderful conversation today.

Gary： I appreciate the invitation. It's been fun.

Lex： Thank you, Gary.

## 一个反直觉的观察：内战真正的门槛不是"仇恨"，而是"程序"
Gallagher 给出的判别标准出乎意料地冷静——他不看情绪温度，而看**制度动作**：德州和加州都"谈过"独立，但没有一个真的召开过 secession convention。1860 年的南方却是"召集了、投票了、离开了"。
这里藏着一个反直觉的洞见：**内战的临界点不是言辞的激烈程度，而是"程序性动词"是否被激活**。愤怒可以无限扩张而不越界，但一旦有人把动词从"威胁"换成"召集"，系统的相变就发生了。今天的美国充满了"名词化的愤怒"（政治极化、文化战争、身份对立），却几乎没有"动词化的分裂"。这也解释了一个悖论：**社交媒体让分裂看起来更近，实际上可能让分裂更远**——因为情绪在语言层被过度释放，反而降低了制度层被激活的概率。这有点像地震学里的"蠕滑（creep）"——持续的小滑动反而释放了应力，防止大地震。
