Gallagher 想象林肯出席奥巴马演讲的画面，看似浪漫，但里面藏着一个**生态学式的结构**。他描述美国是"马赛克"——新来的人嵌进去，然后成为

item.title: [GoldRepublic Global] Why Peter Schiff is Sounding the Alarm Now
item.dc:creator: GoldRepublic Global
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的镜像：日本不是"引爆点"，而是美国的时间机器

大多数人把日本危机看作"外部风险"，但真正令人不安的洞察是：日本正在提前上演美国五年后的剧本。日本是全球第三大债权国，储蓄率高、经常账户顺差、政府长期压低利率——它拥有美国早已失去的所有"缓冲垫"。如果连日本这样"最优等生的债务国"都无法承受利率正常化，那么财政赤字占GDP 6%以上、外债依赖度极高的美国，凭什么认为自己能全身而退？

Schiff 说日本可能是"戳破泡沫的针"，但更深层的模式是：日元套利交易的解绑，本质上是全球流动性从"借入方语言"切换回"储蓄方语言"的过程。过去二十年，全世界习惯用日元这种"零成本燃料"驱动风险资产，就像整个金融系统跑在一种廉价合成汽油上。一旦这种燃料涨价，不是某一辆车抛锚，而是整条高速公路同时减速。

二、跨领域连接：AI 资本开支 = 铁路泡沫 + 思科时刻 + 页岩油悖论

Schiff 提到 Nvidia 给客户提供融资让客户买自己的产品——这不只是"思科时刻"的重演，它同时符合三个历史模式的叠加：

  • 1870s 美国铁路狂潮：过度建设的物理基础设施，最终多数运营商破产，但铁轨本身留下了；
  • 1999 思科的 vendor financing：把自己的收入借给客户来"制造"下一季度收入；
  • 2014-2020 页岩油繁荣：现金流永远为负，用债务补贴增长，直到利率上升让整个模式失效。

真正让人意外的观察：AI 芯片的"折旧曲线"更接近页岩油井而不是数据中心服务器。Schiff 说"这些应该算 opex 而不是 capex"——如果 GPU 三年后就被下一代淘汰，那么整个"AI 基础设施投资潮"在会计意义上是被系统性错分类的。这意味着当前 Mag 7 的自由现金流估值中，可能隐藏着一个数千亿美元的"隐性经营支出黑洞"。

三、被低估的隐喻：Michael Saylor 模式是"金融永动机"的最新变种

Strategy 的机制值得放在更抽象的框架下看：它是一个用股权稀释来支付优先股股息、用优先股融资来购买 Bitcoin、用 Bitcoin 上涨来支撑股价的自反馈循环。这不是新东西——它在数学结构上等同于：

  • 麦道夫的庞氏结构（用新钱付旧息）；
  • 长期资本管理公司的杠杆嵌套（用一个头寸的账面盈利去抵押另一个头寸）；
  • 中国房企"三条红线"前的预售融资模式（用未来现金流为过去债务背书）。

惊人的对称性：当 Saylor "不敢卖 Bitcoin 换股息"时，他和日本央行"不敢加息刺破日元套利"、美联储"不敢让利率反映真实通胀"——处于完全相同的博弈困境：主动承认现实会立即触发崩溃，回避现实则会让最终崩溃规模更大。这三个看似无关的角色（一个 CEO、一个央行、一个储备银行）实际上共享同一种"负外部性时间转移"的结构性懦弱。

四、一个 Schiff 自己没说透的观察

Schiff 反复呼吁大家关注他的社交媒体增长——这本身就是一个信号。当一个通缩派/硬通货派的追随者以每月10万速度暴涨时，通常意味着大众叙事拐点已经比价格拐点先到。历史上黄金/白银的大牛市中段，往往对应"看空法币"内容创作者的粉丝爆发期，而不是牛市顶部。这是一种反向的社会情绪指标：粉丝暴涨还不算见顶，粉丝停止增长而金价仍涨——那才是。

📝 转录文本

开场

"the main looming problem that the financial markets, the global economy are going to be confronted with. But the initial reaction, you know, people are going to panic when when this happens."

Welcome to the Microscopic Podcast. My name is Alex A. Jonof. I'm your host. And today I'm joined by Peter Schiff again.

Peter, welcome back.

Oh, thanks for having me back on your podcast.

Well, Peter, last time we we saw each other was uh in Amsterdam uh we uh we had the 15-year anniversary of our company Gold Republic. Jim Rickerts was there as well. We had also a very long debate in which you you found yourself uh looking very old apparently. I could see in one of your one of your videos. Well, everyone knows how young you look uh how how long you look in real life and and now.

Um but um we we spoke about a lot of very important topics as well and I uh I want to give a bit of a followup based on the topics that we discussed. You also had some disagreements with with Jim uh mostly most uh mostly about bonds where the US treasuries were headed but also about the tariffs with the ruling of the Supreme Court uh ruling uh about the tariffs. And I would like to to start with first um um well a bit of an overall overview about what you think were the most important developments in the last six months since we actually saw each other.

利率、债券与关税裁决

Well, I think if you're going to, you know, bring up the points of disagreements with Rickards, I thought interest rates would rise, and that's exactly what's happened. I mean, bond yields have moved. Uh, in the US, the 30-year Treasury hit a 20-year high. Uh, last week, uh, 10-year Treasury not that far behind. We've seen big increases in rates, uh, in other countries. I think 30-year high in Japan for their 10-year uh Japanese government bond.

Uh and the Supreme Court did exactly what I said they were going to do. They struck down the tariffs as being unconstitutional for the very reasons that I said they were unconstitutional. I don't remember why Jim Rickards thought that they were constitutional or that the court would uphold them, but uh to me it was so clearly uh a violation of law.

In fact, Trump recently announced some more tariffs. They're unconstitutional, too. So, we'll see what happens there. Uh these related to or relate to forced labor, but there there is no forced labor. It's just again he's he's he's manufacturing uh a lie to try to just get around the constitutional requirement that tariffs need to be uh you know, enacted by Congress. They just can't be imposed unilaterally by the president.

Now, there are some uh unique circumstances where Congress has authorized presidential tariffs. Uh but then Trump applies those to areas where they don't belong and and so you can't do that. I mean, if Congress has given you specific authority to do something, you can't do something else but then claim your power relates to that authority when it clearly does not.

Yes. And uh that's that's we actually talked about this with with Jim in the previous interview that uh I recorded with him actually a few days ago. Maybe next time I should have you two at the same time to follow up on those disagreements so you can talk it out live.

日本可能是引爆全球危机的"针"

Um but um yeah so that's one part and then the other one is obviously the fact that uh you also gave a broad warning about the US and the debt and the dollar crisis and now you say also that Japan may be the pin that pops it. And thereby I want to also ask you what uh changed and what probability do you put on that Japan-led global crisis in the next 12 months?

Well, I was talking about that at the time as well because the Japanese yen continues to fall. Uh that's putting more upward pressure on inflation, interest rates, and trade deficits in Japan. The Bank of Japan sees the weak yen as a problem and is trying to use forex intervention uh to stop it, but that's not going to work.

Um, the Bank of Japan still has its policy rate down at 1%. Uh, that's much too low. And the Japanese government is still running deficits, budget deficits, about 2% of GDP. I mean, that's not that high relative to other countries, but given how much debt they have, uh, it's worsening the problem.

So I think we need to see either a substantial increase in the policy rate in Japan and/or uh government spending cuts or tax hikes in Japan. And I think uh those have the potential to cause a lot of problems globally for credit markets, stock markets.

Uh you know I I don't see how that happens in a vacuum when you know Japan is one of the world's largest creditors. You know, it's number three now. It used to be number one for you know three decades. And now a couple years ago Germany passed it and then last year China passed it. But you know America — we're the world's biggest debtor nation, so we're not even included in the group of creditor nations. Uh we haven't been a creditor nation since the 1980s.

Uh but Japan has been a creditor nation for a long time. They own a lot of overseas assets. They own a lot of US assets in particular that would need to be sold. I think if we saw big increase in Japanese interest rates and that would also uh put a lot of pressure on the yen carry trade where the yen is used as a funding currency for a lot of investments — a lot of them in the United States — uh risk on, you know, risk assets like stocks but also treasuries. A lot of US treasuries are bought with borrowed yen and uh unraveling that or unwinding that trade would you know really push US bond prices down and interest rates up and be very problematic for the US.

日元套利交易的解绑

So let's say if if the BOJ raises then towards say 3% and the yen rises, why must Japanese investors then sell foreign assets rather than hedge the currency? Uh maybe accept lower return or even wait out the loss.

Well, if the yen really starts to rise and Japanese interest rates go up, that blows up the whole carry because the cost of the carry is increasing, but now you're you're losing money on the exchange rate. So, it doesn't make sense to maintain those positions. It makes sense to, you know, unwind them.

So you would sell whatever you bought with the borrowed yen when rates were low and you'd pay off those loans now that rates are higher, especially since the yen is rising. So that would be the obvious thing to do. Sell US stocks, sell US bonds and uh repay your Japanese debt. And then to the extent they're going to invest, you know, they could invest in yen denominated assets rather than dollar denominated assets.

Mhm. And how how large do you think is this yen-funded carry trade? Uh you think how much uh uh how much must it unwind? What was the um the bought with it? Uh and how much force?

I don't know exactly the size of it off the top of my head but I imagine it's pretty large because it's been going on for a long time. And especially with you know the yen recently hit a 40-year low against the dollar. So that yen weakness has been a big driver of that trade and if we start to see a reversal of the yen uh that would be a big driver to to unwind the trade.

So walk me through maybe through the the let's say the the first dominoes that would fall in the case of um yeah this this first big margin call. Who would get margin called?

Yeah, I don't know if it's really a margin call, but it would act like kind of a margin call, but there may actually be some margin calls, you know, depending on how a lot of these trades are financed. But even if they don't, if the Bank of Japan doesn't act to aggressively raise rates, um the yen could crash and that creates a whole another set of problems in Japan. But if the yen crashes, then that's going to put even more pressure on the Bank of Japan to hike rates even higher than had they hiked them before the yen crash.

So, you know, there there's a huge crisis building in Japan. But, you know, that's just one of many. There are a lot of problems uh you know, a lot a lot of pins that could prick the bubble. That's just one of them.

美国全面泡沫与 AI 资本开支

You know, the whole US market is in big bubble. Stock market, bond market, real estate market, crypto, you got this, you know, AI um bubble — not necessarily in the potential of AI, which may in fact be underestimated. It's just um the valuations that are being placed on a handful of companies that are perceived to be the beneficiaries and the amount of money that is now being spent that you know is being borrowed and that we really don't have. The amount of capex uh is not sustainable given the savings uh that we have to to finance it and and the other competing needs uh for for the money.

And so I want to bring it back maybe to the — because you also mentioned that uh the Japanese government owns more than $1.1 trillion of of treasuries and could sell them, and this has obviously an impact on on the US market, not just the bond market but also stocks, all kinds of assets. So how much control do you think uh uh the government actually has on on those um on those treasuries, because they're also um split across uh Japan resident holdings, public and private, um?

Yeah look, you know, the Japanese government has about 1.1 trillion of treasuries. Uh so other than the Federal Reserve they're the largest creditor of the US government.

Um, one thing that the Japanese could do to improve their situation would be to sell off a good chunk of those treasuries and buy back their own JGBs. So they could reduce the JGBs outstanding and also take advantage of the strength of the dollar relative to the yen to do this at a good time on the exchange rate — because when they sell their treasuries, they're also selling dollars to buy back yen that are cheap uh to buy back uh the JGB uh that that they they would be retiring. So that would help.

But it's not just the Japanese government that I think would be liquidating treasuries. It would be Japanese life insurance companies, pensions, other private investors who have been riding uh the dollar rally in treasuries. They would need to reverse that, especially if they can get good yields on yen denominated debt. They wouldn't need the dollar denominated debt and they would want to avoid it if the dollar was going to start falling, because that the weakness in the dollar relative to the yen would reverse any kind of gain they were getting by holding higher yielding treasuries. But that yield advantage is going to shrink dramatically if the Japanese really start hiking rates.

中东、能源与日本进口账单

And so now because you also mentioned other externalities — there's lots of crisis going on at the same time at the moment. And obviously the Strait of Hormuz with the energy choke is also one of them. Japan imports mostly all of its energy and the latest oil shock is actually worsening the import bill. Um how much of uh your crisis probability depends on the Iran conflict and the expensive oil that we see at the moment? And how much would take off if the oil would go back to let's say $70 a barrel?

Well, you know, I think oil prices are headed higher regardless of how the Iran war plays out. Obviously, there are certain uh ways it could play out where oil prices go a lot higher, but right now there's a lot of uncertainty surrounding the situation there anyway. And I think that uncertainty is going to persist even if we somehow come to a peace, which seems to be very elusive.

Um, but I think prices are heading higher and yes, that compounds the problem for Japan, especially if the yen goes down. Because if the yen is falling and oil prices are rising in dollar terms, they're rising even more in yen terms and and yeah, that worsens their terms of trade because Japan imports pretty much all of its energy. Uh, unlike the United States where we produce a lot of energy that Japan doesn't. So it's a bigger problem. They also import a lot of food and you know that's getting more expensive too.

AI 资本支出的可持续性

So you've also mentioned just before the AI bubble. And if Japan is then not necessarily the pin, because you've also mentioned that everything is playing out on different fronts. Um is then AI capital spending the next candidate?

Yeah. Well, I think AI capital spending is unsustainable. And what the markets don't yet understand uh or haven't figured out is, you know, will this capex spending um ultimately be justified by the income that the companies who are spending all this money will be able to generate off of that capex?

You know, there's a lot of optimism about just how lucrative the business is going to be. But the problem is providing access to AI may not be as high a margin business as is contemplated. There could be a lot more competition that comes into the market. Uh it could be commoditized. We could have more efficient ways of providing that. And it may turn out that the companies that spent so much money spent too much money. They may never be able to recover a decent return on that capital investment.

And a lot of the capital investment is not even really capex, in that so much of it is going into chips that you know, who knows what their useful life is going to be. Uh they may be obsolete in a few years uh when there are better ones on the market. Uh so a lot of this capex, you know, to me looks more like operating expenses that are going to be recurring. So they spend a lot of money, but now they're going to have to spend it again, you know, buying the the the the better ones that come out.

Uh meanwhile, you know, the companies that were investing a lot in the data centers and all this, they started with a lot of cash to invest. They, you know, they they were cash cows and but they burned through all that cash and now they're borrowing money. And now you're even seeing the recipients like Nvidia is announcing this major financing so that it can loan money to its customers so its customers can keep buying its goods.

But, you know, when you get into that situation, when you're vendor financing, are the earnings real? Because you're you're just earning your own money. You're you're lending your customers money. What if they can't pay you back? I mean, we saw that movie before during the dot-com bubble uh with Cisco and all the vendor financing and all the customers that they loaned money to that ultimately went bankrupt.

And the internet was of course real. I mean, a lot of the hype surrounding the internet was justified. It's just that almost all the stocks related to the internet went bankrupt. And so I think AI is potentially a lot more of a gamechanger than the internet and has even greater potential to improve uh living standards, you know, of humans on Earth. But we could be seeing a repeat of that where most of these AI companies, the early uh companies uh end up losing a lot of money on it, or at least the investors too end up losing a lot of money because they overpaid for a lot of stocks.

Now, you could look back and say, well, look at Amazon. Amazon is a lot higher than it was during the dotcom bubble, which is true, but it went down about 80% or more when that bubble popped. And yes, with the benefit of hindsight, Amazon was one of the few winners, but you know, the vast majority of companies went to zero. So investors lost everything. But yes, Amazon uh found a way to uh really parlay the internet in a way that you know early on Amazon was just a bookstore. They were just selling books online and that was not a viable business model. Had Amazon stayed a bookstore, they probably would have gone out of business. It's because of the way Jeff Bezos ran that company and the way it evolved uh that's why it did as well as it did.

AI 崩盘的传染路径

And so in this whole AI capex bust, um would then become like a banking uh or or credit event? Or is it mainly then just an equity valuation reset? Like how would it spread out in terms of contagion and how would the US stock market also react to that, being also a big proportion of that?

Well, it could be both because um you know rates could be headed higher just due to all the corporate borrowing pushing up rates because of competitive uses for capital. But also if there's defaults, then there have losses and you know now you've got you know that to deal with.

Uh so yeah there you know this is a big problem. And at the same time the US government is borrowing a tremendous amount of money to finance, you know, almost a $40 trillion deficit. So, you've got government borrowing, you've got all this AI related borrowing.

Um, who's doing the saving? You know, there's, you know, the savings are limited and, uh, the borrowing needs are rising. That just pushes up rates, but that makes sustaining the credit that much more difficult because now the debtors have a much higher burden when it comes to paying interest on the debt, which you know may not even be possible. They may not be able to service the debt at the higher rates.

油价、美元与全球滞胀

So just earlier we've talked about Houthis um lightly and you just said also that you see oil going much higher. How much higher and what would be the main catalyst apart from the obvious situation that we see in the Gulf uh with the war in Iran? Um what's your full analysis around that?

Well, you know, I think demand for energy is going to continue to rise not just because of AI but just you know for other factors uh in the economy. But I think the real catalyst would be if we get a breakdown in the US dollar, which we haven't had yet. It's something I've been expecting, but it's something that hasn't happened.

But I think when the dollar really starts to fall, and I'm talking about versus other fiat currencies, not, you know, in terms of gold, where the dollar has already broken down — although it's bounced from its lows uh earlier this year, but I think gold now has a lot of support around 4,000 and is getting ready for another big rally. But when the dollar really starts to fall against other fiat currencies, that's really going to be a catalyst for a much bigger rise in the dollar price of oil. Because as the dollar starts to fall, if oil prices stay the same, that amounts to a decline in oil prices for everybody else. But I think the world will respond to lower prices by buying more and that will push up uh the price in dollars.

And what about then other commodities? Because we've just talked about oil, but there's all kinds of other commodities that are impacted about the choke point in supply. Do you also believe — Jim and I talked about this a few days ago — that this would be the onset of a global economic slowdown with uh a huge rise in inflation that we haven't seen since the 70s, a resurgence of the previous wave we just witnessed a few years ago?

Yeah. I mean I do believe that you know global stagflation, particularly you know maybe in the developed you know Western economies, is going to be what defines uh the next several years. I think we've underinvested in capacity for all sorts of raw materials and I think commodity prices are going to be headed a lot higher um along with overall inflation based on all the money that's been created by the central banks. Especially since COVID, but even going back to the days prior. Before COVID they after COVID rather they kicked it into a higher gear.

So we have a lot of inflationary forces that have been built in that are going to be uh you know rearing their head, as well as increased demand and and uh inadequate supply in a lot of commodities. So that's a recipe for much much higher prices. We're also going to have higher interest rates. Um higher inflation, higher interest rates, more expensive commodities, uh and you know, we could see recession and bear markets uh in stocks.

美联储会加息吗？

And that's actually a good segue to then uh what I've seen lately saying that there's um big likeliness that the Fed will hike interest rates uh with 25 basis points by tomorrow. Uh that those odds have risen above 35% for the first time after the inflation data. Um do you believe this is really likely?

Well, you know, I don't think they're going to hike rates. I guess it is a coin toss, but I think that they're still going to err on uh the side of staying pat. I think um they have at least something to justify it based on. There's some numbers that they can hide behind that might suggest that inflation may have slowed a bit or the economy is weakening a bit.

But I think they're also likely to hide behind these task forces that they created to study the problems and come up with solutions. So they may be saying, "Look, we're waiting to get the results and the recommendations from the task forces."

So that might — and you know, if they don't move in this meeting, I think the odds that they move the next meeting are even lower because now we're getting a lot closer to the election and they don't want to take the chance of spooking the markets uh when the election's around the corner. So, I think if the Fed is going to hike rates before the elections, they got to do it tomorrow.

But I agree, if they do it, it's not going to be a big move. And I think, you know, moving up by 25 basis points does nothing to change the dynamic. So, if the Fed thinks rates are too low, a quarter point rate hike is not going to do anything about it.

Well, it's a bit of a tit for tat as well in terms of the bond market and the fact that they aren't able to also really uh finance all those interest rates on the debt, right? I mean, the next 12 months around $8 trillion of treasuries need to be rolled — the average coupon is around 3.3%, the two years around uh 4.3%. So, that's a huge debt load uh and just an interest payment alone as well. Um the question is can they even hike rates?

Well, yeah. Every time they hike rates, they do make it more difficult for the US government, which has been rolling over more and more of their debt short term, you know. So, they're not even, you know, borrowing for 10 years or 30 years. They're borrowing, you know, for a year or less. But yes, it's going to make it more expensive if they just want to, you know, borrow for 90 days. They're going to pay higher rates.

And yeah, I mean it's already happening. I mean, if you look at the net interest expense annualized in June of the US government, we spent 1.6 trillion on interest. That was the entire federal budget as late as like 1997. And now we're spending that much money just on interest, right? Forgetting about everything else.

And but how much more do you think that they can raise interest? I mean there must be a limit.

Well, there's obviously a limit to how much the market can bear, but rates should be a lot higher given how, you know, much debt we have and how much inflation we're going to have. So, uh, rates are still much too low. They should be a lot higher. The problem is we can't afford to pay the rates that are as high as they need to be. That's why the Fed has been artificially suppressing them. But that has other adverse consequences that you know you're seeing with the rise of the cost of living which is being pushed up and other you know misallocations of resources that result from the artificial suppression of interest rates.

黄金与白银

And now let's talk about gold. Your favorite topic. Um, we've had nearly, I think, 900 billion dollars wiped out from gold and silver in just the last 36 hours. Gold is down 2.4% erasing roughly 680 billion. Silver down roughly 5.5% which is wiping another 190 billion. And then in this whole context, we still have a war in the Middle East. We have inflation fears and market uncertainty rising. So how is gold behaving and what are the mechanics behind — and how yeah how do you see this?

Yeah. Well, you can't look at the loss of value of gold and silver without appreciating the big gain that preceded that loss. Uh even though gold is down again today, we're still above $4,000 an ounce. Uh so up until a few months ago that was a very high price. Uh so the fact that gold is not 5,500 I think is a lot less significant than the fact that it's at 4,000.

And the same thing with silver. Uh you know silver — yes it's not 120 which is where it got — but it's 57 and change. So it broke out. But I mean for years and years silver was trading around 20 bucks and maybe it can get up to 30 and it would come down. Uh so all of that overhead resistance has now been cleared out and silver has positioned itself for another huge bull market even if it's you know had a correction uh in the first breakout of that bull market.

Um and I think right now investors were a bit disappointed in the way gold reacted to the war. Again, ignoring the fact that gold went up before the war started and part of that rally may have been the anticipation of the war. And so it was a buy the rumor, sell the fact.

And now you've got gold traders spooked by all the tough talk coming out of the Fed and about how now there's a new sheriff in town and he's going to be real tough on inflation unlike his predecessors. That's all BS. That's just talk. He's trying to buy some uh some cheap credibility on inflation by just talking about how tough he's going to be. But, you know, even when he was asked uh in the Senate in the hearings the other week, what are you going to do about high inflation? How are you going to bring it down? He had three policies and they all amounted to talking about it and doing nothing because the Fed can't do anything but talk. And the markets will figure this out.

And you know, gold prices are going to hit new record highs if not this year, next year. And the same with silver probably. So you — I would just be buying the pullbacks.

没有天花板的价格目标

Now how do you see this as major factors that will contribute to this way up? And let's say what would be your price target personally with a certain date in mind?

Well, I don't really have a target because I don't think that gold or silver have ceilings. Um because I don't think the dollar has a floor. The dollar could lose all of its value, in which case gold and silver prices would be infinite when you priced them in in something that was completely worthless.

Uh, but I just have a price target of higher. I think that you'll need more and more dollars to buy the same quantity of gold or silver. And so to the extent that you don't want to spend or invest your dollars today, you want to save to potentially invest or spend in the future, you should not hold dollars. You should hold gold or silver instead of dollars. And the same likely applies to a lot of other fiat currencies. Like you know you're in Europe. So you know I would prefer gold and silver to the euro obviously.

矿业股与能源成本

Um and now uh let's like talk a bit more also about miners because miners have also been I would say affected by all of that and there's something in the equation that also increases the cost of output and this is obviously energy. So, how do you think that this — and this is a question from uh from our audience — how do you think that this uh energy supply choke uh will affect the mining sector?

Well, I don't think it's going to have that big an impact. I mean, sure, energy prices are a major cost for the mining stocks. Uh but, you know, the mining stocks didn't get that much of a benefit from the big drop in oil prices relative to gold prices. So, I think the fact that oil's backed up a bit is not going to be the primary driver.

I think earnings of the gold mining companies are going to continue to be very strong. Uh they're going to continue to beat estimates and grow. And I think the stocks are undervalued even if the earnings are less uh than what they're likely to be uh if uh they end up spending more on energy.

And I do think that eventually this short-term negative correlation that we've seen between gold and oil is going to break down. And I do think that eventually if oil prices really start to move up, gold prices will move up along with oil, not down.

So you think that the the ratio would actually be intact and both would move accordingly in the same direction?

Yeah. Despite the way they've traded recently, I think the long-term trend would be that oil and gold move up together.

十年配置视角

And so this is a question for my colleague Bart Branch. You met him as well. And his question was, what would you focus on on a 10-year basis? Uh would it be mining, energy? Uh and does it have a specific focus on area or country or continent, um more specifically?

Well you know I have more mining than energy investments but I have both. And uh so I think both sectors are going to do well and I have you know investments you know around the world uh in in those resources you know including the United States but but but but you know broader up in Canada uh in Australia um some South America. Not as much in Europe. I mean there's not a lot of mining going on in Europe. Um but there are some — there are some energy stocks there that I own you know. Mining, I mean I have some copper names there and you know.

Mhm. Is there any specific stocks that you think are worth looking into?

Well you know I don't really get into the specific stocks so much in these interviews. But you know just in general I mean I like the resource names and uh I like value stocks. I like stocks that offer good dividends that are earning a lot of money today, not companies that just have the promise of future earnings because they may never deliver on those promises. Uh a bird in hand, I think, is is what you want as an investor.

Uh and there are plenty of opportunities right now around the world uh to buy that. And in the emerging markets — I mean broadly speaking uh emerging markets ex-tech, you know, because there's a lot of these AI related stocks that have you know also blown up — uh but apart from that I think there's a lot of value in a lot of the traditional uh you know emerging market names that I believe are really going to benefit once the dollar starts to weaken and the weakness in the dollar translates into higher purchasing power and more economic activity within the emerging market economies.

Bitcoin 与 Michael Saylor 模式

And now let's move to your third most favorite topic which is — Bitcoin. Bitcoin. I'm kidding. But you do talk a lot about Bitcoin and you also do not hold back when there's any type of crash or negative news about it uh to comment about how it's uh yeah — all your views on that. And most likely and most uh yeah more specifically um Strategy, which was MicroStrategy before, and the model that it uses to uh get public capital markets to accumulate Bitcoin and increase Bitcoin per diluted share. So what do you think is uh the Michael Saylor model? Um what makes it so unsustainable?

Well, first of all, the main reason I talk about Bitcoin is because Bitcoin is being marketed to people who might otherwise buy gold. Bitcoin is being sold as a digital alternative to gold, but superior to gold. So, I'm going to push back against that because I am an advocate that people should buy gold. And to the extent that they're being conned into buying Bitcoin instead, that's running counter to what I'm trying to accomplish. So I see Bitcoin as a threat to people who might otherwise have bought gold but end up buying Bitcoin instead. So I want to try to minimize that happening.

Um now moving to Strategy. Yeah. One of the big reasons for Bitcoin's rally has been all of the money that has been spent on Bitcoin by Strategy. Strategy has spent over $60 billion buying Bitcoin. And it's not just that it's bought Bitcoin, but other people know that it's going to buy Bitcoin and so they buy it too uh because they want to, you know, ride on his coattails. And so that's been a big supporter of the market.

Well, now Strategy has stopped buying Bitcoin. Um, and a lot of the Bitcoin that it bought, it issued preferred shares to pay for it, and now it's obligated to make large dividend payments on those preferreds. So, not only is it not buying Bitcoin, it's now selling common stock in order to raise the money to pay the yield on the preferred stock.

So that basically means that the biggest Bitcoin buyer is no longer in the market and I think that is a significant development for Bitcoin. I think the price is going to head a lot lower and so will the price of Strategy shares. Because if Saylor keeps selling them he's diluting uh shareholders, and in fact he used to talk about Bitcoin yield. That was the big measure. Well, two months ago, year to date, the Bitcoin yield was 13.3. As of Monday, it's down to 4 and a half because over the last several weeks, he's been deliberately destroying shareholder value, common shareholder value to raise cash to try to shore up the preferred shares.

And so now Strategy stocks — I think the whole thing is going to unravel with Strategy going down, Bitcoin going down, the preferreds going down, the yields going up, and just a self-perpetuating uh spiral.

So, I'm actually surprised that Bitcoin is still as high as it is. Especially with the sell-off we're getting in tech stocks the last few days, I would think that Bitcoin would go down more. So, it's kind of been held up. So, been a little bit more resilient, but there's a limit, I think, to how long it could defy gravity here.

Bitcoin 财库公司的终局

And you also see more and more I think Bitcoin treasury companies popping up as well. Um, and —

Not anymore. I think those treasury companies already popped up and now they're pooped out. You know, the people that bought stock in these companies have lost a lot of money. So, I think — I don't think that more of these Bitcoin Treasury companies are going to start winding down. I don't think we're going to get more starting up. There's no use for them. It's not even a viable business model. I mean, what kind of business is just buying Bitcoin? I mean, anybody can buy Bitcoin. I don't need a business to do it for me.

Well, I guess it's a bit of a speculative layer on top of the Bitcoin it owns by paying like a premium uh for um —

But they're not paying a premium. Look, Strategy is trading at a big discount to the Bitcoin that it owns. So, nobody's paying a premium to buy a Bitcoin treasury company. Bitcoin treasury companies are being punished. Their shares trade for less. So, when they raise money to buy Bitcoin, they destroy value. They don't create it anymore. The bloom is off that rose.

I meant like at the time — obviously now it's the NAV is below um for at least Strategy. I don't know about the other companies. Uh but do you see like any threshold where in terms of the the the price of Bitcoin or actually the dividends they need to pay where it just fully breaks or uh well what's what —

I mean Strategy is not required to pay the dividends. It can terminate them but that doesn't eliminate the obligation. They still accrue. But if he stops paying the dividend, you know, this whole house of cards he built is going to collapse. So he kind of has to pay the dividend, but he doesn't want to sell Bitcoin to cover it — which he should — because he's afraid that will crash Bitcoin. So instead, he sacrifices the common stockholders, and that's what's happening.

So Saylor did not sell any Bitcoin?

No, they've been selling common stock. I mean, they sold a little bit of Bitcoin uh several weeks ago, but they've mainly been selling their common stock, which is a mistake from an accounting point of view because their stock is trading for such a huge discount, maybe a 40% discount to the Bitcoin per share. So, it makes no sense to be buying back — I mean, to be selling stock. They should be selling Bitcoin and buying back their stock, but he's afraid to do that because he's afraid of crashing Bitcoin.

最大的火：美元储备货币地位

So now to resume the conversation we just had, Peter, um there's been like lots of fires just as we see in different parts of the world at the moment, like literally. Um which fire would you say is the most important from all the topics that we discussed or may have not discussed, by the way?

No, I mean I think the biggest problem for the world is the fact that I think the US dollar is going to lose its status as the reserve currency because of the unsustainability of the US fiscal position — both its current account deficits, its budget deficits. I think all this is going to be coming to a head. I think the markets are dismissing the likelihood of such an event.

But I think a sovereign debt crisis and a currency crisis uh is is is is the main looming uh problem that the financial markets, the global economy, are going to be confronted with. And you know for a lot of countries ultimately this is going to be a very good thing. It's it's long overdue. But the initial reaction, you know, people are going to panic uh when when this happens.

中国、黄金与新金融基础设施

And this is also like one of the topics that's been emerging now, especially last weeks, about, for example, China building uh building well more and more gold reserves. There's all kinds of speculation about how much gold China really owns. And there's different commentators that have different versions of it. Some say up to 30,000 tons. And they are trying to prepare for what you just described now by at least linking gold to their own currencies — in this case the yuan for China.

I think China probably has a lot more gold than they let on, and they probably want to buy a lot more gold than they let on. Uh and they're doing that for a reason. You know, they understand that the dollar's days are numbered and they want to position themselves uh to basically take that position.

They want to have the dominant economy. They want to have the dominant currency. And the way to do that is to have the most gold, to have a currency uh that's backed by something. Because that would be a viable alternative to the dollar, because the dollar is backed by nothing. So if you know we used to be — the dollar used to be defined as a weight of gold. Now it's just you know paper. Uh but our economy doesn't support the dollar's valuation because of our lack of productivity. But China's does. China has all the savings and production that we used to have.

And in this new let's say impulse of what China is doing in terms of building an infrastructure around gold — and we're talking about SG vaults now that are in Shanghai and Saudi Arabia and others maybe planned in Switzerland and other countries, um of the convertibility between gold and yuan and perhaps even commodities — we've seen also with in Iran like the talk of like having Saudi oil paid in gold yuan. Do you see this as a viable infrastructure then to build and rebuild, let's say, the rails of international trade?

Sure. Around China, I mean, look, China is a key factor. I mean, they're a major producer. They're a major creditor. You know, they're the second largest creditor nation in the world behind Germany. Uh they'll soon be the number one creditor nation. They're the largest manufacturers.

Um so, the Chinese economy is going to dominate uh you know, the 21st century. I mean, America dominated in the 20th century, but we won't dominate the 21st.

结语与订阅呼吁

All right, Peter. Uh, thanks a lot for your time. And, uh, if there's anything else that you want to share to your listeners — obviously, you're available on your YouTube channel. You're on X very often. Any other things that you want to share?

I would just encourage people to follow me. Uh, especially on those two particular platforms. You know, I I'm not really sure what's behind it, but over the last few months, uh, I'm getting a lot more popular on social media. I've been adding about 100,000 X followers a month. I'm now at 1,630,000. Um, so, you know, if you're not following me, follow me. Um, repost everything I post. Encourage the people who follow you to follow me.

I think I've got a very important message that needs to get out. It's a message that the mainstream media does not disseminate. In fact, they actively try to suppress it. So, I think the only real way uh for my perspective on the free market, capitalism, you know, uh gold, uh sound money, Bitcoin, that stuff — the only way that my perspective gets out there is really through the internet, through social media.

So follow me. Um, subscribe to my YouTube channel. My, you know, my last, you know, couple of months of podcasts on YouTube have been getting more than double the views I used to get on my YouTube. I used to get maybe 50 to 100,000 views per podcast. Now it's more 150 to 250. Uh that doesn't count the people who listen on Schiff Radio or other places where podcasts — but just my YouTube audience uh in the last couple of months has really shot up there.

So again, if you're not a subscriber to my YouTube channel, subscribe. Make sure and watch the podcast there. You know, tell your friends about it. But the message is getting more popular, but I'm still in the minority. You know, I need to get an even bigger audience than the one I have now. Uh and so you can contribute to that audience and help grow it uh by getting engaged, you know, and then, you know, comment on my videos, like them. Uh, same thing with my posts. Get more engagement so you know the algorithms like that stuff and they'll highlight it and move it up so that more people will organically find me and then start listening and start following.

Great. I think it's noted. So the message is clear. Uh, thanks Peter and uh well take care and talk to you next time.

All right. You too. Bye-bye.

Heat. Hey, Heat.

item.description:
## 一、被忽视的镜像：日本不是"引爆点"，而是美国的时间机器
大多数人把日本危机看作"外部风险"，但真正令人不安的洞察是：**日本正在提前上演美国五年后的剧本**。日本是全球第三大债权国，储蓄率高、经常账户顺差、政府长期压低利率——它拥有美国早已失去的所有"缓冲垫"。如果连日本这样"最优等生的债务国"都无法承受利率正常化，那么财政赤字占GDP 6%以上、外债依赖度极高的美国，凭什么认为自己能全身而退？
Schiff 说日本可能是"戳破泡沫的针"，但更深层的模式是：**日元套利交易的解绑，本质上是全球流动性从"借入方语言"切换回"储蓄方语言"的过程**。过去二十年，全世界习惯用日元这种"零成本燃料"驱动风险资产，就像整个金融系统跑在一种廉价合成汽油上。一旦这种燃料涨价，不是某一辆车抛锚，而是整条高速公路同时减速。
## 二、跨领域连接：AI 资本开支 = 铁路泡沫 + 思科时刻 + 页岩油悖论
Schiff 提到 Nvidia 给客户提供融资让客户买自己的产品——这不只是"思科时刻"的重演，它同时符合三个历史模式的叠加：
- **1870s 美国铁路狂潮**：过度建设的物理基

item.title: [Lex Clips] Historian debunks The Lost Cause mythology about the Civil War | Gary Gallagher and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的真相：失败者反而赢得了记忆之战

最出人意料的一点：南方在军事上彻底失败，却在"叙事战场"上获得了长达一个多世纪的胜利。四种记忆版本里，只有"迷失的事业"（Lost Cause）是失败者构造的，却成为20世纪美国最广为流传的南北战争解释框架——教科书、好莱坞（《乱世佳人》《一个国家的诞生》）、南方各州的铜像广场，都是它的展馆。

这揭示了一条被低估的社会学规律：当胜利者忙着"往前看"（把国家拼回去、开发西部、搞工业化），失败者却拥有一种奇特的时间优势——他们别无选择，只能反复回望和重述。加拉格尔提到的"和解叙事"正是这种不对称的产物：北方白人为了让国家继续往前走，愿意用"共同的美国式勇气"来置换对奴隶制与解放的沉默。换句话说，遗忘是胜利者付给失败者的赎金。

二、跨领域连接：Lost Cause 是一种"叙事债务重组"

如果把它放到金融和心理学的坐标里看，Lost Cause 的四条支柱几乎完美对应企业破产后的"品牌重塑话术"：

Lost Cause 论点 商业/心理对应机制
"这不是为了奴隶制" 重新归因（reattribution）——把动机从可耻切换到高尚
"我们本就不可能赢" 事前宿命论（preemptive fatalism）——把失败从"能力不足"改写成"结构必然"
"别谈 Jefferson Davis，谈 Robert E. Lee" 符号替换（symbol substitution）——用一个可爱的英雄替换掉一个尴尬的决策者
"还有荣誉" 道德资本再融资——用美德叙事偿还历史罪责

Enron 崩溃后的高管回忆录、失败创业者的 LinkedIn 复盘、甚至个体的失恋叙事，都会不自觉地走这四步。Lost Cause 不是一个南方特产，而是所有集体自尊心受到重创后的通用心理协议。你在硅谷的 pivot 故事里就能读到它的近亲。

三、隐藏的系统性洞察：谁被踢出了记忆的桌子？

真正令人震惊的不是四种记忆的内容，而是它们在数量上的不对称。加拉格尔提到 Union Cause、Emancipation Cause、Lost Cause、Reconciliation Cause——注意到没有？没有"黑人自由民的记忆"作为独立版本。Emancipation Cause 主要是白人废奴主义者的叙事，被解放的四百万人本身没有获得一个以他们名字命名的记忆流派。

这暴露出一个更深的系统模式：在任何"多元记忆"框架里，缺席的类别往往比在场的类别更有信息量。就像看财务报表要看"表外负债"、看 UI 设计要看"负空间"，看历史记忆要看"哪个群体连版本命名权都没被授予"。

Lost Cause 之所以能扎根，部分原因就是它填补了这个真空——当被压迫者的直接声音被系统性排除，压迫者的粉饰叙事就自动升级为"中立的历史常识"。这个机制今天仍在运作：任何时候你听到"我们不要再纠结过去了"，都值得问一句：谁在这个"我们"里？谁被从"我们"里安静地删掉了？

📝 转录文本

问：你几次提到"迷失的事业"（Lost Cause）。它究竟是什么？谁创造了它？它主张什么？

四种战争记忆的框架

The Lost Cause is the Confederate memory stream of the war. And let me just say very, very briefly, I think there are four main ways the generation that experienced the war remembered it.

1. Union Cause（联邦事业）

The one remembered by the most people would be the majority of white northerners is what I call the Union Cause — and that the greatest outcome of the war was putting the nation back together. It's also good that slavery was killed, that's important, but the most important thing was putting the nation back together.

2. Emancipation Cause（解放事业）

The emancipation cause memory of the war is: yes, it's a good thing that the Union was saved, but the most important thing is you killed slavery. You got rid of this monstrous institution that had mocked that language in the founding documents.

So those are both winners' versions of the war.

3. Lost Cause（迷失的事业）——南方版本

The Confederate version — the Confederates are in a tough spot. How do we make something palatable out of this catastrophic decision that we made in 1861? We'll do this to save slavery, and four years later slavery's dead and a third of all our white military age boys are dead.

So here's what we're going to do:

第一步：否认奴隶制是原因。 First of all, it wasn't about slavery. Let's pretend it wasn't about slavery. It was about high constitutional principles, about state rights as opposed to central authority oppressing people.

第二步：宣称失败早已注定。 And second, we never could have won. It was a hopeless fight against long odds, and so it was a gallant effort in pursuit of constitutional rights. Okay, that gets us off the hook there.

第三步：选择合适的英雄。 And who are we going to look to? Should we talk about Jefferson Davis? No, we didn't even like him during the war. I know who we'll talk about. Let's talk about Robert E. Lee. He won victories against the odds.

Lost Cause 的核心信条总结

So these are kind of the main tenets of the Lost Cause:

  • It wasn't about slavery.
  • We never could have won.
  • There's no loss of honor in losing a battle you never could have won, but that you waged for high constitutional principle.
  • And let's talk about Lee, 'cuz we don't want to talk about Jefferson Davis — and there's almost no one else to talk about except maybe Stonewall Jackson. Those will be our two boys that we talk about the most.

And that is basically the short form of the Lost Cause.

4. Reconciliation Cause（和解事业）

The fourth way that people remembered — and this came a little bit later — was the reconciliation cause, where you… this is kind of white northerners and white southerners agreeing not to talk about slavery. Don't talk about emancipation. Let's talk about shared American virtues of courage and so forth.

item.title: [Lex Clips] Ulysses S. Grant vs Robert E. Lee: The generals of the Civil War | Gary Gallagher and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"失败者"其实是最稀缺的战争资源

Grant 在战前的连环失败常被当作"逆袭"叙事的调味料，但真正惊人的洞察是：19 世纪美军体系里，几乎所有高级将领都是"未曾失败者"——西点毕业、平顺晋升、社交无瑕。Lee 就是这个系统的完美产品。而 Grant 是唯一一个把破产、酗酒传闻、被迫辞职的羞辱内化成认知工具的人。他那句"别管 Lee 要做什么，让 Lee 去操心我们要做什么"，本质上不是军事勇气，而是一个破产者才有的心理特权：他已经在人生最底层活过，所以对"失败的想象"不再具有瘫痪能力。这与创业研究里的"连续失败创业者反而回报率更高"现象惊人一致——Paul Graham 和 Kahneman 都描述过这种"失败祛魅"效应。战争在这里像一个残酷的风险投资市场：它不奖励最优秀的人，而奖励对失败最脱敏的人。

二、"屠夫"标签的统计学反转：Lee 才是美国历史上最血腥的将领

这是全段最反直觉的事实：Lee 军队士兵的伤亡概率是 73%，而 Grant 在遇到 Lee 之前累计伤亡 3.7 万，Lee 已经 9.8 万——几乎是 Grant 的三倍。但一个半世纪以来，公众记忆恰恰颠倒了两人。这里藏着一个跨领域的普遍规律，可以叫它"美学赦免机制"：当一个人拥有贵族气质、悲剧姿态、优雅失败的完整叙事包装（Lee 的白胡子、灰马 Traveller、"荣誉南方"神话），历史会自动把他的数字暴力转译成诗意牺牲；而一个衣冠不整、被传酗酒、长得像小店主的胜利者（Grant），则会被数字反噬。这跟今天科技行业的现象同构——同样是让员工过劳，穿高领毛衣的创始人叫"愿景家"，穿廉价西装的叫"血汗工厂主"。叙事美学比统计数据更能决定道德判决，这条规律在军事史、商业史、政治史里反复上演。

三、Lee 的选择不是"忠于家乡"，而是一次身份系统的塌缩

大家习惯说 Lee "选择了弗吉尼亚"，好像这是一个地理决定。但 Gallagher 埋了一个精妙的细节：Lee 辞职时弗吉尼亚甚至还没加入邦联。他不是选边站，他是选择了一个身份坐标系：家族—土地—奴隶制—弗吉尼亚精英，这四者是一个不可拆分的语义包。这里最出人意料的联系是——Lee 的偶像是华盛顿，而他做的事情恰恰是几乎摧毁华盛顿一生的作品。这不是虚伪，这是一种非常现代的心理机制："通过模仿偶像的形式来背叛偶像的实质"。华盛顿模式对 Lee 而言是"贵族—战士—弗吉尼亚人"的外壳，而不是"合众国建构者"的内核。他复制了雕像的姿势，却砸碎了雕像的底座。类似的模式在思想史里比比皆是：马克思主义者背叛马克思，禅宗弟子焚烧佛像，硅谷创业者高喊乔布斯却做出反乔布斯的产品。偶像崇拜从来不是继承，而是选择性截取——Lee 只是把这种普遍的人类背叛机制演到了最悲剧的规模。

附：一个隐藏的结构性观察

整段对话里，Grant 和 Lee 其实构成一对"熵"的隐喻：Grant 代表可容错的、可迭代的、允许熵增的系统（今天不行明天再试）；Lee 代表低熵的、追求完美形态的、拒绝混乱的系统（贵族、荣誉、纯净的战术）。战争最终奖励前者——这与热力学第二定律在演化生物学、企业管理、机器学习训练中的规律完全一致：能承受混乱的系统，最终战胜追求秩序的系统。Grant 之所以拿到华盛顿的军衔，本质是因为他是那个时代唯一学会与不确定性共处的顶级将领。

📝 转录文本

Grant：一个被失败雕刻出来的天才

And let's talk about the two other figures which we'll return to time and time again, Ulysses S. Grant and Robert E. Lee. So, who was Grant? So, this is a man who failed at farming, failed at business, failed at his role in the peacetime army. Then, when the war came, the war revealed a genius.

So, he'd known a lot of failure. He'd known a lot of setbacks. And his wartime record shows that he learned to deal with those things. He had a great tremendous relationship with his wife, a very strong family life, a family he loved. I think that was the rock for him.

But, during the war, what he exhibited was an absolute willingness to break rules, to take risks, to take responsibility for what he was doing, whether it was a success or a failure, and not to be cast down by things that didn't work. If something didn't work, he'd say, "Okay, that didn't work. Now, let's do this."

He very famously, when he got to Virginia in 1864 and took over the Army of the Potomac, he had all these subordinates who were saying, "Well, what if General Lee does this? What if General Lee does that?" He finally said, "Why don't we start worrying — let's not worry about what General Lee is going to do and let General Lee worry about what we are going to do."

I mean, he just was unflappable under stress. He was the perfect person to end up heading the Union armies, and he and Lincoln — Lincoln realized that. And he proved indispensable.

"屠夫"标签的真相

But, he has this reputation as a butcher, Grant the butcher. That's something that former Confederates and some Democrats in the North fastened on him. His preferred way of fighting wasn't just kind of slug it out.

It's really interesting to compare his record in the war and Lee's record in the war before they wound up opposing each other in Virginia in a really bloody Overland Campaign. Grant's total casualties in all his great battles before they met were 37,000. Lee's were over 98,000 in the same period. The bloodiest general in US history by far in terms of how many of his men get shot is Robert E. Lee.

The most careful demographic study of any Civil War army is one done of Lee's army by a scholar named Joe Glatthaar, and Joe figured out that if you were a soldier in Robert E. Lee's army, you had a 73% chance of becoming a casualty. 73%.

Grant's casualties get high when he runs into Robert E. Lee, just like everybody else. So, the butcher tag is completely unfair about Grant.

酗酒传闻与华盛顿的军衔

He's also known as a drunk, and people have gone back and forth on that — whether he just had a weakness, couldn't hold his alcohol very well, or was okay as long as his wife was around and he had a key staff officer to help him. The point is, alcohol never got in the way of anything Grant did during the war, and he had a superlative record of delivering victories when the United States needed them, and Lincoln figured that out.

And the absolute proof of his stature because of this is that in the March of 1864, Congress decided to dust off the rank of three-star general, lieutenant general, and give it to Grant. The only person who had ever had that rank was George Washington. The man, Jorge. I mean, he is the man.

And so, they are saying, "Okay, Grant, you get the rank the man had." And that shows — there's never been anyone else who got it. You're the first. And then he would also be the first to get a four-star rank in the United States Army. There couldn't be a better indication of his stature than that he got Washington's rank. Winfield Scott had had it by brevet. Grant got the actual rank.

Overland Campaign 与总司令 vs 军团司令

So, in part, the Grant the Butcher label was from the Overland Campaign that we'll talk about. From the Overland Campaign. It's the military decisions made there. Uh, many would argue that those are critically important for the success of the war.

Yes. He and Lee are often compared, but for the last year of the war, they're operating on — it's not apples to apples — because Grant is general-in-chief and is managing the entire war effort. He's managing what Sherman's doing and what Sheridan's doing and what Nathaniel Banks —

Lee is an army commander.

Mhm.

He can recommend things to Jefferson Davis, but he never commands more than an army. And so, he never operates at the level that Grant did. Very late in the war, he was made general-in-chief when it was so late that it didn't matter.

Robert E. Lee：贵族、偶像与选择

So, who was Robert E. Lee? In April 1861, Lee was offered command of the Union Army. He was. [snorts] And chose Virginia instead. He did. What was he actually choosing in that decision? Was he choosing home? Was he choosing honor? Was he choosing slavery? And maybe just zooming out, what do we need to understand in the early steps about Robert E. Lee? Who was the man?

Well, Lee is sort of the antithesis of Grant in some ways. Lee is from an aristocratic family. Grant was from a solidly middle-class family. Lee's from an aristocratic family at the very top of the Virginia aristocracy. The Lees are all — He has uncles who were prominent, two signed the Declaration of Independence. His father was a famous commander under George Washington. He's — His father's the one who said that Washington was "first in war, first in peace, first in the hearts of his countrymen." That's Lee's father, who was later a prominent Virginia politician.

Lee's idol is George Washington. He patterns himself on Washington. He differs from him in some ways, but he patterns himself on Washington. He considered Washington the most admirable person in United States history. And then, of course, he almost undoes the work that George Washington put in place during the American Revolution.

弗吉尼亚、奴隶制与身份忠诚

He chose Virginia. He didn't resign his commission in the United States Army to go with the Confederacy. He resigned his commission in the United States Army to go to Virginia, which wasn't in the Confederacy yet, and become the head of state forces in Virginia. But then when Virginia went into the Confederacy, he took his Confederate commission and ended up as the third-ranking officer in Confederate service.

And he makes an easy transition to a Confederate loyalty. I think it's his loyalty to Virginia and what that means. That means his family, and of course that means slavery. That's part of what that loyalty is. He's devoted to the slave-holding South as well as to Virginia. Virginia's a subset of that. All of that is in one bundle with Lee.

But he also had been an ardent US nationalist earlier in his career. He was very successful military officer. Winfield Scott thought he was the greatest soldier in the army — and Scott probably really thought "except for me." But Scott is a great soldier that people don't remember that way because he became a kind of Jabba the Hutt figure by the time of the Civil War. He's enormous, weighs 350 lb, has to be winched onto his horse. But he was a very smart guy, and he thought very highly of Lee. Lee was a superb soldier as he would show during the war. But he's on the wrong side.

激进派侧影：Thaddeus Stevens

Maybe just to throw in a few more characters, I do think the folks on both sides that are of the more radical persuasion are quite interesting. Somebody you spoke about — I'm not sure where, I think it might have been in your lecture series — about Thaddeus Stevens. Ah, I know him. Uh [laughter]

Thaddeus Stevens. Thaddeus Stevens is one of the most radical of the radical Republicans. He's a congressman from Pennsylvania who — People say harsh things now in Congress. Thaddeus Stevens just eviscerated people, and he was way out — I mean, he was an ardent abolitionist and for equal rights for women in many ways, and he picked up a number of causes and championed them.

I think in your lecture you mentioned this thing which I just love — this "slime line" of — He had this kind of line. He's sitting in the House of Representatives and one of his opponents — Yeah. and he's speaking, and one of his opponents starts to come down to the floor, and he says — and this is a paraphrase — "I'm going to pause while my colleague from wherever he was from slinks across the floor of this house and adheres to his seat by his own slime."

Yeah, beautiful. Great line, impromptu. Yeah.

He had — women used to ask for locks of hair from famous people, and he was completely bald and wore a full wig. He had a woman stop him on the steps to the Capitol and ask for a lock of his hair. He took his whole wig off and said, "Madam, have them all."

And, no, it's very good.

But of the radical persuasion. Oh, absolutely — yes, he defined it. He is the character in Birth of a Nation — Stoneman, the evil radical Republican. Stoneman is patterned on Thaddeus Stevens.

item.title: [Business of Sport] The Best Sporting Story You Probably Missed
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个被忽略的商业悖论：业余身份其实是一条隐形护城河

大多数分析者读到"GAA 一年营收 1.32 亿欧元却不付球员一分钱"时，会本能地掉进"道德讨论"——这算不算剥削？但真正精彩的洞察在另一个方向：GAA 之所以能维持这套体系，不是因为球员高尚，而是因为盖尔式足球在全球没有职业对手。查理和主持人几乎捅破这层窗户纸却又滑过去了——他们说"如果苏格兰有个职业联赛，顶级球员就都跑了"。换句话说，GAA 的商业模式建立在"体育项目的地理垄断"之上，这与专利药、稀土出口、瑞士手表业的护城河逻辑完全同构。它不是一个体育联盟，它是一个受文化边界保护的单一供应商。

让人意外的观察：这项运动运行在"负工资"上

节目里一句几乎被忽略的话是——球员每年净支出约 5,500 欧元才能参赛。请停下来想想这个数字：这是一个倒转的劳动力市场。运动员不是被雇佣的劳动者，而是付费加入某个身份共同体的成员。这在现代经济里几乎找不到对应，但它有三个远房亲戚： - 开源软件：Linux 内核贡献者大多无偿写代码，价值沉淀在生态而非个人； - 学术终身教职前的博士生：以低于市场价的劳动换取"进入圈子的许可证"； - 中世纪的行会学徒：付学费给师傅，换取一个身份铭牌。

盖尔式足球运动员本质上是"文化学徒"，而不是"运动员"——他们买的是"我代表梅奥郡"这个身份的稀缺席位。这也解释了为什么 74 年不夺冠的"诅咒"能引爆全岛狂欢：因为这从来不是一场比赛，是一个部落对自身叙事的清算。

跨领域连接：为什么"诅咒"是他们最值钱的营销资产

这里有一个 GAA 自己可能都没意识到的深层结构：Paddy Prendergast 四年前去世，让 74 年的诅咒到期——这个故事的戏剧密度，任何一家营销公司都写不出来。它符合叙事经济学里最贵的三个元素：长时间跨度 + 不可复制的偶然性 + 道德暧昧（究竟停没停车致敬？）。这与迪士尼手里的"IP 陈化红利"、日本能剧数百年家元制、甚至苹果发布会的仪式感是同一类资产——时间无法被资本追赶。

再往下推一层，你会发现一个让人不安的洞察：GAA 展示的模式恰恰是英超、NBA、F1 永远回不去的。查理提到英国曾有的郡橄榄球锦标赛、Benson & Hedges 一日板球杯全都塞满 Twickenham 和 Lord's，但一职业化就死了。这是一个残酷的熵增定律——一旦货币化通道打开，"地方性"这种资产会被市场以最高效的方式萃取并蒸发。梅奥郡 15 万人口、球场能装 2.8 万、常年售罄——这种密度在现代职业体育中不可能被"设计"出来，只能被保护下来。

所以真正的元洞察是：GAA 不是一个"落后于时代"的组织，而是一个"故意不进化"的组织——它选择了拒绝复利，以换取无法被复利买回来的东西。这在生物学上叫新奥特尼（neoteny，幼态延续），在货币史上叫金本位，在体育上——就叫盖尔式足球。

📝 转录文本

The Question That Opens It All

What was the biggest sporting event in the British Isles last weekend?

Gaelic football final. The Gaelic football final. Um, the Gaelic football final was um contested on the weekend and as is always the case at a sold-out Croke Park, 82,000 people, um, so pretty much the same number of people that watched the World Cup final live, give or take, watched the um Gaelic football final in Dublin on the weekend.

And the result, Charlie, was —

Mayo. The Mayo, County Mayo, cuz Gaelic football is played on a county basis, okay? County Mayo beat County Kerry. County Kerry being, um, almost like sort of, you know, the Man City of, uh, Gaelic football. They've won, um, the top titles there many, many, many times, but County Mayo have not won the All-Ireland Senior Football Championship final since 1951.

The Myth of the Curse

And it's been the subject of one of the most famous myths in sport of the last century, which is this. This is the myth and this is what's made the big news all around the world. And by big news all around the world, some of the most famous people in the world were tuning in to watch this game. We'll come on to why in a moment.

So, County Mayo last won the All-Ireland Senior Football Championship final in 1951. And it was alleged, not long afterwards — actually, so this is this myth's been going on an awful long time — that on the way back from winning that final, the team um came across a a funeral, um, in County Mayo, and they didn't stop to pay their respects at that funeral, and the priest at that funeral put a curse on the County Mayo players saying, "May Mayo never win the All-Ireland Championship final again whilst you guys are still alive."

Um, and quite extraordinarily, um, the final remaining player from that side died about 4 years ago, a man called Paddy Prendergast. And it was quite interesting really an interview he gave not long before he died about the the story. And he was recalling the journey back from that 1951 final. He says,

"We were all in a truck together um heading from Dublin to Mayo. And I do recall there being a group of people outside the church. But we were on the truck, we couldn't get off the truck. Um it wasn't that we did anything deliberately or anything like that."

So it's never quite been clear whether this story is it is in is true, made up, or a bit made up, whatever it might be. But what is not the what is not in doubt is they lost in the meantime, I think 11 um finals. Um they 11 defeats in 11 finals um between that victory in 1951 and and what happened on the weekend.

The Homecoming

Um so uh and it's a provokes an astonishing outpouring of joy, not just in County Mayo, um where pretty much the entire county — I think there are about 150,000 inhabitants of County Mayo, and it seems like pretty much the entire population of County Mayo turned out to welcome the players back at their home stadium.

Um but also such famous people from around the world with County Mayo antecedents — Joe Biden, the former US president, the Gallagher brothers, um who were wearing Mayo shirts, etc. This this is a big deal, right? This has gone around the world.

What have you taken out of it, Charlie?

Uh embarrassment at my lack of appreciation for actually how important this is to a country and a sporting heritage culture. And you know, from what I've seen as well, like really good sport to to watch and enjoy.

Like great sport. Do you do you know do you know what sport it's sort of closest to?

Aussie rules?

Oh Australian rules. Yeah, it's really it's really close to Australian rules football.

So one of the players, I think one of the star players was part of the commentary was oh they're worried that they'll lose them to the AFL. So, you know, clearly like close enough.

Why why might that happen? Why why might they lose players to the AFL, Charlie?

The Amateur Economy

Well, the second part that was fascinating is this is an amateur sport. So, you have 82,000 people packing out Croke Park. Reportedly, Charlie, I I you'll you'll be able to tell me better, but I mean it was they said 132 million euros generated, right, by the GAA, which is Gaelic football and hurling, I think.

It's it's it's a bit more than that, actually. And that's I mean I think that's kind of where we need to start, right?

So, the GAA is the Gaelic Athletic Association. And it was founded um 125 years ago, maybe even more. And it was really to promote Gaelic Irish sports, but also Irish culture. So, the GAA devotes part of its revenue to promoting Irish music, dancing, and this type of stuff. So, this is a cultural organization.

And the sporting elements of it, which obviously dominate its revenue base and dominate in reality the vast majority of what it does — um you've got obviously Gaelic football, um but also you've got hurling, which is a very big sport um in in Ireland. You've got Gaelic handball. Um you've got Gaelic rounders. Um all of these sports are taking place and being funded or supported by the GAA.

So, they take in all their revenues from their big spectator events, which is the Gaelic football and and they get the hurling, and then they spread that revenue through supporting basically Gaelic culture broadly, but particularly sporting culture um through through throughout throughout the Ireland.

How the County System Works

Um and uh the way they do that is by not paying the players. So, the money that would normally go to paying the performers instead goes to supporting the whole infrastructure of of these sports.

Um and where that spins through to in terms of Gaelic football is it's played on a county basis. Um and as you say on an entirely amateur basis. So, a top Gaelic footballer will play for his county. Um and they play against the other counties in the National Football League. Um and then from the National Football League, if they do well, um they qualify through to the All-Ireland Senior Football Championship, which is for the top counties to then play off against each other. And then that in turn is what County Mayo has just won.

So, it's almost a bit more like an American sports system where you end up with with the playoffs where where the big matches happen and the final um then happens.

Now, of course, that amateur status, which is pursued pretty relentlessly, um but the players do get paid expenses. They do get helped out obviously with certain allowances and, you know, traveling and some maybe some accommodation and and all this type of stuff. But fundamentally, it is still strictly amateur. So, some of those who excel at it at an early age have been transferring across to play Australian Rules Football in Australia.

Players Who Pay to Play

I mean, even looking at it like without, you know, transfer systems and all — players just play for their counties — and understanding why it is structured the way it is was um really interesting because, you know, again, it throws up this piece of well, you know, when you start to generate that amount of money, regardless of whether you want to stay amateur or not, you know, you you have players that create even more value, should we say, from a kind of social element and and what it brings to regions in these counties and how they can leverage it, but you're not paying the key contributors.

In fact, maybe even worse than that, I think I saw and again, could be wrong, but it actually costs — I mean, they're net down about 5 and 1/2 thousand euros a year these players just to compete in it. But you know, it's really funded by that whole system, which means that everyone is volunteering, whether it's the pitches and the facilities and all of this.

So, you know, the the costs completely change the dynamic of the sport completely changes if you professionalize it. We all know what happens when that comes in at a stage where maybe there isn't the right structures in place to manage it properly, so you just lose complete control.

The Hidden Moat: No Competition

Well, they've they've they've got a big advantage, Charlie, right? Which is leaving aside um the the very small number of players who decide to travel to the other end of the world playing in Aussie rules football. Unlike in most other sports, they don't face immediate competition. Right?

So, let's just say for the sake of argument that as well as the amateur league in Ireland, there was a professional league in Scotland. Right? What you would find is that all the top players in Ireland went to play in the professional league in Scotland.

But the absence of there being that competition enables the GAA to carry on with doing what probably all of us would dream of doing really as sports administrators, which is taking in all the revenues and running a cracking business and being able to distribute those revenues to the development of the sport more broadly and not having to pay the performers.

But if we were to try that in football, then obviously those footballers who are good enough to be paid elsewhere would move elsewhere and the same with other sports as well. So, they So, it's a huge advantage it being a sport which is only played really in one country.

An Invitation to Watch

This is probably one of the reasons I love doing this show more than anything else because you it takes you into places that you don't necessarily expect to go. And one of our um loyal followers on Substack, Tom Clark, has been literally begging us uh to take a look at this and it it probably, you know, warrants, well, it does warrant, you know, a far deeper conversation.

Um I would I would encourage everyone though just for this, based on your first exposure to the sport, to just go and check out some of it. If there's one job that we have, you know, opening people's eyes to things they may not have seen before, I think it's a really good one. This is something that you would be really interested in from a sporting perspective. And it's a fascinating —

Scale in a Small County

It is it's a fascinating sport. And it's you know, we mentioned obviously that the the Grand Final got 82,000. But you know, County Mayo, who as I said have a population of about 150,000 people, their home stadium, which is McHale Park, the capacity of McHale Park is 28,000.

Okay, so about you know, 20% of the entire county can fit into McHale Park. And they sell it out regularly.

Yeah.

Right? I mean, it's quite extraordinary. 28,000 capacity stadium. That's about the same size as Crystal Palace. Right? And County Mayo are selling out for Gaelic football. Their their home stadium on a very regular basis. This is the biggest sport in Ireland. Um you know, spectator football isn't anywhere near that.

What England Lost

I do think there's something absolutely amazing about the county system. Because the roots that that gives people, there are there are two things which I think we've lost from the English um sporting infrastructure in the last 30, 40 years sort of during your lifetime is:

First, that we used to have a strong county rugby championship. And the final of that, which was played at Twickenham, used to be a very, very big event and would pack out Twickenham. You know, if you had Cornwall playing against Suffolk or something, that was a massive event and would sell out Twickenham and give people a real reason to follow their county all over the country because they'd know the players, they'd know the backstories, the families and all that sort of stuff. And that was an amateur um event.

Second, um and then the other thing we've lost is is the big one-day county championship finals at Lord's, um the Benson & Hedges um in particular, um which again used to pack out Lord's for Gloucestershire against Northamptonshire or whatever it might be and gave those counties that don't necessarily have a Premier League football team, don't necessarily have a a top, you know, sort of sporting infrastructure, but for that particular thing gave the whole county a reason to travel up to London as a county and some of the atmospheres at those finals were better than for any England game. It was it was absolutely unbelievable.

I think we sort of slightly lost our sense within the our sporting infrastructure in England of that county rootedness. That And I know you're a Londoner.

Yeah.

Um so it's it's a little bit different, but you know, I'm entirely from Oxfordshire and anything to do with Oxfordshire I would follow and yet there's nothing really I can follow Oxfordshire in at the —

Closing the Circle

Totally. This is kind of beautiful full circle to to finish it off with because really, you know, that as sport gets bigger, as it becomes more of a business, as more money comes into it, it's very hard to retain a lot of sometimes that feeling and those structures. You know, when you look at the upset around FIFA, whatever it is, you know, it's just another element of business and money coming into usurp some of the values that people may hold up that —

It's quite it's quite interesting. Just just to just — Yeah, I I get all that and I understand it, but sometimes be careful what you wish for. I've actually been really enjoying watching the Hundred. Um I'm currently I I'm watching it every evening at the moment. It's really convenient. It takes the right length of time for me to watch during the evening, but I will note that the crowds at the Hundred currently would be rather lower than would be rather lower than would have been the case in the Benson & Hedges county tournament of 20, 30 years ago.

Um so, you know, it sometimes newer is always better, but what the GAA are demonstrating is that you can actually have a massive spectator sport which is still rooted in what has always been the case.

The traditionalist in me loves that.

## 一个被忽略的商业悖论：业余身份其实是一条隐形护城河
大多数分析者读到"GAA 一年营收 1.32 亿欧元却不付球员一分钱"时，会本能地掉进"道德讨论"——这算不算剥削？但真正精彩的洞察在**另一个方向**：GAA 之所以能维持这套体系，不是因为球员高尚，而是因为**盖尔式足球在全球没有职业对手**。查理和主持人几乎捅破这层窗户纸却又滑过去了——他们说"如果苏格兰有个职业联赛，顶级球员就都跑了"。换句话说，**GAA 的商业模式建立在"体育项目的地理垄断"之上**，这与专利药、稀土出口、瑞士手表业的护城河逻辑完全同构。它不是一个体育联盟，它是一个**受文化边界保护的单一供应商**。
## 让人意外的观察：这项运动运行在"负工资"上
节目里一句几乎被忽略的话是——球员每年**净支出约 5,500 欧元**才能参赛。请停下来想想这个数字：这是一个**倒转的劳动力市场**。运动员不是被雇佣的劳动者，而是**付费加入某个身份共同体的成员**。这在现代经济里几乎找不到对应，但它有三个远房亲戚： - **开源软件**：Linux 内核贡献者大多无偿写代码，价值沉淀在生态而非个人； - *
